This study explores the perspectives of individuals who actively sought to have ASD and/or ADHD diagnoses reassessed. Within a pilot project in Skåne, Sweden, fourteen individuals aged 17-30 years, originally diagnosed at ages 4-18, participated in semi-structured interviews. Motivations for seeking reassessment, examined using reflexive thematic analysis, clustered around four themes: having capacity, being no different, demanding fairness, and removing barriers. While some initially benefited from resources linked to diagnosis, many described how it had become restrictive-limiting career options, influencing health-care encounters, and shaping identity. Diagnoses were experienced as "sticky": tied to childhood contexts yet continuing to circulate into adult institutions. Although not representative of all individuals with ASD/ADHD, this group constitutes a critical case, highlighting reassessment as a possible response to the temporal durability and institutional reach of psychiatric labels. The very fact that individuals request, and institutions require, a formal act of removal underscores the enduring power of such classifications as both resources and constraints. The study contributes to debates on overdiagnosis by highlighting the temporal and institutional dimensions of diagnostic expansion, and by examining how proportionality between benefits and burdens may shift over time.

title: Cultural adaptation and updating of the ICAST-R child abuse and neglect instrument for Denmark
abstract: We describe the validation, cultural adaptation, and updating of The International Society for the Prevention of Child Abuse and Neglect, Child Abuse Screening Tool, Retrospective version (ICAST-R) for use in a Danish context. Thorough Danish questionnaires on child abuse and neglect exist, but some are proprietary, and their development precedes widespread use of social media. As forms of abuse evolve, including online sharing of abuse material, updated tools are needed, and we are not aware of any recent, comprehensive and validated questionnaires that are culturally adapted for Danish. The free ICAST-R measure has been translated into at least 20 languages and is widely used in the field. To develop a Danish version, the questionnaire has been back-and-forth-translated and has undergone cognitive testing and focus group interviews by eight individuals within the target age range and seven experts by experience with abuse and neglect. Further adaptation was done through focus group interviews with professionals from research and practice. Categorisation of severity of abuse was done through a Delphi process, and acceptability of the adapted measure was assessed in an online survey distributed to 450 Danish adults. The ICAST-R has also been reviewed in focus group interviews with 11 professionals working with child abuse and neglect, representing practitioners, researchers and non-governmental organisations. The final Danish measure incorporates additional questions focused on online sexual abuse, free-text options for other experiences of abuse, and items describing acts of abuse with subcultural attributions of meaning. The neglect section is substantially altered, and the section on sexual child abuse has been restructured into non-contact sexual abuse, non-contact technology-facilitated sexual abuse, and moderate and severe contact sexual abuse. For sexual abuse, the structure was changed so that sexual experiences were recorded and subsequent questions explored consent and age at the event. For all events, a number of questions exploring disclosure was added.

title: Is intersectionality selective? The role of collider bias
abstract: We examine whether observed intersectional inequalities may arise from selection processes rather than underlying social mechanisms. Intersectionality is commonly operationalized using interaction terms in regression models or approaches such as Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA). An implicit assumption is often made that the analyzed sample reflects the population of interest, so that inference from the sample can be extended to that target population. Using theory illustrated by directed acyclic graphs, and empirical evaluation through Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that conditioning on a selection variable influenced by social characteristics and the outcome induces collider bias. That is, it occurs when selection into the analytic sample depends jointly on the intersectional variables and the outcome of interest. In a data-generating process where the outcome is independent of intersectional variables, restricting analysis to a selected sample produces apparent intersectional inequality. These spurious findings emerge regardless of the method used, reflecting the fact that quantitative methods applied to data that have undergone selection processes can produce misleading conclusions. Collider bias may generate, amplify, attenuate, or reverse apparent intersectional inequalities. Importantly, if the data-generating mechanism induces collider bias, it propagates through all downstream quantities that depend on the observed joint distribution, not just interaction components evaluated here. Therefore, general descriptions of inequality, and not just the interaction components, will also be biased relative to the target population. When drawing conclusions about a target population from an analytic sample, accounting for selection is essential for valid estimation and interpretation of intersectional patterns.

title: Violence prevention through legislative change: Qualitative insights on ending the physical punishment of children in the UK
abstract: Physical punishment violates children's rights as outlined in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and has consistently been linked to detrimental outcomes, yet it remains legal in most countries. In the UK, it is prohibited in Scotland and Wales, whereas in England and Northern Ireland, the defence of 'reasonable punishment' remains available to parents. We report findings from a qualitative study that sought to understand how law reform was achieved in Scotland and Wales and why it has been resisted in England and Northern Ireland. We interviewed 29 stakeholders across the four UK nations and a broad range of sectors. Data were analysed using framework analysis. Two advisory groups of young people provided their perspectives on the research throughout. In line with Kingdon's Multiple Streams Framework, our findings suggest that law reform becomes possible when three elements align: recognition of the problem, a feasible solution, and a favourable socio-political climate. Successful advocacy for reform centred arguments around physical punishment's incompatibility with children's rights, evidence of harm, and the need to address the ambiguity of what constitutes 'reasonable punishment'. Ultimately, the case for reform required strong cross-sector coalitions and a receptive political environment. Participants also highlighted the importance of careful implementation, including public education, parenting support, guidance for frontline professionals, and monitoring. These findings provide transferable lessons for efforts to reform legislation in England, Northern Ireland and internationally, and add to the wider understanding of how research evidence and rights discourses can be translated into policy.

title: The gender pay gap and women's sexual health outcomes: Could closing the gap close the risk?
abstract: The United States has one of the highest rates of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among high-income countries, with women-particularly young Black women-bearing the greatest burden. Gendered power dynamics are a driver of women's STI risk, yet most research has focused on couple relationships, rather than the structural gender inequalities that shape power imbalances. This study investigates the extent to which the gender pay gap, a key indicator of structural sexism, is associated with women's sexual health outcomes in the US. Drawing on theories of household bargaining and gendered power dynamics, we hypothesize that wider gender pay gaps reduce women's agency in relationships and dating markets, thereby increasing their risk of STIs. We analyzed surveillance data from 2012 to 2023 on chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis incidence rates among women aged 15-44. The primary exposure was the lagged state-level female-to-male earnings ratio within racial groups. We used fixed-effects linear regression models to estimate associations that adjusted for key economic and demographic covariates. A one-percentage point increase in female-to-male earnings ratio was associated with significant declines in chlamydia (-20.4 cases per 100,000) and gonorrhea (-8.2 cases per 100,000) rates. These associations were strongest among women aged 15-29 and among Black women. Results were robust across model specifications and geographic levels. Associations with syphilis were smaller and less robust. Findings suggest that the gender pay gap functions as a structural determinant of women's sexual health and that narrowing the gap may enhance women's agency in couple and dating relationships and reduce STI risk.

title: Accountability displacement in health systems integration: A study of the English National Health Service
abstract: Governing complex public services increasingly requires coordination across multiple organisations, yet the collaborative arrangements intended to achieve this create new governance and accountability challenges. In England, the National Health Service (NHS) has pursued successive reforms to better integrate the planning and delivery of health and care. The most recent Health and Care Act 2022 aimed to strengthen horizontal accountability mechanisms by establishing a statutory basis for Integrated Care Systems (ICS) and enabling organisations to delegate responsibilities to each other locally to achieve subsidiarity. However, the Act did not particularly change vertical accountability mechanisms and lacked guidance on how horizontal accountability should operate. This paper explores what happens when a metagovernor simultaneously promotes horizontal collaboration and enforces vertical oversight, and through what process one accountability mechanism prevails over another. We analysed the formal governance structures in all 42 Integrated Care Board (ICB) governance handbooks and conducted 17 semi-structured interviews with ICB directors of strategy. Our findings reveal that ICBs faced conflicting accountability demands from NHS England, and that stronger felt accountability towards vertical mechanisms consistently outweighed horizontal ones. Most ICBs retained decision-making authority, resulting in limited delegation and weak horizontal accountability. We conceptualise these dynamics as accountability competition, where vertical and horizontal mechanisms coexist and create tension, and accountability displacement, where stronger hierarchical controls crowd out collaborative forms of accountability. We conclude that without clearer policy guidance, the prevailing hierarchical context will continue to prevent the development of effective horizontal accountability, undermining the collaborative aims of the Act.

title: Escaping in-work poverty and mental health: A longitudinal study of Swedish workers
abstract: In-work poverty (IWP) affects individuals who are employed but have an equivalised disposable household income below 60% of the national median. While IWP is associated with poorer mental health, it remains unclear whether escaping IWP reduces mental health risk or whether adverse effects persist after upward mobility. This study examines whether escaping IWP reduces mental health risk in Sweden, and whether moving moderately versus substantially above the poverty line differentially affects outcomes. This cohort study included 93,962 Swedish workers aged 24-60 who were in IWP in 2012. Escaping IWP was defined as moving from IWP in 2012 to either "moderately above" (60-100% of the median) or "substantially above" (>100% of the median) the poverty line in 2013, with those remaining in IWP as the reference group. Outcomes were first-diagnosed mental health disorders and first SSRI prescriptions during 2014-2019. Sex-stratified Cox regression models estimated crude and adjusted hazard ratios (AHRs) with 95% confidence intervals. Moving moderately above the poverty line was not associated with a significantly lower risk of either outcome. Men who moved substantially above the poverty line had a significantly lower risk of diagnosed mental health disorders (AHR 0.65, 95% CI 0.50-0.84) and SSRI prescriptions (AHR 0.85, 95% CI 0.74-0.97). No significant associations were observed among women. Escaping IWP yields greater mental health benefits for men than women, and only substantial income gains were associated with improved outcomes. Policies should address not only IWP reduction but also the adequacy and stability of upward mobility pathways.

title: Hate crimes hurt: State-level hate crime rates and racial health disparities
abstract: Despite the growing prevalence of hate crimes in the United States, little is known about whether and how state-level institutional and cultural climates surrounding bias-motivated violence pattern health and health disparities. This study conceptualizes state-level hate crime rates as composite indicators of these climates-reflecting the underlying incidence, institutional recognition and reporting, and political-cultural context-and examines their association with individuals' mental and physical health. Linking FBI Hate Crime Reporting Program data with individual-level data from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (2011-2023) (n = 3,827,446), we first document substantial variation in hate crime rates across states and over time. Using two-way fixed effects models, we find that higher state-level hate crime rates are associated with more days of poor mental and, to a lesser extent, physical health, with associations concentrated among Black respondents and little evidence of associations among White or Hispanic respondents. By contrast, state-level violent crime rates show weak, racially undifferentiated associations with health, underscoring that state hate crime climates likely operate through distinct pathways from general crime rates to shape health risks. Taken together, findings are consistent with the notion that state-level hate crime rates capture a meaningful dimension of institutional and cultural context relevant to population health, with especially concerning implications for the health of historically marginalized populations, particularly Black Americans.

title: Going the distance? A meta-analysis of leadership styles, social distance, turnover intention, and organizational commitment
abstract: Retention of healthcare personnel is a global challenge with severe implications for securing stable, high-quality healthcare services. The common saying that 'people do not leave a bad job, but they leave a bad boss' stresses the influence a formal leader has on employees' turnover intentions (TI) and organizational commitment (OC). Understanding what makes an effective leader is essential for understanding managers' agency in dealing with employee retention; yet, few systematic reviews compare the effectiveness of leaders. This study conducts a systematic review and identifies 54 studies that include 147 correlation effect sizes from public hospitals worldwide. Conducting a multi-level meta-analysis, we find that leadership is significantly associated with employee's TI (r = -0.158, [-0.213; -0.102]) and OC (r = 0.266, [0.194; 0.336]); however, the meta-regression reveals that the correlation effect sizes of leadership styles vary significantly across studies where leader-member exchange (LMX) (OC: r = 0.32; TI: r = -0.37), servant (OC: r = 0.40), supportive (OC: r = 0.35; TI: r = -0.36), and ethical (OC: r = 0.43) leadership styles are most strongly associated with the employee outcomes. A deeper dive into the leadership styles reveals that social distance moderates the relationship between leadership styles and OC and TI as correlation effect sizes decrease when social distance increase (TI: r = 0.161, std error = 0.046, p = 0.032; OC: r = -0.298, std. error = 0.072, p = 0.008). With minor exceptions, findings remain relatively stable across cultures, methods, and participant characteristics. These findings nuance previous leadership research in healthcare and public management and have important implications for research and practice.

title: The habitus of care: Overdose normalization, reversal expertise, and the invisible moral labor of people who use drugs
abstract: BACKGROUND: People who use drugs represent a significant yet underrecognized frontline against overdose fatality. While overdose education and naloxone distribution programs provide basic training, little is known about how expertise develops through repeated real-world encounters with overdose. METHODS: We conducted semi-structured interviews with 74 people who had administered naloxone within the past year, recruited through harm reduction programs in Pennsylvania, Michigan, and California between October 2024 and March 2025. We conducted reflexive thematic analysis, with the Critical Decision Method guiding our elicitation and coding of decision points and contextual cues during overdose response. Bourdieu's theory of practice provided the interpretive framework for understanding how response skills develop and are enacted as embodied expertise in community settings. RESULTS: Most participants had reversed multiple overdoses, with 34 reporting more than ten reversals and four reporting hundreds. Three themes emerged: (1) overdose response became normalized as an expected, obligatory feature of everyday life rather than exceptional heroism; (2) repeated exposure cultivated tacit expertise characterized by calm and confidence, automatic recognition, and intuitive decision-making; and (3) during overdoses, experienced responders described entering focused flow states, taking charge, and improvising effectively under pressure. Despite demonstrating practical mastery comparable to professional emergency response, participants deflected recognition and minimized their contributions. CONCLUSIONS: People who use drugs develop sophisticated, embodied expertise through repeated overdose encounters, yet this labor remains invisible, unsupported, and uncompensated. Public health systems rely on peer response without providing parallel structures of protection, trauma support, or legitimization afforded to professional first responders. Promoting sustainability and equity in community overdose response requires acknowledging and supporting this essential workforce.

title: When class silences disclosure: Working-Class women, sexual violence and classed gender stigma in healthcare
abstract: Feminist sociology has illuminated how sexual violence both reflects and reproduces gendered inequalities, yet its intersection with social class remains comparatively under-theorised in health research, particularly in relation to healthcare and disclosure. This study advances critical social science research on health and healthcare by theorising classed gender stigma as a mechanism through which class and gender intersect to shape working-class women's willingness to disclose sexual violence within healthcare encounters. Drawing on episodic interviews with working-class women in Scotland, the analysis focuses on disclosure within healthcare and related professional support context, including specialist mental health services and third-sector provision. The findings show how classed histories of dismissal, material constraint and respectability norms shape women's expectations of being believed and their assessments of whether healthcare encounters are safe spaces for disclosure. Disclosure within healthcare emerges as a socially organised process shaped by classed relations of care and institutional practices, including appointment structures, referral pathways and access to paid support. The analysis develops the concept of classed gender stigma to show how healthcare encounters shape whose disclosures are recognised as credible and deserving of care following sexual violence. The paper advances understanding of how health inequalities are reproduced through silence within healthcare contexts and highlights the importance of integrating analyses of class and institutional practice into health-focused research on sexual violence disclosure.

title: Doing understanding during triadic decision-making with people living with dementia
abstract: This paper examines how patients with dementia reveal their level of understanding during the complex process of making decisions around their medical care. Using Conversation Analysis, we examined 172 decision-making sequences across 64 memory clinic consultations and found that understanding is best viewed as an interactionally constructed continuum that patients can move along with the help of their interlocutors. We identified specific behaviours, both spoken and embodied, that patients, their companions, and the healthcare practitioners display, which index the patient's location on the continuum of understanding. This has consequences for the patient's level of involvement in decision-making, and who ultimately contributes to the decision. Patients who display clear understanding are frequently treated as the primary decision-maker, while situations in which patients are treated as showing a lack of understanding typically result in the companion becoming the primary decision-maker. Only when the patient is revealed to sit between these two poles does the decision-making become more of a shared endeavour. We highlight the need for patient understanding to be assessed continuously within the decision-making sequence due to the potential for patients to move along the continuum of understanding as the talk progresses.

title: Embodied well-being: Energy, exhaustion, and bodily difference among Danish schoolchildren
abstract: The well-being of children and adolescents is debated globally, and school settings constitute important sites in which well-being is lived and managed. In contemporary well-being debates, schoolchildren's embodied experiences receive little attention, and well-being is often treated as synonymous with mental health. In this study, we explore and conceptualize embodied well-being in everyday school settings. While Danish media discussed a proclaimed 'well-being crisis' and the government established an expert commission targeting children and young people's well-being, we conducted ethnographic fieldwork at a Danish public primary and lower secondary school. Between February and June 2025, we followed and observed three classes (2nd, 4th, and 7th grade) for 60 days, and pupils and teachers were interviewed in focus groups. Staying close to pupil perspectives, we propose 'exhaustion' as a conceptual lens that, in dialectical relationships with 'energy', points to sensed, embodied dimensions of their fluctuating everyday experiences of well-being. We characterize exhaustion as a condition in which the mental, physical and social intertwine, manifesting differently in different bodies and situations, and show how movement narratives are central to how children and teachers understand and manage exhaustion. Our analysis is inspired by Merleau-Ponty's understanding of the embodied 'I can' and a critical phenomenological attention to a socially conditioned 'I cannot'. These concepts illuminate how well-being and ill-being are shaped and articulated through embodied abilities and disabilities. Overall, we argue that the environment and structure of the school day contribute to making exhaustion a recurring, socially shared mode of being-in-the-world for Danish schoolchildren.

title: Leaving no one behind: Assessing declines in early neonatal, late neonatal, post neonatal, and child mortality for the richest and poorest children in 38 low-and-middle-income countries
abstract: The United Nations Sustainable Development Group suggests that the rate of decline should be the fastest among the most vulnerable to close equity gaps for goals aiming to zero. Using under-five deaths as a case study, this study highlights that target rates of decline should be disaggregated by dimensions of vulnerability within countries. In this study, we examine rates of change in the early neonatal, late neonatal, post neonatal, and child mortality periods in 38 countries using Demographic and Health Survey data. Overall, we find that in most countries, the rate of decline for the four outcomes was faster among the poorest children than the richest children. However, we show that in many countries, the poorest children in the most recent time point experience higher rates of death than the richest children in the earliest time point. Additionally, the poorest children are not on track to meet our proposed SDG targets despite experiencing faster rates of decline than the overall rate of decline. Our findings highlight the importance of establishing target rates of decline that are disaggregated by dimensions of vulnerability.

title: No one wins: Mapping the gendered pathways of structural sexism and health
abstract: Existing scholarship defines structural sexism as systematic inequality in power and resource distribution across political, economic, and social institutions within a given gender system. Despite growing recognition of structural determinants of health, researchers have not adequately addressed the specific pathways through which early exposure to structural sexism shapes later health outcomes. Using data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (N = 10,009), we examine the link between adolescent exposure to structural sexism and self-rated health in midlife, focusing on mediation through health behaviors, psychosocial strain, and socioeconomic resources. We find that the relationship between structural sexism and health is asymmetric, gendered, and pathway-specific, yet the direct association with midlife health is small for both women and men. For women, structural sexism is associated with poorer midlife self-rated health and is mediated across behavioral, psychosocial, and socioeconomic domains, with individual pathways accounting for 9-25% of the total effect. For men, the direct association with self-rated health is weaker and less consistent, but structural sexism remains linked to health primarily through behavioral mechanisms such as smoking (24%) and unhealthy eating (17%). These findings suggest that structural sexism shapes health less through large direct effects than through the behavioral and socioeconomic pathways by which gendered inequalities become embedded over the life course, and raise further questions about how structural inequalities may reconstitute themselves as gender norms shift, potentially creating new forms of health stratification.

title: From blood disorders to data disorder. The thwarted path from onco-haematology clinic to occupational cancer epidemiology
abstract: The promise of big data in public health has fueled expectations for leveraging electronic health records (EHRs) to advance epidemiological research, particularly in occupational health. Yet, hospitals-where patients' occupational histories are routinely collected-often do not transform this information into usable epidemiological data. This article examines the organisational and infrastructural barriers that hinder the use of hospital data for studying occupational cancers, focusing on blood cancers in France. Drawing on interviews, questionnaires, and ethnographic observations with onco-haematologists and Occupational Diseases Consultation Centers (ODCCs), we document two key mechanisms: (1) inscription practices, where clinicians collect but rarely record occupational histories in a structured, epidemiologically useful format; and (2) delegation practices, where referrals to specialised ODCCs are erratic and depend on local, ad-hoc relationships. Despite onco-hematologists' awareness of occupational risk factors, their documentation in medical records is fragmented, and referrals to ODCCs are inconsistent, resulting in non-representative data, unfit for epidemiological research. Considering the hospital as a whole as an information infrastructure (Bowker and Star, 2000) allows us to describe how it absorbs substantial information about patients' jobs and potential exposures, both through routine clinical work and specialised consultations. However, we also demonstrate that it converts only a small fraction of this information into standardised data that can be reliably incorporated into epidemiological research infrastructures. This study highlights the need for structural reforms aiming at stronger integration between clinical and occupational health services to bridge this gap. Our findings shed light on the social production of data disorder, which jeopardizes big data promises in the field of occupational health epidemiology. We call for greater attention to organisational and infrastructural constraints in hospital settings.

title: Effects of requiring active parental consent on participation, sample composition, and mental health outcomes in school-based adolescent surveys: A cluster randomized trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Requiring active parental consent in school-based adolescent surveys may reduce participation rates and introduce response bias, particularly in studies assessing sensitive outcomes such as mental health. However, experimental evidence on its impact remains limited. METHODS: A cluster randomized controlled trial within 20 Norwegian lower secondary schools: 259 classes were randomized to either (1) active parental consent, or (2) adolescent self-consent. Data were collected with online questionnaires administered during school hours in the autumn of 2025. Differences in class-level participation rates were examined, as well as sample composition (sex, age, immigrant background, subjective socioeconomic status) and a broad range of mental health-related measures. The data were analyzed using fixed-effects regression models. RESULTS: Requiring active parental consent substantially reduced participation (average marginal effect: -32.2 percentage points, 95% CI -35.5, -28.8). Despite this large difference, sample composition was highly similar across conditions with respect to sex, age, and socioeconomic status. However, a lower proportion of students with two parents born abroad participated in the active parental consent condition (average marginal effect: -7.1 percentage points, 95% CI -9.4, -4.7). For mental health outcomes, no statistically significant differences were observed. CONCLUSIONS: Requiring active parental consent can markedly reduce participation in school-based adolescent surveys, but it does not appear to meaningfully bias sample composition or estimates of mental health outcomes, although students with immigrant backgrounds may be underrepresented. These findings can inform ethical and methodological debates regarding adolescent autonomy, survey validity, and consent procedures in public health research.

title: Life-course stress exposure and cognitive decline in middle-aged and older Chinese adults: The role of sex differences and educational protection
abstract: Abstract Background Stressful life events (SLEs) across the life course have been associated with cognitive decline, but evidence on their cumulative impact and potential modifiers remains limited. We aimed to examine the associations between SLE exposure in childhood, adulthood, or both life stages and cognitive trajectories, and to investigate whether these associations vary by sex and level of education. Methods We used data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), a nationally representative cohort of adults aged 45 years and older. Participants with complete data on SLEs, cognitive function, and covariates were included (n=5,922). SLEs were assessed retrospectively for childhood and adulthood periods. Cognitive function was measured using a composite score (range 0–21) across three waves (2011–2015). Linear mixed-effects models were used to examine longitudinal associations, adjusting for sociodemographic factors, health behaviors, and chronic health conditions. Interaction analyses were performed to explore effect modification by sex and education. Results Of 5,922 participants, 2,428 (41.0%) reported no SLEs, 1,374 (23.2%) experienced childhood-only SLEs, 1,294 (21.8%) experienced adulthood-only SLEs, and 826 (14.0%) had cumulative SLE exposure (both childhood and adulthood). In fully adjusted longitudinal models, cumulative SLE exposure showed the strongest association with cognitive decline (β = –0.52, 95% CI –0.69 to –0.35, p<0.001), followed by childhood-only (β = –0.34, –0.48 to –0.20, p<0.001) and adulthood-only exposure (β = –0.22, –0.37 to –0.07, p<0.01). Sex significantly moderated the associations for childhood-only and cumulative exposure (interaction β = –0.21, 95% CI –0.36 to –0.05, p<0.01; interaction β = –0.25, 95% CI –0.43 to –0.07, p<0.01), with women showing greater cognitive vulnerability than men. Higher educational attainment buffered against single-period stress effects but provided only partial protection against cumulative life-course adversity. Conclusion Life-course stress exposure, particularly when cumulative, is associated with accelerated cognitive decline in Chinese middle-aged and older adults. Women show greater vulnerability to stress-related cognitive effects, whereas higher education appears to buffer against such impacts across both sexes. These findings underscore the importance of sex-sensitive, education-informed approaches to stress reduction and cognitive health promotion across the life course.

title: The political economy of universal health coverage reform in Kenya: executive dominance, elite alignment, and populist strategy (2004-2023)
abstract: Why do some ambitious social health insurance reforms get enacted, while others stall, even within the same country, and under similar structural constraints? This article compares Kenya's failed 2004 National Social Health Insurance Fund Bill, with the reform enacted in 2023. It combines Kingdon's Multiple Streams Approach (MSA) with political economy and populism theory, drawing on 48 elite interviews, and policy documents. Using outcome-explaining process tracing, the study explains why enactment became possible in 2023 but not 2004. MSA highlights how adoption depends on coupling across problem, policy and politics streams. Kenya's case shows that in executive-dominant presidential systems, leaders can also make this coupling happen. Three mechanisms distinguished the 2023 episode: (i) executive dominance and institutional bypass, that compressed procedures and reduced veto points; (ii) elite re-alignment including a fiscal gatekeeper buy-in, which ensured a supportive political settlement; and (iii) populist strategy that moralised inequities, delegitimised opponents and justified expedited enactment. In 2004, the reform faced executive and elite fragmentation, which enabled organised resistance and presidential veto. By integrating MSA with political economy and populism theory, this study conceptualises populism as a coupling mechanism that can align streams by reshaping political feasibility and coalition incentives. Empirically, it provides a rare within-country comparison of health financing reform enactment in an LMIC, clarifying how power, elite bargains, and political strategies shape whether redistributive reforms become law. While these three mechanisms helped ensure the reform's enactment, they risk limiting the reform's ability to increase coverage, specifically for the informal sector populations that it aimed at serving.

title: Diagnostic infrastructuring: Biomarkers, pharmaceutical marketing and governance in Taiwan
abstract: This ethnographic study examines the role of pharmaceutical companies in the era of precision medicine. Focusing on PD-L1 biomarker testing for cancer immunotherapy under Taiwan's National Health Insurance reimbursement policy, we trace how these diagnostics are introduced, adopted, and governed within the policy regime that frames therapeutic access. We propose the concept of "diagnostic infrastructuring" to describe how corporate entities act as "infrastructural architects," actively remodeling material platforms and clinical practices to facilitate the routinization of biomarker tests. Extending Sergio Sismondo's discourse on "assemblage marketing," this study reveals a shift toward material and practice governance. In this model, firms mobilize technical objects, standardize practices, and negotiate interpretive discretion and leniency to align with rigid policy frameworks, thereby bridging infrastructural gaps. By governing diagnostic routines, companies embed commercial interests directly into the clinical and reimbursement infrastructures of precision medicine. Ultimately, this industry-driven infrastructuring illuminates an evolving political economy where the capacity to deliver precision medicine is contingent upon the power to configure biomarker diagnostic practice.

title: A scoping review and examination of conceptual frameworks of cognitive changes in Indigenous communities across Canada
abstract: Recent studies of cognition in Indigenous communities have documented an increased prevalence of cognitive impairment and dementia in Indigenous communities. However, Indigenous conceptualizations of both cognitive changes in aging and community health and wellness challenge methodologies and conceptual frameworks used in these studies. With Haudenosaunee Knowledge Keeper guidance, we conducted a scoping review that aims to better understand the following questions: 1. How do concepts of cognitive function and impairment differ in clinical studies and Indigenous knowledge systems? 2. How are the voices of Indigenous communities reflected in the literature in terms of both participation and leadership? We reviewed 44 relevant articles published between 2001 and 2024 on mild cognitive impairment, dementia, and other neurodegenerative diseases in Indigenous communities in Canada. We find that: 1. Inclusion of Indigenous peoples as experts in cognitive-related research produces research with outcomes relevant to and resonant with Indigenous people. 2. There are different definitions of cognitive impairment in Indigenous communities that do not align with biomedical definitions. 3. Existing cognitive assessment tools are not culturally appropriate for all Indigenous peoples and may specifically reproduce historical traumas. 4. There are significant gaps to be addressed regarding Indigenous experience of cognitive changes in aging and appropriate supports.

title: Intersectional parental health inequities one year after childbirth: race/ethnicity, sex/gender and social class in the elfe birth cohort
abstract: Social inequities in health are shaped by interlocking systems of oppression that differentially structure experiences across populations and over the life-course. This study examines intersectional inequities in parental health one-year post-birth, focusing on the articulation of race/ethnicity, sex/gender, and social class. Using data from a French population-based birth study, Elfe cohort, we applied intersectional multilevel analysis (I-MAIHDA) to self-reported mental (SF-12 MCS) and physical (SF-12 PCS) health scores among 24,108 parents (mean age 32.8 ± 5.3, included in 2011) nested in 42 intersectional strata. Substantial intersectional inequities were observed in parental health in the cohort, with a more pronounced gradient for mental health than physical health. Inequities were primarily driven by additive effects, on average: racialized parents scored lower on both mental and physical health than non-racialized parents; women scored lower on mental health than men; and parents from less advantaged social classes scored lower on physical health compared to the most advantaged ones. The magnitude of racial/ethnic inequities was comparable to that of sex/gender in mental health and social class in physical health. Additionally, the protective effect of sex/gender on mental health seemed modulated by social class (significant interaction effect). We further open a critical reflection on how categorization choices shape the visibility of health inequities. These findings highlight how systemic forces-racism, sexism, and classism-jointly structure parental health around childbirth. They underscore the importance of intersectional approaches that account for the intertwining effects of social positions within society when studying population health.

title: Optimizing health, financial risk protection, and equity in health benefits package design toward universal health coverage
abstract: Health policymakers are often challenged with balancing multiple objectives within the constraints of a limited budget. These objectives typically include enhancing (i) population health, (ii) providing financial risk protection, and (iii) improving health equity. We introduce quantitative methods to guide the design of essential benefits packages (EBPs) that explicitly account for trade-offs across these three critical objectives under budgetary limitations. We develop a mathematical optimization model that evaluates the fulfillment of these objectives for a spectrum of potential candidate health interventions under various options of public funding. Utilizing tri-criterion integer programming, our model identifies an optimal set of interventions for inclusion. We illustrate the approach with a case study of EBP design in Ethiopia. We found that the optimal EBP's intervention mix is sensitive to the comparative prioritization of the three objectives and the available budget; and that the number of Pareto-optimal intervention combinations changes nonlinearly with the available budget. When all three objectives are integrated, the composition of the optimal EBP is strongly influenced by the relative preferences placed on each objective. The mathematical optimization framework proposed can empower policymakers to design health policies that synergistically address multiple efficiency and equity objectives within defined financial limits.

title: Social status in a complex society: Examining multidimensional prestige as a social driver of health in the U.S.
abstract: Across the social sciences, measures of social status are used to explain social, economic, and health outcomes. Yet existing measures typically conceive of status as singular and overlook the multigroup status problem: individuals in modern societies are embedded in multiple status hierarchies and therefore have multiple statuses. To address this problem, we draw from evolutionary accounts of prestige hierarchies and Ernest Becker's theory of cultures as hero systems to introduce a conception of general social status (GSS) as multidimensional, internalized prestige. We evaluate the Hero Systems Status Scale (HSSS), which assesses perceived prestige and social role identity centrality across five status arenas. GSS was calculated using prestige ratings weighted by identity centrality across four bounded arenas: workplace, leisure group, family, and social media. In a broadly representative U.S. sample of 774 adults (aged 25-54), factor analyses supported the HSSS's hypothesized five-factor structure, indicating prestige varies by status arena. GSS was distinct from the MacArthur subjective socioeconomic status (SES) scales and objective socioeconomic factors. It was less strongly associated with objective SES indicators than was subjective SES. GSS demonstrated incremental validity beyond subjective SES in explaining physical impairment, internalizing and externalizing problems, and life satisfaction. In comparative models, GSS produced greater model improvement for physical impairment and explained more variance in internalizing problems, whereas subjective SES explained more variance in life satisfaction. Findings suggest GSS is a distinct and consequential social driver of health. The HSSS offers a psychometrically sound, context-sensitive framework for studying multidimensional prestige in the U.S.

title: Do financial incentives affect rural physician supply? Empirical evidence from a Canadian experiment
abstract: Rural physician shortages remain a persistent challenge in health workforce planning, and financial incentives are commonly used to improve geographic physician distribution. This study exploits Saskatchewan's Rural Physician Incentive Program (RPIP), introduced in 2013, as a natural experiment to evaluate the impact of direct annual payments for rural practice on the rural-urban distribution of family physicians. Using administrative physician counts from the Canadian Institute for Health Information and population data from Statistics Canada, we construct health region-area type-year panels for short-run (2009-2017) and long run (2009-2021) windows, comprising 72 and 104 observations, respectively. We first document distributional patterns using location quotients, and then implement a two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences (DiD) design comparing rural and urban areas within mixed health regions (regions containing both rural and urban populations) of Saskatchewan before and after policy introduction. To strengthen identification, we conduct multiple robustness checks, including a triple DiD framework that incorporates Manitoba as a comparison province, selected for its geographic proximity, similar rural-urban population structure, and absence of a comparable contemporaneous incentive program. Distributional results indicate that rural physician rates remained persistently below urban rates throughout the study period. Main DiD estimates show no statistically significant narrowing of the rural-urban physician rate gap within mixed health regions of Saskatchewan following the program implementation. The Triple DiD estimates similarly fail to detect a significant policy effect relative to Manitoba. Taken together, the results provide no evidence that financial incentives altered geographic physician maldistribution. The findings suggest that, depending on size and scope, stand-alone incentives may be insufficient to meaningfully address family physician maldistribution without integrated, multi-component workforce strategies.

title: What's Behind the ‘Digital Front Door’? Building a digital care infrastructure in a fragmented healthcare system
abstract: With alarming demographic and workforce developments in healthcare systems globally, digital health innovations are often heralded as solutions. Despite promises, empirical work points towards the complexity of such endeavours. Various sources of fragmentation complicate scaling up local initiatives and collaborations between different care institutions. In this paper we take fragmentation as ontological reality and conceptual starting point. Mobilizing literature on sociotechnical infrastructures and alignment work, we follow how a hospital-based innovations programme developed a digital care infrastructure in a major urbanized region. Combining these theoretical notions allows us to trace how digital infrastructure is 'done' in practice and continuously 'under construction'. Drawing on longitudinal ethnographic methods (observations, interviews and document analysis) conducted over an extensive period of time (17 months), we examine how various actors involved in a digital innovations programme try to build a digital infrastructure in a healthcare system characterised by fragmentation. We focus on how actors within the programme attempt to align social, technical, organisational and professional elements within the fragmented context. Our approach allowed us to identify five types of alignment work: narrative, internal, organisational, regional, and technical alignment work, and address emerging tensions and interactions between them. We argue that by using this more granular and comprehensive typology, and through conceptualizing infrastructures as moving targets, we can better appreciate the complexity and variety of alignment activities that support 'the' digital transformation in healthcare.

title: Embodiment of sociopolitical stress during pregnancy and coping strategies among perinatal Filipina women
abstract: Fear and uncertainty surrounding contemporary sociopolitical environments are emerging as global concerns for maternal and fetal health. However, limited research has examined how pregnant individuals perceive and embody these conditions and their implications for health. We focus on the Philippines, a country marked by intense State violence, to explore how fraught sociopolitical environments shape the impacts of stress during pregnancy among Filipina women. Through the lens of embodiment, this study investigates how perinatal women perceive sociopolitical stress and the coping strategies they employ to manage these stressors. We interviewed 21 pregnant and recently pregnant Filipina women across multiple regions of the Philippines. Participants reflected on their experiences of the current political climate and its perceived impact on their pregnancies. We found that stress arises from an interplay of everyday and sociopolitical stressors, and that awareness of and interaction with Filipino news and media contributed to levels of perceived stress. Using thematic analyses, we identified two primary forms of agentive coping strategies aimed at mitigating potential harm. These themes were (1) reframing stress (i.e., community viewing, familial support, humor): and (2) exercising agency through political apathy (i.e., disengagement, bahala na, avoidance, silence). This is one of the first studies to examine how perinatal women navigate and manage the embodied effects of sociopolitical stress. Our findings highlight the importance of considering sociopolitical contexts in shaping maternal health during pregnancy.

title: Clinical, organizational and institutional levers to ensure low-coercion psychiatry: an ethnographic study of four French psychiatric hospitals
abstract: Coercion in psychiatry refers to a continuum of measures applied against the patient's will. Epidemiological studies demonstrate that beyond the observation of frequent use in most countries, there are significant disparities between locations where coercion is used, even within a single country. Such is the case in France, where in certain hospitals restraints continue to be used with most patients, while in other institutions restraints are not used at all and wards employ an open-door policy. From a salutogenic perspective, we will turn out attention to the latter category in order to examine the protective factors, which we shall refer to as levers of least coercion. Adopting an interactionist and contextualized approach, we carried out an ethnographic study of four hospitals which in decades past have rarely, if ever, resorted to seclusion or mechanical restraint, and in which wards are left unlocked. This study, which took place between February to June 2022, was led by sociologists and nurse-researchers. It combines observations (62 days) and interviews among a diverse sample (mental health care professionals including psychiatrists, administrative staff, service users) (n = 78). It allows us to confirm that in comparable patients, and without increasing the level of violence or recourse to other methods of restraint, it is possible to keep wards open and still see infrequent or non-existent use of seclusion or mechanical restraint. Facilitating this state of affairs is the activation of relatively ordinary clinical measures based upon the quality of the caretaking relationship, the skills of caretaking teams, and a favorable therapeutic environment. Such clinical levers must be supported by both organizational methods and an institution, emphasizing the essential role played by the management team, the community of psychiatrists, and directors. The importance of a common culture and value system has also been pointed out - a culture which is equal parts caretaking and institutional organization.

title: Evaluating the effect of social mobility on the incidence of HIV/AIDS in low-income populations: A dynamic microsimulation study with large cohort data
abstract: The control of the HIV/AIDS epidemic remains a significant challenge for public health in Brazil, a country marked by profound social inequalities. In this study, we aimed to use the integration of large data analyses with microsimulation models to evaluate the effect of alternative income-based social mobility policies on AIDS incidence, both in the overall population and in specific vulnerability groups. We created a dynamic microsimulation model of a cohort of 1 million individuals starting from a large dataset of low-income people in 2012 in Brazil, integrated with input parameters from the analysis of a large retrospective cohort of 28.3 million individuals. We incorporated national, subnational, and municipal-level demographic, social and economic changes into the population, and simulated the impact until 2030 of five different scenarios of income social mobility based on income quintiles. A high-coverage, income-based social mobility intervention could reduce the overall incidence of AIDS by 11.8% (IRR 0.88, 0.81-0.96) by 2030. Among people living in extreme poverty, the reduction could reach 24% (IRR 0.76, 0.56-0.96). For those with no or limited literacy, a 17.9% (IRR 0.81, 0.62-1.03) decrease in AIDS incidence could be achieved, while the Black population could see a 12.4% (IRR 0.87, 0.42-1.24) reduction. Income-based social mobility policies could significantly reduce AIDS incidence in low-income populations, particularly in the most vulnerable individuals. These policies should be considered an important strategy for achieving the Sustainable Development Goal of ending AIDS by 2030 in Low- and Middle-Income Countries.

title: The symbolic power of natural beauty: A qualitative inquiry into the practices of cosmetic surgeons and aesthetic doctors
abstract: Social scientific research into the world of cosmetic surgery and aesthetic medical interventions shows that notions of natural beauty are used to gauge what procedures (not) to perform and who (not) to treat. In this article, we approach natural beauty as a beauty taste to examine how the professional practices of cosmetic surgeons and aesthetic doctors, what we call their beautifying bodywork, shape social inequalities. Drawing on in-depth interviews with aesthetic practitioners and non-participant observations during client-patient consultations and an international plastic surgery conference in Belgium, we find three types of mutually reinforcing mechanisms that hinge on a preference for natural beauty. The first type of mechanism involves the establishment of the superiority of natural beauty, e.g. by deeming a preference for it innate and unequivocally superior to other beauty tastes. This consensus underpins the perceived legitimacy of the other identified mechanisms. The second type of mechanism shows how the meaning of natural beauty is configured and enacted through an agreement of "appropriate" procedures informed by intersections of gender binaries, race, and class boundaries. Finally, we find mechanisms that advance the superiority of natural beauty through pedagogical practices of inclusion and exclusion. These different mechanisms feed into each other to produce the symbolic power of natural beauty, which has the capacity to perpetuate gendered, racialised, and classed beauty ideals and practices; something we urge the broader medical industry to acknowledge.

title: Health impact bonds as an innovative payment model for health prevention programs: A scoping review
abstract: Health impact bonds (HIBs) are an innovative outcome-based financing model increasingly applied in public health programs. This study aimed to comprehensively summarize their applications, benefits, and challenges in health prevention programs. In this scoping, 31 peer-reviewed papers and 19 websites were eligible for inclusion. Key characteristics of the programs were extracted, including details of the interventions, health and financial outcomes, and stakeholders' involvement. We identified 23 HIB programs across 13 countries, with durations ranging from 2 to 7.5 years. These programs targeted various health issues, including non-communicable diseases, cancer screening, maternal and child health, infectious diseases, mental health, and assistance for older people. Of completed programs with disclosed financial outcomes, 11 programs fully met their targets. Initial investments ranged from under US$100,000 to over US$29 million, with investor returns varying from 5% to 27.4%. Benefits included risk transfer, innovation, cross-sector collaboration, and improved accountability. Key challenges were investor risk, high transaction costs, outcome attribution complexity, limited evidence, and stakeholder coordination issues. HIBs may be a promising complementary model for financing health prevention initiatives to alleviate burdens for healthcare systems. However, some major challenges, including modest return relative to risk, limited investor participation, and stakeholder misalignment, need to be addressed to enable a broader adoption across diverse health issues and healthcare contexts.

title: Housing environments, social isolation, and mortality among low-income older renters in the United States
abstract: Housing environments constitute a fundamental social determinant of health in later life, yet little is known about how different housing contexts shape survival among economically vulnerable older adults. This study examines whether mortality among low-income older renters follows a graded housing ecology and whether the consequences of social isolation are conditioned by residential context. Using twelve waves (2011-2022) of nationally representative data from the National Health and Aging Trends Study, we analyze 2790 low-income renters (9337 person-wave observations). Mortality risk was estimated using longitudinal discrete-time hazard models with weighting to address attrition and housing selection. A clear mortality gradient emerged across housing types. In fully adjusted models, residents of traditional rental housing exhibited significantly higher mortality hazards than those in subsidized senior housing (SSH) (HR = 1.56, p < .01), while non-subsidized congregate housing showed intermediate risk (HR = 1.32, p < .10). Social isolation independently predicted mortality (HR = 1.51 for isolated; HR = 1.41 for severely isolated, p < .05). However, the mortality consequences of isolation varied by housing context. Socially isolated residents in non-subsidized housing faced nearly double the mortality risk relative to socially integrated SSH residents (HR = 2.00, p < .05). Predicted probabilities were similar across housing types among socially integrated older adults (6-7%) but diverged under isolation, rising to 9-13% outside SSH. These findings suggest that housing environments function as meso-level social ecologies that structure exposure to relational risk. Structural supports embedded in subsidized senior housing appear to buffer the life-threatening consequences of isolation, whereas less institutionally embedded contexts amplify vulnerability in later life.

title: Does who is counted matter? Comparing disability measures and self-rated health
abstract: BACKGROUND: People with disabilities experience significant health disparities compared to those without disabilities. However, analysts disagree on which measures should be used to identify the disabled population. Differences in disability measurement hamper efforts to accurately estimate health risks experienced by people with disabilities. This study investigates how self-rated health differs based on responses to two common population measures of disability. METHODS: Using weighted data from the 2011 and 2012 National Health Interview Survey (N = 25,096), this study employed logistic regressions to estimate the predicted probabilities of reporting poor or fair self-rated health based on responses to the disability measures from the American Community Survey (ACS-6) and the Washington Group Short Set (WG-SS). RESULTS: While the ACS-6 identifies a significantly higher prevalence of disability (16.9%) than the WG-SS (7.9%), the adjusted predicted probabilities of poor/fair health did not differ significantly between measures (0.329 for ACS-6; 0.358 for WG-SS). However, individuals counted only by the ACS-6, those who would be excluded if federal surveys adopted the more restrictive WG-SS, were roughly 20 percentage-points more likely to report poor/fair health than non-disabled respondents. CONCLUSION: The WG-SS excludes a considerable proportion of the disabled population who experience significantly worse health than non-disabled people. Relying solely on the more restrictive WG-SS may omit millions of individuals, potentially hampering federal efforts to achieve health equity.

title: Economic uncertainty shocks and cause-specific mortality
abstract: Economic uncertainty negatively impacts employment and production. However, little is known about the associations between uncertainty shocks and health over time. We employ a time-series econometric model to analyze the propagation patterns of uncertainty shocks on mortality, using daily data from the Economic Policy Uncertainty Index and the UK national death registry. We observe immediate increases in suicide, drug poisoning deaths, and in cardiovascular mortality at weekly horizons. Suicide and drug poisoning deaths rise by up to 2.3%, with the positive association persisting for three weeks before returning to baseline by week six. Cardiovascular mortality rises by 0.9%, persists for one week, and increases modestly again during weeks five and six. Our results demonstrate transmission patterns of uncertainty shocks across causes of death, reflecting both individual and systemic responses during uncertain times.

title: Working while living with cystic fibrosis: Why symptom severity tells us little about employment outcomes?
abstract: This article examines the vocational and employment trajectories of people living with cystic fibrosis in French-speaking Switzerland. Drawing on qualitative data, it reveals that clinical severity alone is an ineffective predictor of these trajectories. These are dependent on the resources available within individuals' families. Furthermore, illness serves as a site of socialization: it fosters contrasting attitudes towards effort and pleasure. An ascetic orientation, characterized by discipline and long-term planning, fosters ambitious professional goals, whereas a hedonistic orientation cantered on immediate gratification inclines individuals towards more pleasure-oriented activities. The study also identifies four types of orientations to work: career-oriented, work-at-all-costs, withdrawal, and secondary gain. These types explain divergent employment outcomes. This article highlights the analytical yield of articulating Bourdieusian concepts of capital and dispositions with medical sociology's concern for the modes of adjustment to chronic illnesses.

title: Physicians’ viewpoints on initiating invasive mechanical ventilation in older persons: A Q methodology study in Japan
abstract: Initiating life-supporting invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) is a complex yet crucial decision, characterised by prognostic uncertainty and a wide range of outcomes, with profound consequences for patients, families, and healthcare systems. Older persons are at increased risk of poor outcomes. In Japan, IMV use is relatively intense in older persons. Moreover, in contrast to other countries, IMV initiation is often considered irreversible. IMV initiation in such a context is crucial, yet understudied. We used Q methodology, a hybrid quantitative and qualitative technique, to explore viewpoints on initiating IMV in older persons among Japanese physicians. A purposive sample of 42 physicians ranked 39 opinion statements on a quasi-normally distributed grid. The statements ranged from patient to societal level considerations, and participants explained their rankings in interviews. By-person factor analysis identified shared ranking patterns, interpreted as distinct viewpoints and supported by interview data. An additional question addressed ways to improve decision making. Three distinct viewpoints were identified. While the patient's expressed or inferred wishes were prioritised in all three, differences emerged in how these were weighed against family preferences and physicians' clinical judgment. This may give rise to dilemmas when preferences diverge, as current regulatory frameworks and guidelines leave room for interpretation. To improve decision making, respondents pointed to clearer guidelines enabling reassessment and reconsideration. Greater clarity and guidance may support these deliberations and promote greater consistency, particularly regarding the role of the family, requests for potentially low-value treatment, and the use of time-limited trials before definitive decisions.

title: The effect of internal migration on blood pressure among a cohort of young adults in South Africa
abstract: Given global concern over rising hypertension prevalence, especially in low-and-middle- income countries, we investigate whether migration and urban exposure is associated with higher blood pressure (BP). We use data collected over four waves between 2018 and 2022 from the Migrant Health Follow-Up Study, a longitudinal cohort study of young adults aged 18-40 at baseline who were members of households within the Agincourt Health and socio-Demographic Surveillance System located in rural northeast South Africa. Our analytic sample consists of the 1037 women and 994 men for whom we have BP measurements at both Waves 1 and 4, and who have complete socio-economic, demographic, and migration information collected in Waves 2 and 3, which we use to predict Wave 4 BP. Descriptively, our analysis shows that migration is still more common among men in contemporary South Africa compared with women, as it has been historically. However, a significant share of young adult women increasingly migrate away from their rural homes. We find evidence that migration is associated with higher longitudinal BP, net of various health and health behavior measures. This finding is especially robust for women. Further, residence in the highly urbanized Gauteng province is associated with increased BP for both men and women, but these negative effects are buffered by higher levels of education for women, and by employment for men. Our findings suggest that migration processes and urban exposure may result in experiences that result in increases in BP over 3-4 years, especially among women.

title: Corrigendum to “Does additional education affect memory consistently? An analysis of compulsory schooling reforms across Europe and U.S.” [Soc. Sci. Med. 403 (2026) 119377]
A longitudinal ethnographic exploration of actor power and agency in healthcare systems: The role of human and non-human actors in shaping care delivery and outcomes
abstract: Healthcare systems are complex socio-material assemblages shaped by the interactions between human and non-human actors. This study applies Actor-Network Theory (ANT) to identify the actors influencing healthcare delivery within three Community Healthcare Networks (CHNs) in Ireland. A 23-month longitudinal ethnographic design combining photo-ethnography, ethnographic interviews, and focus groups was applied to comprehend the natural setting through which care is delivered and to trace the actors influencing care delivery. 47 site visits provided contextual observations of everyday practices and interactions. Additionally, 22 interviews identified actors influencing the delivery of care, while 3 ethnographic focus groups explored the scope of actors' power and agency. The study revealed the presence of human (22%) and non-human actors (78%) within the healthcare network, and although agency and power were distributed relationally across human and non-human actors' interactions, this distribution was uneven, with actors possessing varying capacities to shape interactions and control outcomes. A novel actor typology, mapping combinations of power and agency, was developed to classify actors within the network. The study suggests the importance of granting analytical symmetry when considering human and non-human actors in the delivery of healthcare, and the varying levels of power and agency occupied by these actors. Further, this study extends ANT's analytical scope, providing a more advanced theoretical perspective for understanding the complex socio-material realities of contemporary healthcare networks.

title: A call for standardization: A case study of theoretical ambiguity in mental illness labeling and stigma research via systematic review
abstract: Despite more than 60 years of research, the specific effects of mental illness/psychiatric labels on stigma remain unclear. As pointed out in prior systematic reviews, one reason for this ambiguity is that researchers conceptualize key variables differently. Since conceptualization is derived from theory, we conducted a pre-registered systematic review to investigate the definition and operationalization of mental illness stigma. On one hand, we find that fewer than half of the reviewed studies define stigma, and among those that do, definitions vary-even when citing the same foundational sources. On the other hand, there is an increasing use of social distance as a measure of stigma-a trend which suggests the beginnings of methodological consensus. We hope these convergences will inspire theoretical consensus and methodological cohesion, particularly if paired with more rigorous attention to how social distance is defined and measured. Such theoretical consensus would allow knowledge to accumulate, paving the way for the development of more effective evidence-based interventions to reduce mental illness stigma.

title: Neighborhood social structure, criminal convictions, and substance use disorders in Sweden: a population-based sibling comparison study
abstract: PURPOSE: We investigated how multidimensional neighborhood types, capturing the complexity of neighborhood social structure, related to criminal convictions and substance use disorders (SUDs) in Sweden while accounting for residential mobility and shared familial influences. METHODS: Using nationwide Swedish register data (1991-2020), we followed 1.82 million individuals born 1985-2002 across five neighborhood types previously identified using latent class analysis. These were defined by socioeconomic and demographic indicators, with the most common type (rural low-diversity neighborhoods) serving as the reference category. Associations between neighborhood types, violent and nonviolent convictions, and SUDs were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models with hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Neighborhood type was modeled as a time-varying exposure, capturing residential changes over time. Sibling comparison models were applied to account for familial confounding. RESULTS: Risks of violent convictions, nonviolent convictions, and SUDs were highest in resource-limited neighborhoods (i.e., socioeconomically deprived areas with high residential turnover; violent: adjusted HR (aHR) = 4.70, 95% CI 4.26-5.19; nonviolent: aHR = 2.07, 95% CI 1.92-2.22; SUDs: aHR = 3.36, 95% CI 3.09-3.65). Moderate increases were observed in urban high-diversity neighborhoods (i.e., characterized by ethnic heterogeneity), whereas risks were lowest in socioeconomically advantaged urban areas. Associations were attenuated but remained statistically significant in sibling comparisons. Sex differences were modest and followed similar patterns across outcomes. CONCLUSION: Neighborhoods marked by socioeconomic disadvantage and residential instability, rather than ethnic diversity, were linked to higher risks of criminal convictions and SUDs. Remaining associations after familial adjustment suggest modest but meaningful contextual effects.

title: Racism, mortification and carcerality: Three concepts needed to understand the experiences of racially minoritised people diagnosed with severe mental illness
abstract: This paper argues to understand racially minoritised people's experiences of mental illness and mental healthcare, we must expand the focus from inpatient stays to understanding a series of interactions with state institutions. We extend Goffman's concept of mortification beyond the inpatient unit to demonstrate how carceral practices are routinely used by state institutions, contributing to the worsening of racially minoritised people's mental health. Drawing upon 22 in-depth interviews from participatory action research (PAR) with racially minoritised people diagnosed with severe mental illness in the UK, we show mortification and carceral practices experienced by racially minoritised patients are related to their racialised identities. This is shown in our data by: institutions' failure to act on reported incidents of racism; controlling and withholding information and services related to patients' mental healthcare; and the assumed criminality and threat of racially minoritised people, often resulting in increased police involvement and surveillance. Specifically, we show (1) mortification is not a process that happens solely inside the physical psychiatric hospital. It happens in a series of interactions with state institutions with harmful effects and (2) mortification is not a discrete event that takes place within one period, in one type of institution. Instead, degrading, racist experiences are interspersed throughout the life course compounding the feelings of identity loss and erosion. We conclude it is vital to bring together the concepts of racism, carcerality and mortification to develop a thorough understanding of the experiences of racially minoritised people diagnosed with severe mental illness.

title: Living through rupture: The social dynamics of cancer and selfhood in Türkiye
abstract: This study analyses the intersection between risk medicine and biographical disruption from a sociological perspective, drawing on cancer patients' experiences. The research aims to determine how the deterioration in the quality of life affects the subjective self and how the coping strategies influence health behaviors and experiences of receiving support. Using a phenomenological approach, the study examines how individuals cope with the deterioration of their living standards and what strategies they produce when faced with medical risk, existential anxiety, and social stigma. The sample of the study consists of three categories: newly diagnosed with cancer, actively fighting cancer, and cancer survivors but at risk. Karabük province, characterized by high levels of air pollution and an increased incidence of cancer, was selected as the study population. Türkiye is important for two reasons. The first is the emphasis that the social field in Türkiye produces a strong form of stigmatization of cancer patients. The second is that religious well-being practices in Türkiye offer vital support for individuals facing biographical disruption and fear of death.

title: Gentrification, policing, and potential pathways to health: A scoping review
abstract: Policing is a social determinant of health that disproportionately affects racially, socially, and economically marginalized communities. Gentrification is hypothesized to alter policing, yet findings have not been synthesized across studies. We conducted a scoping review of studies examining gentrification's effects on direct policing (e.g., person-police encounters) and indirect policing (e.g., vicarious exposure through media or word-of-mouth) and related outcomes. Searches across multiple electronic databases identified 2680 records; after screening titles and abstracts, 42 full texts were reviewed and 26 were included (14 qualitative, 9 quantitative, 3 multi-method). Studies varied widely in how gentrification was defined; few were from public health or medicine. No study examined indirect policing in the context of gentrification. We identified three pathways through which gentrification increases direct policing: resident-led calls for service (via 911/311), police-led expansions of order-maintenance policing in gentrifying areas, and investment-led policing to protect new commercial development. Adverse effects were concentrated among longer-term Black, Latine, unstably housed, and gender minority residents. Health-related studies reported significant negative psychosocial impacts linked to these dynamics. Overall, gentrification appears to increase population-level exposure to direct policing via residents, police, and investors, with potential contributions to poorer mental health among longer-term residents. The review also highlights critical gaps, including sparse health-specific research and the absence of research on indirect policing.

title: Emotional labour in therapeutic work – the case of physiotherapists and psychotherapists in Poland
abstract: This article presents a comparative analysis of emotional labour among physiotherapists and psychotherapists in Poland, based on 26 in-depth interviews conducted separately with practitioners working primarily in private practice. Despite differences in therapeutic modality - physiotherapists intervening through the body, psychotherapists through the psyche - the analysis reveals structural convergences in their emotional experiences. Drawing on Hochschild's concept of emotional labour and Bolton's typology of emotion management, the article examines how practitioners employ both surface and deep acting. The article's key contributions are threefold. First, it offers an innovative comparative approach, providing empirical evidence of professional similarities across therapeutic modalities (and some differences). Second, it reconceptualises therapy sociologically as a normative and relational setting. Third, it clarifies the boundaries between emotional labour and self-care.

title: Scale matters: Patterns of inequity in measures of structural racism can reverse direction when using the relative vs. the absolute scale
abstract: Quantifying the effect of structural racism on health is a subject of sustained interest. To measure structural racism, analysts often calculate contrasts between marginalized and privileged groups on measures of social determinants in health. These contrasts are predominantly calculated on the relative scale, rather than the absolute scale. In this paper, we investigated the rank ordering of 38 US states in terms of the relative and absolute difference in education and incarceration between Black and White individuals using 2015-2019 data from the American Community Survey and the National Prisoner Statistics.
