The state-level Black/White ratios and Black-White differences in education were highly correlated (Spearman's rank coefficient = 0.99) and resulted in few rank changes. Conversely, ratios and differences in incarceration were only modestly correlated (Spearman's rank coefficient = 0.43), and resulted in thirteen rank changes of ten or more positions. For incarceration, broad trends in state ordering reverse when considering differences rather than ratios. We contend that for incarceration, the absolute difference is the more meaningful contrast, as it counts the number of additional Black individuals incarcerated. For education, the decision between the relative and absolute scale matters less since the differences and ratios are so highly aligned that states generally fare the same regardless of the measure chosen. Before linking measures of structural racism to health outcomes, researchers are advised to decide the scale for each measure based on conceptual theory and an explicit value judgement.

title: Patient-made knowledge networks: Long COVID discourse, epistemic injustice, and online community formation
abstract: Long COVID represents an unprecedented case of patient-led illness definition, emerging through Twitter in May 2020 when patients collectively named and legitimized their condition before medical recognition. This study examines 2.8 million tweets containing #LongCOVID through topic modeling followed by content analysis of a purposively sampled 5100 tweets, and exponential random graph modeling (ERGM) to understand how contested illness communities construct knowledge networks. User roles were identified through analysis of Twitter biography fields and review of 1000 tweets (10 per user) from the 100 highest-centrality accounts. We identify seven discourse themes spanning symptom documentation, medical dismissal, cross-illness solidarity, and policy advocacy, alongside a differentiated ecosystem of four user roles. ERGM results demonstrate that tie formation centers on epistemic practices-knowledge sharing and community building-rather than policy debates, supporting characterization of this space as an epistemic community in Haas's (1992) sense. Long COVID patients achieved World Health Organization (WHO) recognition within months, contrasting sharply with decades-long struggles of similar conditions. These findings illuminate how social media affordances enable marginalized patient populations to construct alternative knowledge systems, form cross-illness coalitions, and contest traditional medical authority.

title: Beyond socio-economic disadvantage: Religio-cultural practices and the Muslim advantage in child survival in India
abstract: Background Despite declining child mortality in India over three decades, religious disparities persist. Muslim children consistently exhibit lower under-five mortality than Hindu children, despite Muslims occupying a more disadvantaged socio-economic position on average. Explanations based solely on urban residence or caste composition remain incomplete. Objective This study examines the persistence of the Muslim child survival advantage in India and investigates whether religio-cultural practices, beyond conventional socio-economic determinants, help explain this paradox. Methods Pooled data from five National Family Health Survey (NFHS) rounds (1992-2021) are analysed using Cox proportional hazards models, controlling for socio-economic, demographic, and health-related factors. A complementary mixed-methods field study conducted in North-East Delhi between August 2022 and June 2023 integrates household survey data (n = 400) and qualitative interviews (n = 45), analysed using the Framework Analysis Method, to capture cultural mechanisms not measurable in large-scale surveys. Findings Muslim children exhibit consistently lower under-five mortality across all five NFHS rounds; in NFHS-5 this stands at 8.4%. The advantage persists - and in some specifications strengthens - after adjusting for socio-economic, demographic, and healthcare factors, despite Muslims being disadvantaged on 15 of 25 key mortality determinants. Factors favouring Muslim children include better sanitation, higher dietary protein intake, alcohol abstinence, lower son preference, and community-based redistribution. Field evidence indicates these practices are embedded in religio-cultural norms. Conclusion The findings suggest that socio-economic explanations alone are insufficient to account for religious differentials in child survival in India. Religio-cultural practices are associated with patterns of child survival and represent plausible pathways through which observed differences may arise. Policies aimed at reducing child mortality must therefore engage not only with material deprivation and healthcare access but also with culturally embedded practices that influence caregiving, nutrition, hygiene, and social support.

title: Changing cannabis use among diverse adolescents over a 12-year period of policy change: Trends and disparities
abstract: Purpose Cannabis use has decreased among adolescents over the past decade, in spite of more permissive policies. Prior studies are limited in their ability to examine numerous social identities over a meaningful period of time. The present study therefore uses a very large school-based survey to examine how rates of cannabis use and disparities in use have changed from 2013 to 2025. Methods 9th and 11th grade students provided survey data on the 2013, 2016, 2019, 2022, or 2025 Minnesota Student Survey (Ns = 45,180 to 75,551 by wave). The prevalence of any past 30-day cannabis use was compared across survey year, using harmonized measures of assigned sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, racial and ethnic identity, and poverty experience. Logistic regression (adjusted for grade) was used to test if disparities in past-30 day cannabis use had widened, stayed the same, or narrowed over time. Results The prevalence of any past 30-day cannabis use declined from 2013 to 2025 for the full sample, from 12.7% to 5.0%, and this downward trend was evident for all subgroups examined. In almost all cases, marginalized youth had significantly elevated odds of reporting past 30-day cannabis use compared to their privileged group counterparts. In many groups, observed disparities decreased significantly from 2013 to 2025, with some nuance by group and intermediate years. Conclusions Health equity should be the focus of ongoing cannabis use prevention efforts, particularly reducing stigma, which previous research has shown to be a substantial contributor to cannabis use disparities.

title: Abuse and disrespect of family members in pediatric hospital wards in Sierra Leone: The role of emotional culture and spatial practices for emotion management
abstract: Delayed care seeking is a major source of pediatric mortality in low-income countries. Disrespect and abuse by healthcare providers are widely recognized as critical barriers to care, but few studies consider how these problems manifest in pediatric care settings. Based on interviews and observations of 110 nurses on pediatric hospital wards in Sierra Leone, this study suggests that nurses likely exacerbated problems of delayed care seeking by publicly blaming and berating parents and other family members. These expressions of anger and frustration violated professional expectations that nurses manage their emotions to create a caring environment for patients. To understand the nurses' actions, I analyzed the emotional cultures of these wards, including the norms, beliefs, artifacts, and practices that governed which emotions were considered appropriate and acceptable. I found evidence of complex and often contradictory emotional cultures from three possible sources: global contemporary professional nursing culture, an apparent residual influence of British colonial medicine, and the emotional expressiveness of Sierra Leonean society. These three sources contained conflicting expectations for emotion management, which may have contributed to instances of disrespect and abuse toward patients' families. However, when nurses were able to create momentary private space in otherwise intensely public wards, they did not express anger toward patients' families; instead, they adhered to professional norms of compassion and comportment. This research identifies spatial practices for emotion management and suggests a renewed focus on emotional culture to help reduce disrespect and abuse of patients and families.

title: Filling the void: Compensatory expertise and psychiatric care continuity among Russian migrants in Georgia
abstract: This article introduces the concept of compensatory expertise to explain how psychiatric treatment is sustained when the coordination required for ongoing care becomes unreliable. It examines how Russian-speaking migrants who left Russia after the onset of the 2022 Russo-Ukrainian war navigate mental health care in Georgia. Drawing on qualitative analysis of a Telegram support group with approximately 3000 members, the study focuses on an urban, university-educated cohort whose relocation disrupted established therapeutic relationships and access to medication. Participants used digital infrastructures to preserve diagnostic histories, interpret psychological distress through psychiatric categories, evaluate practitioner reliability, and coordinate treatment through peer exchange. Compensatory expertise refers to a form of lay expertise that emerges when patients assume interpretive and organisational roles typically performed by clinical systems, thereby allowing psychiatric knowledge to remain useable despite institutional instability. The findings show that participants continued to rely on biomedical psychiatry as the framework guiding treatment, even as they expressed scepticism toward individual providers.

title: “I want to be able to say that I did everything I could”. Exploring the negotiations between the logic of care and the logic of research in clinical trials
abstract: Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTs) are considered the "gold standard" for producing medical evidence due to their emphasis on standardisation, control, and scientific rigour. However, staff often face challenges in adhering to protocols, as running trials can generate tensions with caring for participants as individuals. In this article, drawing on Annemarie Mol's concept of the 'logic of care', we explore how care and research are continually negotiated within clinical trials. We conducted a 17-month ethnography at a UK clinical trial centre. The study draws on 330 h of observation of 170 staff and participants to examine how healthcare professionals navigate competing demands while managing hypertension. Our findings show that strict adherence to research protocols was maintained when deemed essential for running the trial, even when doing so generated discomfort or potential harm for participants. However, there were also moments in which staff prioritised participant wellbeing, for example by offering dietary advice, even when such actions risked influencing trial outcomes. Our analysis offers four contributions to this literature. First, it illustrates how the logic of care and the logic of research co-exist within the everyday conduct of trials. Second, our study highlights how the relationship between care and research is not resolved through the prioritisation of one logic over the other, but through ongoing negotiation. Third, our findings show how these tensions are embodied in the role of the clinician-researcher. Fourth, our analysis contributes to broader debates on the ethics of clinical research.

title: Trajectories and inequalities in routine healthcare uptake from adolescence to retirement: A sequence analysis across 14 European countries
abstract: BACKGROUND: Regular uptake of routine healthcare services can support disease prevention, early detection, monitoring, and timely treatment. Socioeconomically disadvantaged populations often face barriers to healthcare use. However, little is known about how routine healthcare uptake, and inequalities within it, unfold across the life course, or whether these trajectories differ by gender and birth cohort. METHODS: We used retrospectively collected SHARELIFE data from wave 3 (2008/09) of the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) (n = 27'960). We constructed annual binary sequences of self-reported regular uptake from ages 16 to 65 for blood pressure measurement, blood tests for sugar or cholesterol, vision checks, mammography, and gynecological visits. We used sequence analysis to identify service-specific clusters of routine healthcare uptake trajectories. We then used multilevel multinomial regression models to examine associations with life-course socioeconomic disadvantage and birth cohort and assessed gender differences where applicable. RESULTS: Regular healthcare uptake generally increased with age across all services. In the pooled analyses, three broad trajectory types were identified across services: low uptake, uptake mainly in later life, and uptake throughout life. Trajectory membership differed by life-course socioeconomic disadvantage, country, and birth cohort, but not meaningfully by gender. Higher life-course socioeconomic disadvantage was associated with lower odds of belonging to high uptake trajectories compared with low uptake trajectories. CONCLUSIONS: Routine healthcare uptake across adulthood followed age-patterned trajectories that varied by socioeconomic disadvantage, birth cohort, and country of residence. These findings suggest that social stratification influences long-term patterns of routine healthcare uptake across the life course and highlight the importance of addressing inequalities in access to and engagement with routine healthcare services.

title: Spirit of the Hawk: Colonial intensity and alcohol use disorders across 178 countries
abstract: Qualitative research links colonial history to alcohol-related harms in specific populations, and econometric studies show that colonial institutions shape long-run health trajectories, yet no study has connected these literatures by testing whether colonial intensity predicts national-level alcohol outcomes in a spatially explicit panel framework. We construct a colonial intensity composite (the duration of colonial rule weighted by colony type-extractive versus settler) from COLDAT 3.0 and estimate panel Spatial Durbin Models on 178 countries over 21 years (2000-2020), using geographic contiguity and shared-colonizer spatial weights across four WHO alcohol outcomes. Colonial intensity shows a significant positive direct association with alcohol use disorder (AUD) prevalence across all eight specifications (0.065-0.238 percentage points per unit), accompanied by negative spillover effects (associations transmitted to geographically neighbouring or co-colonized countries). The AUD association emerges only after controlling for cultural confounders (suppression effect) and shows no temporal decay, while consumption effects weaken over time-a pattern consistent with intergenerational trauma persistence. Effects concentrate in British colonies. Standard alcohol policies reduce consumption but not AUD, suggesting regulatory tools alone cannot close the colonial legacy gap in disorder prevalence. These findings provide the first large-scale quantitative evidence linking colonial intensity to contemporary AUD.

title: Navigating aging and health with limited family ties across societies: Challenges, adaptations, and policy responses
abstract: This overview introduces a special issue on aging with limited family ties, developed from an international workshop held at the National University of Singapore in February 2025. The special issue brings together nine articles examining how older adults navigate later life with constrained family availability across Brazil, rural China, India, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, the United States, and a 25-country cross-national sample. The papers examine diverse forms of limited family ties, including childlessness, spouselessness, kinlessness, sonlessness, and sole family survivorship, and consider their implications for health, mortality, subjective well-being, social connection, advance care planning, and anticipated living arrangements. This overview synthesizes three key lessons. First, limited family ties should not be treated as a homogeneous experience, as different missing family ties carry distinct meanings and support implications. Second, the consequences of limited family ties are conditional rather than uniformly negative, which produces vulnerability in some contexts while also prompting adaptation and planning in others. Third, the capacity to adapt among older adults with limited family ties depends on available resources and relationships, which are further shaped by gender, socioeconomic resources, cultural norms, and formal or informal support options. This article concludes by outlining future research and policy directions for building more inclusive care, housing, health, and planning systems for older adults with diverse family circumstances.

title: Educational attainment and social isolation trajectories from midlife to later life in four high- and middle-income countries
abstract: Social isolation is an important public health concern, yet its variation by educational attainment across life stages and sociocultural contexts is not well understood. This study uses harmonized longitudinal data from the Gateway to Global Aging Data (2010 to 2018) to examine trajectories of social isolation from midlife to later life in the United States, England, China, and Mexico. We analyze both an overall isolation index and four dimensions of isolation: partnership status, contact with children, contact with friends, and social participation. Growth curve models assess differences in social isolation trajectories across educational groups and whether these disparities change with age. Less educated adults experienced higher overall isolation in all four countries, with larger gaps in China and Mexico and smaller gaps in the United States and England. Educational disparities in overall isolation widened with age in the United States and Mexico, consistent with cumulative disadvantage processes over the life course, but remained stable in England and China. Domain-specific analyses show notable cross-national variation. Education-related differences in social participation and friend contact were consistent across contexts, while differences in family-based ties varied in direction and size. These findings document cross-national educational disparities in social isolation and highlight the importance of considering structural barriers and domain-specific patterns in future research and policy discussions.

title: Producing antibiotic practices from guidelines, clinical assessment and health insurance in Kilimanjaro, Tanzania
abstract: Antibiotics are crucial medications for healthcare delivery. The regulatory frameworks that govern the prescription and consumption of antibiotics vary widely. In Tanzania, over-the-counter sales of antibiotics are illegal, yet widespread. In contrast, prescription of antibiotics in Tanzanian hospitals is constrained through regulatory tools, such as Standard Treatment Guidelines (STG). This paper examines what moves, limits and accelerates antibiotic prescription and use in rural hospitals of the Kilimanjaro region. The study draws on four months of ethnographic fieldwork, including participant observation and semi-structured interviews, between January and July 2022. We demonstrate that antibiotic prescription is influenced by drug availability, resource constraints, and linkages between guidelines and insurance systems. Doctors aim to create paper trails to adhere to the STGs which are closely linked to reimbursements from the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF), thereby balancing adherence to guidelines with their efforts to make antibiotic treatment work for their patients. Furthermore, resource constraints contribute to use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as Ceftriaxone. Through the theoretical frameworks of tinkering and standards in medicine, we argue that tinkering occurs at the individual, institutional and state levels. The STGs are not simply followed or violated but absorbed into broader repertoires of practice shaped by procurement systems, insurance logics, and clinical uncertainty. While concerning from an antimicrobial resistance perspective, it is analytically revealing from an ethnographic perspective, as antibiotic guidelines are reworked in practice rather than simply enacted. The findings of this study can inform policy on the effects of guidelines coupled with health insurance on antibiotic use.

title: Beyond the visible: Centering adolescent voices in conceptualising violence in conflict settings
abstract: Measures of violence against children (VAC) categorise violence as physical, emotional, sexual violence and neglect. While used globally, these measures may not reflect how conflict-affected adolescents conceptualise harm. Drawing on child rights, structural violence, and feminist frameworks, this study explores how adolescents living in conflict-affected Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) conceptualise violence. METHODS: We conducted four same-sex group discussions with 36 adolescents (20 girls, 16 boys) aged 13-17 years old in the DRC. Participants discussed daily experiences in their community: things they like, and good and bad things they experience. Inductive and deductive thematic analysis were used to identify forms of violence discussed, which were then mapped onto measures of VAC to explore how well existing tools capture their experiences. RESULTS: Adolescents described experiences of violence consistent with physical, emotional and sexual violence, child neglect and labour, which are all commonly recognised in existing tools. Less commonly recognised forms described included economic control, negative social perceptions and ill-labelling, taking on parental responsibility, and environmental hazards and safety concerns in the community. Gender differences emerged with economic maltreatment predominantly described by boys and sexual exploitation linked to unmet needs described only by girls. CONCLUSION: When adolescents define harm in their own terms, they reveal forms of violence not captured by standard measures. These forms of harm also reflect the stage of development and positioning of adolescents in society. Research tools for conflict-affected adolescents should be co-developed with adolescents to ensure evidence and prevention strategies reflect and address the interconnected forms of harm.

title: Socioeconomic inequalities in inflammation in childhood and adolescence: an international study across five cohorts
abstract: Chronic inflammation may be a key mechanism driving social to biological transitions across the lifecourse. We investigated the effect of early-life socioeconomic position (SEP) on inflammatory biomarkers in childhood and adolescence and assessed mediation by body mass index (BMI). We conducted cohort-specific analysis in five birth cohorts: the Barwon Infant Study (BIS, Australia, n = 708, 4-5 years); Born in Bradford (BiB, United Kingdom, n = 4576, 7-11 years); the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children's Child Health CheckPoint (LSAC-CP, Australia, n = 1874, 11-12 years); the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1986 (NFBC1986, Finland, n = 9467, 15-16 years); and the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC, United Kingdom, n = 4875, 17-18 years). Exposures were neighbourhood disadvantage, household economic conditions, and maternal education, in pregnancy or infancy. Outcomes were log-transformed high sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) and glycoprotein acetyls (GlycA) levels. We conducted confounder-adjusted linear regression to estimate the effect of exposures on outcomes, and mediation analysis using interventional effects to assess mediation by BMI. Lower early-life SEP, particularly neighbourhood disadvantage and lower maternal education, was associated with higher inflammation from the age of 7-11 years. Effects were most apparent for GlycA (e.g., mean GlycA difference between BiB children in most and least disadvantaged neighbourhoods: 0.1 SD [95% CI 0.03-0.2]; between NFBC1986 adolescents with most and least educated mothers: 0.2 SD [0.02, 0.3]). BMI partially mediated many of these effects (20-100%). Neighbourhood disadvantage and lower maternal education may increase inflammation in children and adolescents, in part through higher adiposity. This underscores the importance of addressing socioeconomic conditions in early life and of preventing excess BMI.

title: Association between socioeconomic status, lifestyle factors and mortality: A scoping review
abstract: BACKGROUND: Lifestyle factors have been widely discussed as potential mediators of the association between socioeconomic status (SES) and health outcomes. However, no comprehensive review has synthesized existing evidence on the mediating role of lifestyle factors in the association of SES with all-cause mortality and cancer-specific mortality. Therefore, we conducted a scoping review to sum up current evidence and highlight research gaps. METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science from database inception to March 31, 2026 for observational studies that explicitly assessed the mediating role of lifestyle factors in the associations between SES and all-cause mortality or cancer-specific mortality. RESULTS: Twenty-five longitudinal studies published between 2008 and 2025 were included, predominantly from high-income countries. The median proportions of the associations between SES and mortality mediated by lifestyle factors were modest, ranging from 5.4% to 28.0% for all-cause mortality and from 10.7% to 25.6% for cancer-specific mortality, with substantial heterogeneity across SES indicators, population subgroups, lifestyle measurement approaches, and analytic methods. Smoking consistently showed the strongest mediating role, whereas BMI contributed minimally. Studies using repeated or non-baseline assessments of lifestyle tended to report larger mediation effects. CONCLUSION: There is evidence that lifestyle factors (in particular smoking habits) partially mediate the association between SES and all-cause and cancer-specific mortality. However, the magnitude of this mediation is highly sensitive to measurement strategies and study context. Future studies should adopt longitudinal and life-course designs with repeated measures of SES and lifestyle factors, and expand research to low- and middle-income countries to provide globally relevant evidence.

title: Incarceration, inclusion, and health equity: A global challenge
Corrigendum to “Why we need political values in epidemic modelling: parameters, populations, and public health policy goals” [Soc. Sci. Med. 404 (2026) 119532]
Birth cohort trends in activity limitation among U.S. adults in established adulthood: an intersectional approach to examine the effects of persistent inequality on health
abstract: This study uses an intersectional framework to evaluate age, period, and birth cohort trends in activity limitations among adults aged 30-45. We estimated cohort effects for activity limitation prevalence using cross-sectional data from the National Health Interview Survey between 1973 and 2016. We conducted an Age-Period-Cohort (APC) analysis using the median polish approach to calculate the prevalence ratios (PR) estimating birth cohort effects. We then calculated stratified estimates for Black and white women and men. The overall prevalence of activity limitations was higher in more recent birth cohorts than the earliest cohorts identified in the study. The cohort effect was 1.04 (95% CI:1.00, 1.07) for the 1979-1982 birth cohort and 1.04 (95% CI: 0.99-1.08) for the 1983-1986 birth cohort relative to referent 1943-1946 birth cohort. When stratified by race and gender, this cohort effect was only seen in White men. For Black men, significant cohort effects were pronounced in individuals born between the late 1940s and mid-1950s. There were no significant cohort effects for Black women or White women, however Black women had higher prevalence across time periods and age groups relative to White Women. Modeling race and gender separately obscures important differences in activity limitation trends across populations. Findings highlight the importance of an intersectional approach to understanding health inequities with respect to activity limitations, an outcome that reflects the interaction of health, the social environment, and structural ableism.

title: Caring for children with special healthcare needs and parent health in later life
abstract: Guided by the life-course perspective and the stress process model, this study examines the long-term health associations of parent caregiving for children with special healthcare needs. Using the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), we linked retrospective caregiving histories from the 2017 and 2019 Life History Mail Survey to later-life health outcomes from the 2020 core survey. The analytic sample included 7003 participants (parent caregivers: n = 185; other caregivers: n = 1469; non-caregivers: n = 5349). We examined caregiving group membership and, among parent caregivers, six caregiving characteristics: multiple care, start and end age of caregiving, number of episodes, accumulated duration, and concurrent caregiving. Compared with non-caregivers, parent caregivers reported more functional limitations and more depressive symptoms in later life, whereas other caregivers differed from non-caregivers only on functional limitations. In caregiver-only comparisons, parent caregivers continued to report more depressive symptoms than other caregivers but no longer differed on functional or cognitive health. Parent caregivers also began caregiving earlier, ended later, and accumulated nearly three times the caregiving duration of other caregivers. Among parent caregivers, our exploratory analysis showed that a later caregiving start age was associated with better cognitive health, whereas a later end age was associated with more functional limitations. The findings indicate that depressive symptoms are a distinctive later-life correlate of parent caregiving, while functional and cognitive health may be dependent on caregiving timing. The study underscores the need for prospective longitudinal research and targeted long-term support for parent caregivers of children with special healthcare needs.

title: Looking back and moving forward: Reflections on twenty editions of the international medical geography symposium and the state of the field
Navigating opioid overdose risks in a vulnerable social network
abstract: This study uses mixed methods social network analysis (MMSNA) to examine the concentration of opioid overdoses among highly vulnerable people embedded in an administrative proxy network in an overdose hot spot. Descriptive network analyses are used to understand the contours of individual and relational overdose risk in an administrative proxy network of people who use and sell opioids. Interviews with market participants are then used to understand the strategies used to mitigate individual risk of death. People who use and sell both develop interactional rules and cultural scripts as prophylactic measures that are tragically limited in preventing unwanted consequences from continued opioid use.

title: Soft skills as mediation competencies in digitally mediated healthcare
abstract: Digital transformation is reshaping healthcare delivery, with growing but uneven incorporation of artificial intelligence into clinical practice. While often framed in terms of efficiency, access, and performance optimization, less attention has been paid to its relational consequences for everyday professional work. Limited empirical insight exists into how healthcare professionals experience digitally mediated care and how soft skills are enacted, constrained, and sustained. This qualitative study examines how healthcare professionals conceptualize and experience soft skills in digitally mediated environments. Based on semi-structured interviews with 46 physicians, nurses, and emergency care professionals across hospitals, health maintenance organizations, and emergency medical services, the study analyzes how soft skills are enacted, what constrain their use, and how professionals learn and adapt over time. Data were collected in 2023-2024, transcribed verbatim, anonymized, and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. The findings identify four themes: (1) Digitally Driven Changes in Healthcare Practice; (2) Enacting Soft Skills in Digitally Mediated Healthcare; (3) The Compression Paradox: When Digital Efficiency Intensifies Relational Strain; and (4) Learning to Sustain Soft Skills - Adaptation, Reinforcement, and Professional Re-Skilling in Digitally Mediated Healthcare. Overall, the study shows that in digitally mediated healthcare, soft skills remain essential for maintaining trust, clarity, and relational care, while also being reconfigured by changing interactional conditions. The findings introduce interactional intensity and a compression paradox to explain how digital transformation reshapes relational work, making it more time-pressured, effortful, and context-dependent. By conceptualizing soft skills as mediation competencies, the study shows how abilities often treated as stable individual attributes are enacted and transformed in digitally mediated care. Their effective use depends on supportive organizational conditions and may erode without them. Rather than framing soft skills solely as trainable competencies, the study highlights their situated role under shifting organizational, interactional, and temporal demands in digitally mediated care.

title: Climate change experiences among women with psychiatric illness – a qualitative exploration of lived experiences and service needs
abstract: People with pre-existing psychiatric illnesses are recognized as a high-risk group in climate-health research, yet few qualitative studies explore their experiences. This study explored the gendered experiences of women with psychiatric illnesses in relation to climate stressors and identified the tailored supports they perceive as necessary to maintain their mental health and wellbeing. Between January and December 2025, 23 participants took part in four focus groups at an academic psychiatric hospital in Toronto, Canada. The study used a service-user-informed qualitative design in collaboration with people with lived experience, who contributed to developing the interview guide and interpreting the findings. Codebook analysis with an intersectional lens was applied to examine pathways linking climate stressors to mental health impacts and service needs in this under-studied population. Three main domains emerged: (1) mechanisms by which climate stressors exacerbate psychiatric symptoms, (2) how these impacts intersect with gendered roles and responsibilities, and (3) patient-identified priorities for climate-informed mental health interventions. Participants reported disrupted care, forced isolation, difficulties with medication adherence, strained communication with clinicians, and bidirectional interactions between physical and mental health. Women described reproductive guilt, caregiving burdens, reactivation of sexual trauma, and feelings of disempowerment. Participants identified actionable priorities, including accessible climate preparedness resources, clinician training, peer support spaces, and hospital-based programs fostering social connection and adaptive coping strategies. These findings reveal social and institutional pathways linking climate stressors to mental health risks, and provide guidance for gender-responsive, service-user-informed interventions to enhance resilience in the context of climate change.

title: The feminist care work in abortion funds
abstract: We contribute to the research on care work and emotion work through a focus on abortion fund workers in an abortion restrictive landscape. We utilize interview data collected from 23 abortion fund staff and volunteers serving Texans after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic and a subsequent Texas Executive Order that suspended abortion care for 30 days. We find that abortion restrictions led to increased workloads for abortion fund workers and more desperate situations for callers, which then necessitated fund workers to provide intensive emotional support to callers. This led some volunteers to experience burnt out, and staff described strategies to mitigate burnout, including delving into a community of care model for the workplace. These findings add to the literature on abortion funds, and on human services workers and emotion and care work, which is particularly timely in the current post-Dobbs landscape where abortion fund staff and volunteers are facing similar and new challenges.

title: Financial incentives and social messaging for repeat SARS-CoV-2 antibody testing among the underserved: A randomized trial
abstract: Financial incentives may influence health behavior beyond their expected monetary value, and their effectiveness may depend on how the behavior is framed. Behavioral theories of decision making suggest that individuals may value protection against small-stakes losses more than expected utility predicts, while theories of family-centered health behavior suggest that messages emphasizing benefits to family members may strengthen participation in preventive health activities. We tested these ideas in a 2×2 factorial randomized trial involving 625 households recruited from a Federally Qualified Health Center serving low-income Latino/Hispanic communities. Participants completed repeat SARS-CoV-2 antibody testing. The trial crossed two messaging strategies (Family vs. Personal) with two incentive structures (Loss Protection vs. Lottery) that offered equivalent expected monetary value. Family Messaging emphasized protecting one's family from COVID-19, whereas Personal Messaging emphasized protecting oneself. Loss Protection allowed participants to secure an at-risk reward through repeat testing, whereas the Lottery condition offered a chance of a large reward. Repeat testing was approximately 8 percentage points higher under Family Messaging and 7 percentage points higher under Loss Protection. Baseline trust in medical providers, financial barriers to vaccination, and risk aversion were associated with initial testing, whereas household characteristics were not associated with repeat testing. Incentive design may matter beyond expected monetary value and that framing health behaviors in terms of family welfare may increase participation in repeated healthy activities. Broadly, the results support behavioral theories emphasizing loss aversion, anticipated regret, and family-centered motivations, and suggest practical approaches for improving engagement in repeat health behaviors. CLINICALTRIALS.GOV REGISTRATION NUMBER:: NCT01901624.

title: Intersectional sampling in health research: A scoping review of approaches and structural constraints
abstract: BACKGROUND: Intersectionality, rooted in Black feminist praxis, holds that systems of power configure unique positions of disadvantage and privilege irreducible to single-axis analysis. Quantitative methods to estimate intersectional effects have advanced rapidly, but less attention has gone to a prior question: how samples are designed to make intersectional positions analytically visible. Prior systematic reviews have catalogued analytic methods without examining sampling as a distinct methodological object. METHODS: We conducted a scoping review following JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards, searching seven international and three regional databases (AJOL, LILACS, Global Index Medicus) from inception to February 2026, restricted to English-language publications. Screening used machine-assisted prioritization (ASReview); two reviewers conducted full-text screening, charting, and appraisal. FINDINGS: Of 51,154 records, ten studies (<0.02%) met inclusion criteria. All ten were conducted in the United States, United Kingdom, or Canada; none in low- or middle-income countries. This absence is consistent with prior reviews of the indexed, English-language methodological literature. We propose two provisional analytic instruments: a diagnostic framework (the Triad) and a four-category Taxonomy. Cross-cutting patterns included an implementation gap, a probability-intersection divide, a dimensional ceiling, and a recurring audit pattern. INTERPRETATION: Intersectional sampling in the indexed methodological literature remains rhetorical rather than operational. The Triad and Taxonomy are bounded starting tools, not global standards; their transnational application requires LMIC-led methodological reconstitution, not validation. We hypothesize five candidate mechanisms for the LMIC absence: infrastructure dependency, missing identity variables, digital access requirements, methodological hegemony in global health, and cell sparsity at population scale. These are to be tested empirically rather than treated as findings. Sampling designs that operationalize only marginalized positions are methodologically incomplete and should be reconsidered against intersectionality's bidirectional analytic of power.

title: Pesticide suicide as a relational structural event: linked lives, gendered kinship and reputational governance in rural China
abstract: Background Pesticide self-poisoning was a major cause of suicide in rural China. Although mortality has declined, little is known about how earlier suicide waves continue to shape bereaved families, kinship relations and village life decades later. Aims To examine how a past wave of pesticide suicides shaped linked lives, gendered kinship obligations and intergenerational inequality in rural China, and to theorise these deaths as relational structural events. Methods Between October 2024 and March 2025, we conducted a qualitative life-history case study in a Hunan village where multiple pesticide suicides occurred in the 1980s-1990s. After identifying all 12 known bereaved households in the relevant settlement, we interviewed 28 relatives and 7 key informants. Data were analysed using framework-informed thematic analysis, with life course theory as the primary framework. Results Pesticide suicide redirected linked rural lives through four mechanisms: role substitution and trajectory resequencing in schooling, labour and care; gendered moral accounting that allocated earning, caregiving, silence and blame across kin positions; reputational transmission through village memory, marriage screening and informal governance; and unequal repair through ritual containment, kin-based rescue, informal monitoring and reverse investment in children's education. Conclusion We develop a relational structural-event model showing how sudden, stigmatised death can become intergenerational inequality through linked lives, gendered kinship, reputational governance and uneven social repair. Public health postvention matters, but the primary contribution is to theorise how suicide loss is socially transmitted across kin and community life.

title: Indicator menus: Intentional reorientation in global maternal and neonatal health measurement
abstract: There is strong impetus for internationally standardized measurement for maternal and neonatal health (MNH) to facilitate global benchmarking and accountability. Recent funding cuts have sharpened debates about whose priorities should guide measurement and what role international-level actors should play. This qualitative study combined observations and 24 semi-structured interviews in 2023-2025 with experts across multilateral agencies, bilateral donors, academia, and philanthropic organizations to explore how global-level MNH measurement actors understand challenges of indicator standardization and prioritization amid shifting funding and governance dynamics. Our findings show a field grappling with an appetite for increasingly comprehensive measurement which has outpaced feasibility and local relevance. The expansion from mortality and coverage indicators to quality-of-care measurement represents progress to many, but has also generated indicator proliferation and 'overloaded plates'. Underlying this are deeper questions of purpose and power: global MNH measurement was widely perceived as designed primarily to serve upward accountability rather than local decision-making. Interviewees proposed indicator menu approaches - curated but selectable sets of indicators from which countries choose based on their own priorities and capacities - as a meaningful step towards contextualisation and flexibility, while acknowledging that menus alone do not alter the accountability architecture within which measurement operates. Funding disruptions exposed the structural fragility of donor-dependent measurement systems and were viewed with cautious optimism as a potential catalyst for reorientation. Substantive change, however, was seen as demanding more than redesigning indicator lists. It requires building local measurement capacity and centering people who produce and use data closest to the point of care.

title: Patients’ perceptions of suspected Lyme borreliosis in a non-endemic area: A qualitative study in French Guiana
abstract: Lyme borreliosis (LB) is the most frequently reported tick-borne disease in Europe, yet no autochthonous case has ever been confirmed in French Guiana (FG). Despite this, patients in FG sometimes attribute persistent, non-specific symptoms to the controversial entity named chronic Lyme borreliosis. This study explores how patients living in a non-endemic region construct and interpret their illness experiences, and how these interpretations shape their interactions with the healthcare system. We conducted a qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews with nine patients previously followed for suspected LB at Cayenne Hospital. Only two had a confirmed or possible LB acquired outside FG; the remaining seven showed no evidence of active or past infection. Thematic analysis revealed four major patterns. First, uncertainty surrounding unexplained symptoms led participants to seek coherent explanatory frameworks, with LB emerging as a meaningful interpretive narrative. Second, a strong epistemic tension was observed between patients lived experience and biomedical knowledge, often resulting in mistrust and perceptions of delegitimization. Third, participants engaged in autonomous diagnostic strategies, relying on online communities and lay expertise to reinterpret symptoms and question biomedical authority. Finally, patients described a state of liminality marked by chronic suffering, social consequences, and a strong desire for recognition and attentive care. Our findings highlight how diagnostic uncertainty, limited local expertise, and structural healthcare constraints contribute to the emergence and persistence of contested diagnoses in non-endemic regions. Beyond biomedical controversies, this study underscores the need for empathetic, rigorous, and dialogical care to restore trust and address the suffering of these patients.

title: Who cares? Exploring the socio-economic dynamics of informal caregiving trajectories in England
abstract: Informal care is a core component of England's long-term care system, yet demographic shifts and austerity threaten its sustainability. This study examines socio-demographic and structural factors shaping informal care trajectories, leveraging newly linked data from the ONS Longitudinal Study 2001-2021 and local-level datasets on adult social care expenditure, care home availability, and area-level deprivation. Guided by the Informal Care Model, we use logistic regression and Fairlie decomposition to analyse transitions into caregiving (n = 550,644) and repeated care (n = 85,500), focusing on care intensity, gender-specific patterns and temporal changes. Results showed that caregiving trajectories were primarily shaped by individual-level factors and barriers to care. Predictors of entering caregiving differed from those associated with intensive and sustained caregiving. Poorer health, lower educational attainment and non-homeownership showed limited associations with caregiving entry overall but were more strongly associated with intensive caregiving among those who became carers. Repeated caregiving was associated with poorer health and non-homeownership, while employment constrained both caregiving intensity and repeated caregiving. Gendered patterns diverged by 2011-2021; employment and poor health increasingly constrained women's transitions into caregiving, whereas poor health remained a positive predictor for men. While women initiated high-intensity care, men were more likely to report it at consecutive censuses. Decomposition analysis showed that changes in health and formal care infrastructure contributed most to the explained component of observed transitions, though much of the overall decline remained unexplained by observed characteristics. The findings highlight a growing inequality, as systemic constraints and demographic pressures concentrate intensive caregiving among the most vulnerable populations.

title: Between 'liquids' and 'Poisons': Sensory-Practical rationality within the social representations of pesticide risk among chilean farmworkers
abstract: Occupational pesticide exposure is a significant global health concern for agricultural workers, and research aimed at addressing it has long been shaped by the "knowledge deficit" framework, which dominates pesticide safety research and treats workers as rational actors who lack adequate information. This framing fails to account for how risk perceptions are socially organised, culturally reproduced, and structurally embedded within specific occupational contexts. This study applies Abric's Central Core Theory (CCT) of Social Representations to examine how 20 Chilean farmworkers in the Maule Region construct and organise their understanding of occupational pesticide exposure. Using open-ended interviews analysed through Rodríguez (2007) qualitative methodology, central and peripheral elements were identified across four representational domains: pesticide identity and risk, routes of exposure, prevention conditions, and health and environmental effects. The analysis suggests a coherent representational system organised around a paradoxical central core: pesticides are simultaneously objectified as "liquids", normalising their use as routine agricultural matter, and recognised as "poison," acknowledging their danger. The functional logic sustaining this paradox is characterised as sensory-practical rationality: risk is perceived, graded, and managed according to sensory detectability rather than toxicological magnitude, producing a stable pattern of conditional risk acceptance. Sensory cues structure how exposure routes are represented (visible oral and inhalation risk versus the invisible dermal hazard), anchor the hierarchy of health effects (from immediately witnessed poisoning to intergenerational malformation and cancer), and constrain the salience of environmental harm to what can be materially apprehended. This representational architecture is not a product of ignorance or cognitive error, but rather a culturally embedded and structurally reproduced form of lay expertise shaped by precarious labour conditions, limited regulatory enforcement, and export-market compliance pressures. The findings carry implications for how occupational health interventions are designed and how risk communication can engage invisible cumulative hazards beyond the limits of sensory-practical knowledge.

title: “We all agree” – or do we? Strategic participation in health echo chambers among mothers on Facebook
abstract: Access to health information and the "information environment" are now understood as social determinants of health. Correspondingly, researchers are increasingly concerned about the potential impacts of internet "echo chambers" - ideologically insular online spaces - on health beliefs and behavior. Understood as "health managers" for their families, mothers are a population of particular interest, yet little research has explored their experiences in online echo chambers. This manuscript draws on findings from an 18-month internet ethnographic study of ideologically-insular Facebook parenting groups - one "science-based", the other focused on "natural parenting". Through inductive analysis, I assert that the apparent ideological homogeneity of echo chambers is not a structural feature, but a side effect of mothers' strategic participation. Five categories capture mothers' strategic participation: (1) appreciating the echo chamber; (2) concealing differences to avoid rebuke; (3) plural membership; (4) hacking the algorithm; and (5) evolving participation. These findings reframe engagement with echo chambers as an active, intentional process, casting mothers as strategic architects of their health information environments. In this framework, mothers treat echo chambers as only one option among many in the broader information landscape. This study has implications for how researchers, clinicians, and health educators understand the relationship between parenting ideology, maternal health learning, and the evolving online information environment.

title: Retrospectively appraised life changes since the German reunification and health: gender-differentiated indirect associations via psychosocial resources
abstract: BACKGROUND: The German reunification (1989/1990) was a period of rapid socio-structural transformation, with heterogeneous consequences for work, finances, and personal life in East Germany. Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, this study examined whether retrospectively appraised changes since the reunification are associated with later-life health and whether psychosocial resources show gender-specific indirect associations. METHODS: Data came from a 2022 cross-sectional survey of 1,295 adults who lived in East Germany before and after reunification and were aged 16-64 in 1990. Multi-group structural equation models (men / women) estimated associations between perceived occupational, financial, and personal changes and current depressive symptoms and self-rated health status, including indirect associations via resilience, optimism, low pessimism, and social support. RESULTS: Perceived deteriorations were more consistently associated with poorer health than improvements with better health, especially for personal change. Occupational deterioration showed more consistent associations with poorer health and resources, particularly among men, whereas financial improvements were positively linked to resources among women. Personal deterioration was associated with lower resources and more depressive symptoms in both genders. Indirect association patterns varied by domain, gender, and outcome; pessimism showed the most consistent associations, particularly for depressive symptoms. CONCLUSION: Findings were consistent with COR theory in that retrospectively appraised deteriorations were more consistently associated with poorer current health than improvements were with better health. The cross-sectional and retrospective design limits causal interpretation, but the findings point to gender- and domain-specific resource-related association patterns after major social change.

title: Trends in sleep duration among U.S. population aged 15 Years and older, 2003–2024: A sociodemographic analysis of ATUS data
abstract: Background Healthy sleep is essential for physical health, cognitive function, and overall well-being, yet many U.S. participants do not achieve the recommended sleep duration. Sociodemographic disparities in sleep are well documented, but evidence on long-term population trends are mixed. This study updates national estimates by examining 2003-2024 trends in diary-reported sleep duration and assessing whether changes differed across key population subgroups. Methods We conducted a repeated cross-sectional analysis of American Time Use Survey (ATUS) data from 2003 to 2024, excluding 2020 due to COVID19, comprising approximately 239,930 person-days from individuals aged 15 years or older. Total daily sleep minutes were derived from 24-h time diaries. Survey-weighted linear regression models estimated changes in sleep duration overall and tested year-by-subgroup interactions across sex, age, race/ethnicity, education, income, marital status, and household caregiving responsibilities. Fully adjusted models controlled for all covariates. Results Average daily sleep duration increased significantly over the study period, rising from approximately 8 h 30 min in 2003 to 8 h 55 min in 2024. Unadjusted models estimated gains of 1.21 min per year (≈25 min total), while fully adjusted models estimated 1.73 min per year (≈36 min total). Improvements were seen across most groups, with no meaningful sex differences in trends and unadjusted age-related divergence was attenuated after adjustment. Racial/ethnic differences in unadjusted trends were largely explained by socioeconomic factors. Higher-income and higher-educated adults consistently slept less, although disparities narrowed modestly. Co-residence with an elderly household member was found associated with persistently shorter sleep. Conclusions Sleep duration increased modestly over time, but socioeconomic and caregiving-related disparities remain.

title: Are public preferences over health distributions guided by principles of distribution? A social choice experiment
abstract: Objectives Policymakers must decide how to distribute limited healthcare resources and may wish to draw upon public preferences to identify whom to prioritise. However, little is known about the reasons underlying these preferences. The aim of this study is to examine public preferences over health distributions and the extent to which the reasons underlying them reflect one of the following principles of distribution: equality , need , responsibility , or efficiency . Methods In an online experiment administered among members of the general public in the United Kingdom, respondents (n = 648) distributed resources to determine the health of hypothetical recipients identified by sex, income or smoking-status. They provided the main reason for their choices in an open text response, and we classified their responses into one of the four principles. We used multinomial logistic regression models to examine the relationship between the preferences and principles. Results The majority of respondents gave equal priority to male and female recipients (83.9%) and low- and high-income recipients (52.8%). Those who prioritised, distributed more resources for health to low-income recipients (40.2%) and non-smoking recipients (69.3%). The most prominent principles were equality for sex, equality and need for income, and responsibility for smoking-status. These principles were strongly and significantly associated with preferences over health distributions ( R 2 > 0.34), and explained more variation in preferences than socio-demographic characteristics ( R 2 < 0.06). Conclusions These findings can inform health policy and policy messaging regarding the distribution of healthcare resources and increase their legitimacy.

title: Empowerment or exclusion? Exploring perspectives on health data sharing through the lens of marginalisation and inequality
abstract: There has been growing emphasis on the need to enable and make use of electronic healthcare records for research and to improve health services. Alongside this, there has been raised awareness of digital (and broader) health inequalities in the UK context. This paper explores perspectives towards health data sharing amongst marginalised groups, addressing a research gap in which previous research has not been inclusive of such groups. There is a lack of theoretically informed research exploring perspectives of such communities, which negates underlying inequities and institutional disadvantage to be un-earthed analytically. We present findings from a co-produced qualitative research project with marginalised groups in the Greater Manchester (UK) region. We explore the perspectives of 58 individuals regarding different contexts for health data sharing, including data shared in relation to direct personal healthcare, and where shared for research purposes. We use a critical approach to explore how intersectional disadvantage shapes views towards data sharing. The findings indicate that participant perspectives reflect embedded structural and institutionalised power dynamics as part of existing inequalities in health and care. Perspectives were nuanced and complex in framing data sharing as potentially empowering or disempowering depending on the context and purpose of data sharing and in relation to intersectional disadvantage. The critical approach drawn on here makes visible a contextualised understanding of perspectives towards health data sharing which illustrate (via lived experience) that socially situated vulnerabilities risk compounding institutionalised inequalities and multiple forms of disadvantage.

title: Corrigendum to “The habitus of care: Overdose normalization, reversal expertise, and the invisible moral labor of people who use drugs” [Soc. Sci. Med. 405 (2026) 119560]
Corrigendum to “Life course socio-economic effects in later life cognitive functioning by cohort, gender and origin” [Soc. Sci. Med. August 2026 119333 402]
Immigration enforcement as structural exposure: Provider moral distress in U.S. health and social care—An integrative review
abstract: Immigration enforcement shapes access to and quality of U.S. health and social services, positioning frontline providers as mediators between care and immigration control. Although a growing body of empirical work documents provider experiences of ethical conflict and moral distress in immigration policy-affected settings, this literature has not been synthesized in relation to the policy, legal, and institutional ecology of U.S. immigration enforcement. Following Whittemore and Knafl (2005) and PRISMA 2020, we conducted a comprehensive database search for U.S.-based studies on provider experiences in settings serving immigrant populations or under immigration enforcement; 25 studies (20 qualitative or qualitative-adjacent, 5 quantitative cross-sectional or mixed-methods; 2012-2025) were included. Thematic synthesis used deductive coding anchored to structural vulnerability and ethics of care frameworks, extended inductively to capture provider perceived policy-to-practice mechanisms. Three interlocking themes explain how policy becomes practice and why distress follows: the moral landscape, in which providers report encountering preventable suffering and dual-loyalty tensions that accumulate as moral residue; policy as intervention, wherein enforcement-linked rules reconfigure triage and documentation, shifting providers into gatekeeping roles and narrowing clinical discretion; and institutional mediation, whereby organizations variably buffer provider exposure through sanctuary protocols, legal consultation, and protected debriefing, and where those buffers are absent, ad hoc workarounds substitute. Immigration enforcement operates as structural exposure producing patterned moral distress; durable change requires decoupling enforcement from care settings, status-neutral access, and institutional levers including information-protection policies, legal consultation pathways, and protected debriefing.

title: The management of daily topics in conversations with individuals with Alzheimer's disease in Chinese residential care
abstract: Background Individuals with Alzheimer's Disease (AD) often experience difficulties managing topics in daily interactions, which can hinder their participation in interactions and affect their social engagement. There is a gap in exploring the interactional dynamics and the maintenance of personhood when interacting with individuals with AD in asymmetric institutional settings. Objectives This study aims to examine the interactional competence of individuals with AD and how their vulnerabilities are managed in daily-topic interactions within institutional healthcare settings. Methods This study adopts Conversation Analysis (CA) to examine video-recorded conversations between a trained researcher and individuals with mild cognitive impairment due to AD residing in two residential care facilities in China. Findings Individuals with mild AD demonstrate agency within asymmetric interactions by reshaping conversational frames, preserving face, and situating themselves within relational contexts to maintain their personhood. This agency emerges only when interlocutors actively engage, providing validation and recognition while accommodating temporary incoherence. These findings underscore the collaborative nature of sustaining identity in dementia care and highlight the particular significance of such interactional practices within the Chinese cultural context. Implications Conversation partners can support agency in individuals with AD by ratifying frame reconfigurations, sustaining topics, acknowledging repetitions, and responding flexibly to disengagement. Care facilities are also expected to create more opportunities for residents to engage in casual conversation.

title: Income inequalities in cardiovascular health among children and adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in Canada: A nationwide trend analysis, 2007-2019
abstract: While socioeconomic inequalities in cardiovascular health are well-documented among older adults, evidence in younger populations is limited. This study assessed income inequalities in cardiovascular health among children and adolescents (6-17 years), young adults (18-39 years), and middle-aged adults (40-64 years) in Canada from 2007 to 2019. This serial cross-sectional study included 25,538 respondents from six biennial cycles of the nationally representative Canadian Health Measures Survey. Equivalized annual household income quartiles were used to measure socioeconomic position. Sub-optimal cardiovascular health was defined as the presence of obesity, hypertension, diabetes, or dyslipidemia, based on age-specific biomarker thresholds and medication use. Relative and absolute income inequalities in cardiovascular health were quantified using the relative index of inequality (RII) and slope index of inequality (SII), estimated using age group- and sex-stratified generalized linear models (RII>1 and SII>0 indicate pro-rich inequality). The prevalence of sub-optimal cardiovascular health decreased from 2007 to 2019 for children and adolescents (23.0%-17.1%, p trend <0.01), but remained stable for young (28.4%-27.0%, p trend =0.44) and middle-aged adults (55.4%-54.6%, p trend =0.88). Among children and adolescents, income inequalities in cardiovascular health increased over time (RIIs=1.39-3.60, p trend =0.01; SIIs=0.08-0.22, p trend =0.03), with trends more pronounced in males (RIIs=1.10-4.63, p trend <0.01; SIIs=0.02-0.29, p trend =0.01) than females (RIIs=1.85-2.47, p trend =0.27; SIIs=0.13-0.13, p trend =0.42). Income inequalities in cardiovascular health were present in young and middle-aged adults, with no significant temporal trends but divergent patterns by sex, decreasing in females and increasing in males. While cardiovascular health improved over time among children and adolescents in Canada from 2007 to 2019, persistent and widening income inequalities in cardiovascular health were evident during this period.

title: Decentralising health management: Heterogenous effects on health behaviours and health outcomes
abstract: Many countries have implemented decentralisation reforms to address efficiency and equity concerns in health management. Most evidence on their impact focuses on average health outcomes and provides mixed results. We examine effects of administrative decentralisation of population health management on health behaviours in Greater Manchester, England, in 2016. Using data on 26,773 adult respondents to the UK Household Longitudinal Study between 2009 and 2020, we use a generalized random forests framework to examine how the effects of the decentralisation vary across individuals. We find that decentralisation was associated with reductions in smoking, alcohol misuse, and poor diet, but had no impact on physical inactivity. Individuals with higher socioeconomic status and better health and well-being before decentralisation experienced the largest beneficial impacts. Lifestyle improvements following decentralisation were unequally distributed, suggesting that more targeted interventions are needed for more disadvantaged groups.

title: Trust strategies in healthcare: A cross-disciplinary scoping review of quantitatively studied approaches to building, maintaining, and repairing trust
abstract: Trust is foundational to the functioning of health systems and public health initiatives, yet it is increasingly strained by misinformation, politicization, and persistent structural inequities. Although multiple disciplines have examined how trust is built, maintained, and repaired, evidence remains fragmented and often lacks sufficient specification to support comparison or practical application. We conducted a scoping review to map empirically examined trust-related strategies across disciplines and to clarify how these strategies are articulated in actionable terms. We searched seven databases from inception to March 15, 2024, and included experimental, quasi-experimental, and observational studies assessing trust-related strategies. Screening and data extraction were completed in duplicate. Strategies were coded using the Action, Actor, Context, Target, Time (AACTT) framework and categorized by trust phase (building, maintaining, repairing). A reproducible, human-verified Python workflow supported data standardization and thematic clustering. Across 327 studies, we identified 1017 strategy instances (919 unique) spanning disciplines including psychology, sociology, political science, economics, technology, and healthcare. Strategies clustered into 14 themes, most commonly values-based approaches, structural assurances, transparency and disclosure, humanizing framings, and interpersonal communication. Strategies were predominantly enacted by individual actors within institutional contexts and primarily targeted individual trustors, with limited emphasis on structural or post-violation repair interventions. Overall, findings highlight the dominance of relational and informational strategies alongside structural safeguards, while underscoring gaps in institutional-level approaches. This review advances an interdisciplinary, action-oriented understanding of trust, offering a foundation for developing more explicit, evaluable, and contextually responsive trust-building strategies in health and social systems.

title: Residential context and epigenetic age acceleration among older-age black and white Americans: Findings from the health and retirement study, 2010-2016
abstract: This study examines whether residential contexts account for Black-White disparities in epigenetic age acceleration (EAA), a key biomarker of premature aging. Relevant hypotheses are tested by merging survey, biomarker, and contextual data from non-Hispanic Black and White older-adult participants of the Health and Retirement Study who provided venous blood samples in 2016 (n = 3187; mean age = 69). Using multigroup structural equation modeling techniques, we decompose direct and indirect paths between a latent variable of EAA-comprised of GrimAge, PhenoAge, and DunedinPoAm38 clocks-and five features of residential contexts: racial clustering of residents, air pollution, greenspace, household incomes, and perceived disorder. We find that White respondents who lived in areas with a high clustering of other White residents in 2010 exhibit lower EAA in 2016, relative to White peers who lived in areas with fewer White residents. Higher household incomes in predominantly White areas account for around 25% of this association. With one minor exception, we find no significant paths between residential contexts and EAA among Black participants. These findings are also robust to numerous control measures and sensitivity analyses. Our study highlights concentrated privilege in predominantly White areas as potential drivers of Black-White health and aging disparities. We discuss the broader implications of our study and outline several avenues for future research that could advance our findings.

title: Platformed care, platformed harm: how social media function as conditional informal infrastructure across eating disorder trajectories among young people in China
abstract: Eating disorders (EDs) among young people in China are rising amid service barriers and stigma, prompting many to rely on social media for interpretation, support, and coping. While existing research often treats social media's influence as static "mixed effects", we reconceptualize social media as conditional informal infrastructure and explore how this infrastructure interacts with users' offline structural scaffolding to shape divergent illness trajectories. We conducted qualitative interviews with 21 young people with EDs, including 5 "dual-role" peer supporters, focusing on their experiences with algorithm-driven platforms (e.g., Xiaohongshu) and super-apps (e.g., WeChat). Through abductive analysis, we identified three analytical segments: (S1) early naming to make distress legible, (S2) constrained navigation for coping resources, and (S3) recovery work to maintain daily routines. Beyond baseline individual traits, outcomes at three critical breakpoints were conditionally shaped by an interactive hierarchy of users' offline scaffolding, including life stressors, social support, stigma, and service barriers. When offline scaffolding was robust, users could bypass digital reliance entirely, or social media facilitated illness validation (S1), routing to bounded support (S2), recovery routine integration and reciprocal care labor (S3). Conversely, when offline scaffolding failed, users relied on symptom-escalation instructions and misleading severity benchmarks (S1), became digitally dependent (S2), and faced recovery scrutiny and systemic overload (S3), triggering stagnation or relapse loops. Overall, platformed care and harm emerge as processual outcomes of offline conditions. Meaningful intervention requires moving beyond content moderation alone to repairing the offline structural deficits that drive young people into digital dependency.

title: Patient trust in community-based interventions versus health-facility care: an economic experiment in Cameroon
abstract: Trust in patient-provider relationships is central to healthcare utilisation in health facilities, but also in community-based interventions, particularly in contexts embedded within weak health systems. Neglected tropical disease (NTD) control programmes rely heavily on community-based mass drug administration (MDA) to reach over one billion individuals worldwide each year. However, empirical evidence on behavioural trust in any community-based interventions remains limited, especially in sub-Saharan Africa. We measured trust across two healthcare settings in Cameroon: health facilities and community-based MDA for schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminthiases (STH). In 2024, we conducted a cross-sectional mixed-methods study in Bafia health district among households seeking care at health facilities (n = 117) and those eligible for community MDA (n = 109). Subjects completed (i) patient surveys, including the Trust in Physician Scale, (ii) trust games, and (iii) provider knowledge surveys administered to 17 health-facility and 11 community-based providers. Multivariate regression models identified trust determinants. Behavioural trust was high across settings (mean = $1.14; p = 0.99). However, self-reported trust was significantly higher in health facilities (mean = 43/55) than community-based (mean = 38/55; p < 0.01). Provider communication - greeting (β = 1.70; SE = 0.48), eye contact (β = 1.62; SE = 0.46) - and key sociodemographic characteristics, such as isolation (β = -1.88; SE = 0.34), ethnicity (β = -1.39; SE = 0.68), strongly predicted self-reported trust, whereas behavioural trust was primarily associated with socioeconomic status. Providers in both settings demonstrated high trustworthiness, but health-facility providers showed greater disease knowledge. This study provides the first behavioural evidence of trust in a community-based health intervention. Lower self-reported trust in community-based interventions highlights the importance of strengthening provider training and communication to enhance programme effectiveness and support progress toward NTD elimination.

title: Diets, politics, and camel economies: a qualitative One Health study of zoonotic disease risk in pastoralist regions of eastern Ethiopia
abstract: One Health research on the social, behavioral, and political factors that drive zoonotic disease risk are often limited in conflict-affected and politically insecure locations, and within informal and extralegal economies. This study therefore examines zoonotic disease risk in eastern Ethiopia, where conflict, political insecurity, and forced displacement are prevalent, where pastoralist economies are mostly informal or extralegal, and where camels are central to diets, health practices, and livelihoods. Using multi-sited qualitative data collection between 2021 and 2024, we examined camel herding, transit, trade, care and slaughter, as well as the production and consumption of various camel products including milk. We found that humans and camels in eastern Ethiopia lived and moved in close proximity, and unpasteurized milk remained a staple food and common medicinal product. Slaughtering, grazing, herding, trading and exporting of camels involved mobility and frequent multispecies interactions including with wildlife. Camels were often sold in informal or extralegal markets, and camel dairy products were also typically processed, sold, and consumed outside of regulated markets, licensed facilities, and disease surveillance mechanisms. Internal conflicts, political insecurity, and displacement throughout eastern Ethiopia increased livestock grazing and travel within national parks, wildlife preserves, and remote trails and secondary roads in wilderness areas-potentially also increasing multispecies interactions. Qualitative research including ethnographic data collection helped us examine unexpected contexts where multispecies interactions occurred, as well as the specific policy changes and conflict dynamics that potentially shape zoonotic disease risk. Long-term ethnographic engagement also helped build trust with interlocutors and therein explore politically sensitive and extralegal dynamics.
