METHODS: Using content analysis of contracts, we examined 663 clauses from 42 multi-year contracts between Dutch hospitals and health insurers initiated in 2017, 2018, and 2019. RESULTS: The analysis shows that contract clauses cluster into distinct groups. Clauses with a control function and a prevention frame dominate in operational and technical sections of contracts such as financial arrangements, dispute resolution, and monitoring. By contrast, coordination- and promotion-oriented clauses are more prevalent in collaborative sections, including shared objectives and operational coordination. At the contract level, variation is observed across health insurers in how these clauses are combined. Some contracts show a relatively balanced mix of contractual and relational elements, while others rely predominantly on control- and prevention-oriented clauses. CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate that clauses supporting both contractual and relational governance coexist within the same contract, albeit to varying degrees across health insurers, contracts, and contractual domains. The observed variation suggests differences in strategic orientation, contracting capabilities, and market position rather than a single optimal contracting model.

title: Early career health shocks and long-run labour market outcomes
abstract: The economic literature on health shocks and labour market outcomes largely focuses on acute health shocks at older ages, leaving limited evidence on long-term labour-market consequences. By examining the consequences of incident hospital-diagnosed back disorders among early-career workers, this study addresses that gap in the literature. We link population-wide Danish administrative registers (1996-2017) to follow a cohort of 157,692 individuals who were aged 28-31 in 2006. We apply a staggered difference-in-differences design, to identify the impact on both earnings (productivity) and disposable income (financial burden). We find persistent adverse effects: eight years post-diagnosis, annual earnings have declined by 8% for men and 13% for women relative to the controls. We document a distinct gender divergence in the mechanisms driving these losses. While men primarily adjust through the intensive margin (temporary reduction in hours) and stabilize over time, women face a progressive decline driven by labour market exit (extensive margin). Although the Danish welfare system acts as a significant buffer, compensating for 55-65% of earnings losses, a substantial private financial burden persists. These findings suggest that early-career back disorder shocks initiate long-term trajectories of cumulative disadvantage, particularly for women.

title: Labor pain relief and women's evaluations of childbearing: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in China
abstract: As governments respond to fertility decline with pronatalist policies centered on economic and childcare support, childbirth itself remains undertheorized as an embodied and gendered experience. This study contributes to fertility research and maternal health scholarship by documenting unmet demand for labor pain relief in China and examining how access to pain management shapes women's evaluations of whether conditions are favorable for having a child. We draw on an original study of 2866 women of reproductive age that combines a conjoint experiment with survey questions on childbirth experiences and attitudes. To our knowledge, this is the first large-sample study to examine labor pain relief and evaluations of childbearing conditions together. We estimate the causal effects of epidural access and family support for its use alongside commonly studied factors such as household income and childcare support. Results show substantial unmet demand: most respondents regard childbirth pain as important for fertility decision-making, yet nearly half of those with recent vaginal delivery experience did not receive epidural analgesia during labor. Experimental results further suggest that, compared with sometimes-available access, always-available epidural access improves these evaluations by approximately 70% of the effect of receiving childcare support, while family support for epidural use increases these evaluations by an amount comparable to that of moving from sufficient to comfortable household income. These findings underscore the importance of integrating maternal health and childbirth experiences into theories of fertility decision-making and reproductive policy debates.

title: Parental education and children's old-age mortality: Evidence using college expansions
abstract: This paper examines the intergenerational effects of parental college education on children's old-age mortality, focusing on health benefits flowing from parents to children. We utilize historical data of college expansions in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, employ Social Security Administration death records linked with the full count 1940 census, and implement a difference-in-difference approach to exploit parental cross-cohort variations in exposure combined with spatial and temporal expansions in colleges. We document that parental exposure to new college openings during adolescence is associated with significant increases in children's later life old age longevity, with treatment-on-treated effects ranging from 4.2 to 15.4 months. Heterogeneity analyses uncover dynamic complementarities with educational policies whereby the effects of parental exposure to college expansions amplify in states with more stringent compulsory schooling and child labor laws. Furthermore, we provide evidence of improvements in parental education, income, and socioeconomic status, along with significant increases in children's education as key mechanism channels. Monetizing the implied gains in children's life expectancy using standard value-of-statistical-life estimates suggests aggregate benefits on the order of $6-8 billion per additional college opening.

title: Firearm violence and racial capitalism: A conceptual framework for understanding the persistence and prevalence of gun violence in the United States
abstract: Firearm violence is a leading cause of death in the United States and is marked by profound racial and socioeconomic disparities. Existing research has identified many of the conditions that make interpersonal firearm violence more likely, and intervention research shows that firearm regulation, targeted policing, and community-based programs can reduce harm. Yet firearm violence remains high, persistent, and unequally distributed. This article develops a racial capitalism framework to explain that persistence. Building on structural racism approaches, it asks how the conditions associated with firearm violence are linked to accumulation, extraction, and profit. Drawing on a structured database of 395 citations, the article situates research on segregation, economic precarity, illicit markets, firearm availability, policing, and community intervention within a broader political-economic system. It shows how labor market exclusion, housing extraction, informal economies, firearm production and circulation, and state harm management jointly produce conditions in which violence becomes more likely and more lethal. In this account, firearm violence is not simply an unintended consequence of inequality. It is a predictable feature of systems that make insecurity profitable while concentrating harm in racially marginalized communities. The framework extends public health research and policy by directing greater attention to the political-economic arrangements that reproduce violence.

title: The lasting association between interrupted medical care during US immigration detention and mental health outcomes
abstract: Detained immigrants with chronic health conditions face heightened exposure to health-harming conditions, including interrupted medical care for chronic conditions, with potentially long-lasting health consequences, including for mental health. Drawing on a unique longitudinal referral sample of 192 individuals with chronic conditions released from US immigration detention between 2020 and 2021 and followed through 2023, we find that 42% experienced interrupted medical care during detention. We then use longitudinal multivariable random-effects regression to examine the relationship between interrupted medical care while in detention and long-term psychological distress. We find that psychological distress decreases over time after release among those with and without medical care interruptions, but remains elevated when benchmarked against the US general population, even three years following release. We also find that those who experienced interrupted medical care during detention had higher and more persistent distress, even after adjusting for socio-demographic characteristics, prior health status, and post-detention conditions. Building on scholarship on the stress process within carceral settings and on organizations as sites of stratification, we conceptualize immigration detention as a stratifying institution that may shape health trajectories in durable ways. Our findings suggest that interrupted medical care in detention is not just a temporary hardship, but an organizational feature that contributes to enduring mental health inequities that can extend well beyond the period of confinement.

title: Socioeconomic adversity and child health following the COVID-19 pandemic: A convergent integrated mixed-methods review of household and neighbourhood inequalities
abstract: Children experience inequalities in health at household and neighbourhood level, even in wealthy countries. Measures to contain the COVID-19 pandemic such as school closures, followed by the cost-of-living crisis, did not affect all children equally. This review aimed to understand the impact of socioeconomic adversity on child health and development following the COVID-19 pandemic. Systematic literature searches used the SPIDER tool to identify studies, and a convergent integrated approach to combine and synthesise quantitative and qualitative data. A mixed methods appraisal tool was used to appraise for risk of bias. Three integrated findings were identified from 125 studies: 1. Socioeconomic adversity and unequal exposure to risk; 2. Community support and professional input as protective influences. 3. Structural and system-level requirements to address socioeconomic adversity. COVID-19 restriction measures were associated with worsening family finances and health of disadvantaged children who experienced cramped living conditions and insecure food and housing. COVID-19 amplified existing health inequalities. These inequalities could potentially be reduced through public health interventions such as improved availability of community services, greater consideration of sociodemographic factors in healthcare settings, and by professionals using their collective voice to influence policy development, for example through improved data sharing to help public-sector services make the best use of available data to support vulnerable families.

title: Impact of housing improvements on childhood hospitalization rates in a large cohort of low-income families in New Zealand
abstract: The global burden of disease arising from exposure to inadequate housing is a significant public health concern. In New Zealand over 25,000 children are hospitalized annually with preventable housing-related conditions, with Māori and Pacific children particularly at risk. The Healthy Homes Initiative (HHI) is a community-led, government-funded, multicomponent intervention aimed at improving health outcomes for children at risk of housing-related illness in low-income families. In this study, we examined hospitalizations for children enrolled in the HHI between 2014 and 2023. Using Poisson regression, we show that the HHI was associated with a 29% five-year reduction in childhood hospitalizations, equal to approximately 2,817 hospitalizations or 16,027 hospitalizations per 100,000 people. Community-led interventions such as the HHI are an effective mechanism to address housing as a social determinant of health. When given sustained government support, they have the potential to make a significant impact on health outcomes and contribute to the wider public good.

title: Ecologies of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) transmission across One Health interfaces: Waste, food and changing metabolic relations in rural China
abstract: Within the One Health framework applied to global health issues including antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and zoonoses, ecological linkages between animals, wastes, soil, water, and humans are increasingly being interpreted through the lens of pathogenic transmission. This framing problematises waste practices and cross-species contact in many parts of the Global South, where rural livelihoods are often closely integrated with farm animals and organic materials. In this study, we use metabolic relations as an analytical tool to understand One Health linkages in AMR ecologies, moving beyond transmission pathways. We examine the entangled and often ambivalent relationships surrounding waste, food and environmental health in rural China, where interactions involving these elements are associated with both wellness and harm. Drawing on ethnographic research into everyday agricultural practices and waste management, we explore the tensions between positioning organic wastes as hazardous and metabolic dependencies on them for livelihoods. We show how co-existing governance imperatives for separation and circulation in waste treatment bring into focus the collision between long-standing integrated farming practices and the hazardous inputs of industrial farming. We further illuminate the lived experiences of ambivalent metabolic relations, wherein local communities are caught between material dependencies on subsistence agriculture and exposure to potential toxic fallout from urban-oriented commercial production. We argue that One Health responses to antimicrobial resistance must transcend a narrow focus on hygiene and biosecurity to engage with the latent political-economic configurations of uneven exposure.

title: Paternalism, parsed. Presenting empirical insights into the actions of physicians under the Austrian law on assisted dying
abstract: RATIONALE: In all jurisdictions with laws standardising the process of assisted dying, physicians play a key role. That they do is a concern in the academic literature, with critics accusing physicians of medical paternalism, particularly in relation to their role in assessing requests for assisted dying. OBJECTIVE: By exploring how physicians handle medical assessments under the 2022 Austrian Dying Decree Act, we aim to add empirical insights to the overly theoretical debate on medical paternalism in the context of assisted dying. METHOD: After employing a maximum-variation sampling strategy, we conducted episodic interviews with 16 assessors recruited among 51 preselected physicians. Thematic analysis was used to interpret the interview data. RESULTS: When conducting assessments, it was crucial to physicians that they could relate to the request and empathise to the extent of imagining making the same choice if they found themselves in the requester's circumstances. They did not support requests that they could not relate to, even when the requester met the legal access criteria for assisted suicide. They did so for self-protective reasons. CONCLUSION: Criticising the practice of assessing requests for assisted dying through the lens of paternalism leads to oversimplifying the real-world complexities of the matter. Denying or shaming physicians for considering self-interested motives in their assessment practice will not make them disappear.

title: Structural threat as a theoretical driver of trans health inequities
abstract: Transgender and nonbinary (trans) people in the United States are increasingly exposed to structural conditions that undermine their safety, belonging, and inclusion. Existing theoretical frameworks focus on how anti-trans stigma and discrimination impact health, but structural drivers of trans health inequities remain undertheorized. This paper introduces Structural Threat to explain how cultural, legal, administrative, and institutional systems destabilize and withdraw social safety and protection for trans communities. Structural threat places trans people in a constant state of uncertainty, driving health inequities via weathering processes. We situate Structural Threat within established frameworks of the structural production of health inequities, including Fundamental Cause Theory and social determinants of health frameworks. Our analysis attends to how intersectional structural oppression shapes both exposure to structural threat and its health consequences with disproportionate effects for trans people of color. Conclusions highlight implications for research, policy, and practice that promote safety, belonging, and inclusion to reduce trans health inequities.

title: Gamete selection in gay male surrogacy: Procreative labor beyond gestation
abstract: This article examines gamete selection as a central yet understudied dimension of procreative labor in gay male surrogacy. Drawing on a qualitative study of French intended fathers pursuing transnational surrogacy in Colombia, it analyzes how choices regarding sperm and oocyte donors constitute a form of emotional, reflexive and politically situated labor that extends beyond gestation. While reproductive labor has traditionally been theorized through women's embodied work of pregnancy and care, this article mobilizes and empirically extends the concept of procreative labor to account for reproductive practices that are non-gestational, male, and technologically mediated. The findings show that gamete selection involves intensive reflexive work through which intended fathers negotiate equality within the couple, manage genetic asymmetries, anticipate social stigma, and articulate moral responsibilities toward egg donors. These choices are shaped by biomedical constraints, legal frameworks, and market logics, but also by emotional and ethical considerations, including efforts to recognize and symbolically compensate women's procreative labor in contexts where donor bodies are structurally anonymized and commodified. At the same time, strategies aimed at protecting children from discrimination often reproduce racialized and gendered hierarchies embedded in reproductive markets. By focusing on a triply specific configuration-same-sex male couples, non-compensable genetic choices, and the absence of pregnancy-this article highlights how procreative labor operates as a site where structural inequalities are both made visible and re-enacted through individual decision-making. Without presupposing procreative labor as an analytical framework, the study demonstrates its empirical relevance while extending it to include reflexive, emotional, and political dimensions that remain underexplored in existing scholarship.

title: Changes in health inequalities before and after a major urban greenway intervention: Evidence from a 6-year follow-up in the UK
abstract: BACKGROUND: Evidence concerning health inequalities following urban green and blue space UGBS) interventions is limited. This study examined the changes in health inequalities after a major urban regeneration project, the Connswater Community Greenway (CCG), in Belfast, UK. METHOD: Cross-sectional household surveys were conducted in 2010/11 (baseline), 2017/18 (immediately after completion), and 2023/24 (long-term follow-up) with a sample of approximately 1000 adults each wave. Using concentration indices (CI), income-related health inequalities for three outcomes (physical activity, mental wellbeing and quality of life) were measured. A regression-based decomposition of concentration index examined the contribution of sociodemographic factors to the observed inequalities underpinning each outcome over time. RESULTS: Across three waves, there was widening of inequalities over the 15-year period across all three health outcomes, with those from high-income groups reported higher levels of physical activity (CI = 0.33, SE = 0.026), better mental wellbeing (CI = 0.03, SE = 0.003), and better quality of life (CI = 0.09, SE = 0.008). The widening inequalities mainly occurred during the construction phase of CCG (2010-2017) and remained stable post-intervention (2017-2023). Decomposition analysis revealed that the pro-poor concentration of long-term illness and unemployment was the key driver that together explained approximately 51%-76% of the inequalities. CONCLUSION: The CCG was limited in reducing health inequalities which were mainly driven by long-term illness and unemployment - factors beyond the direct scope of the UGBS intervention - resulting in low-income groups likely to fall further behind the wealthier groups. The widening of inequality is consistent with findings from other public interventions that did not have a primary equity focus.

title: Effects of primary care visits on preventing chronic conditions and avoiding hospital care in the context of China's health system reform: a nationwide panel study
abstract: Background Primary care is widely recognised as essential for the prevention and management of chronic conditions and has been a major focus of China's health system reform. However, evidence on its effects remains mixed. This study examined whether primary care visits was associated with preventing the development of additional chronic conditions that are considered preventable or manageable in primary care, and with reducing hospital outpatient and inpatient care utilisation among people already living with these conditions. Methods We used data on 11,425 individuals across four survey waves between 2011 and 2018 from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. We estimated the effects of primary care visits using the individual fixed-effect model with inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting to account for selection bias. Results An additional primary care visit was associated with a lower number of additional chronic conditions acquired in the following wave (-0.011, 95% CI: -0.017 to -0.004). This association was stronger among urban residents (-0.016, 95% CI: -0.027 to -0.005), respondents with at least primary school education (-0.014, 95% CI: -0.024 to -0.003), and those with a single chronic condition (-0.018, 95% CI: -0.034 to -0.002). By contrast, among individuals with at least one such chronic condition, primary care visits were not significantly associated with hospital outpatient visits (-0.010, 95% CI: -0.029 to 0.009) or inpatient admissions (0.010, 95% CI: -0.020 to 0.040). Conclusion In China, among adults aged 45 years and older, greater primary care use may help prevent the development of additional chronic conditions, but it does not appear to reduce short-term hospital use among people with existing conditions. Primary care strengthening may therefore contribute more to long-term chronic disease prevention than to immediate reductions in hospital utilisation. Further reforms should focus not only on increasing use, but also on improving the quality and targeting of primary care.

title: The impact of fiscal food policies on the macro-economy: The case of the UK soft drinks industry levy
abstract: The UK government announced the 'Soft Drinks Industry Levy' (SDIL), a tiered tax on sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs), in 2016 and implemented the tax in 2018. Traditional economic assessments of SSB tax interventions focus on assessing healthcare cost implications using standard Cost-of-Illness methodology. No studies have so far attempted to apply macroeconomic assessment methods to assess net macroeconomic impacts of SSB taxes, including anticipated standard tax-efficiency losses and macroeconomic gains from reduced diet-related illness, or to assess trade-offs between macroeconomic and health outcomes. We established a novel framework consisting of a dynamically-recursive sectoral macroeconomic Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model of the UK economy linked to the nutrition-focused multi-state lifetable PRIMEtime epidemiological model, and applied this framework to estimate the future macroeconomic impacts of the SDIL, and trade-offs with future health gains, over 2018-2040. Overall, the SDIL is estimated to lead to future health gains of 86,951 Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) saved, and health-related macroeconomic gains of £2.49bn, including £1.33bn due to shifting consumer demand exposures, and £1.15bn due to SSB product reformulation. Due to additional tax-efficiency losses, the SDIL is estimated to result in a limited overall cumulative real GDP cost of £2.01bn (0.004%), and in an SDIL cost-effectiveness ratio of £23,116 per DALY saved, which suggests that the SDIL is cost-effective. Since product reformulation accounts for 46.2% of macroeconomic gains and makes up for 25.6% of overall tax-efficiency losses, this demonstrates the importance of SSB tax schemes to incentivize product reformulation to ensure that they maximize health impacts and cost-effectiveness.

title: Targeting therapies: Analysing the social and normative dimensions of ‘targeted’ approaches to biomedicine and public health
abstract: Today, much in biomedicine and public health seems to involve the 'targeting' of therapies. By this, we mean that multiple forms of biomedical and public health praxis are aimed at discovering and delivering increasingly specific therapeutic modalities to individuals and populations. This includes varieties of medicine that have variously been termed 'personalised', 'precise', or 'stratified'. It also entails public health approaches that purposely or otherwise eschew such characterisations, but which nevertheless involve and propel congruent logics. The praxis of targeting by its very nature of course impacts therapies - including what the 'the therapeutic' per se might be taken to be. Importantly, it also actively shapes what diseases are or become, how knowledge about them is produced, and who is (not) able to access (what kinds of) care. Targeted therapies are thus not simply more precise medical or public health tools: they are sociotechnical interventions which simultaneously reconfigure markets, access, normativities, patient subjectivities, and disease ontologies. Metaphors, idioms, and imagery associated with targeting permeate many national and transnational healthcare and innovation ecosystems. The ubiquity and import of targeted therapies demand wider social scientific scrutiny that must ultimately cut across case studies and contexts.

title: When uncertainty becomes guilt: The moralisation of home urinary stoma care after bladder cancer surgery in China
abstract: In post-discharge urinary stoma care, family members are often expected not only to perform technical tasks but also to interpret bodily problems and decide when professional help is needed. Existing research has documented caregiver burden, distress, and psychological strain extensively, but less is known about how guilt is produced through family relationships, uncertainty, and moral expectations of care. This study examines how informal caregivers of bladder cancer patients with urinary stomas in China described guilt, self-blame, and uncertainty in home care, and under what conditions uncertainty became morally charged or remained primarily practical. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 21 family caregivers recruited through a tertiary hospital and analysed using framework analysis, the findings show that caregivers framed urinary stoma care as a moral responsibility tied to protecting the patient's comfort, dignity, and family role. Ordinary care difficulties, including leakage, skin irritation, delayed response, pouch insecurity, and symptom appraisal, became consequential when caregivers interpreted them as evidence of inadequate care. This moralisation was patterned by kinship position and constrained availability, but it was not inevitable. In some accounts, uncertainty remained closer to practical troubleshooting, especially when caregivers had access to professional guidance, reassurance from patients or family members, and direct explanations or follow-up communication from healthcare professionals. The study contributes to research on informal caregiving, uncertainty, moral experience, and home-based care by identifying the relational and interpretive conditions under which caregiver guilt emerged. Supporting family caregivers may therefore require interpretive support that clarifies the boundaries of reasonable family responsibility.

title: The environmental racism index: Estimating the strength of association among environmental risk/benefit, mortgage lending disinvestment, and racial/ethnic density across US geographies
abstract: Although environmental racism is a fundamental cause of health inequities, measurements in the US are lacking. In this paper, we developed an area-based, scalable Environmental Racism Index (ERI) to measure the strength of the associations among neighborhood environmental quality, mortgage lending disinvestment, and racial/ethnic density across US geographies. The ERI was estimated for both Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs) and states using 2015-2019 Census data, Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data, and various environmental databases. The associations between ERI and racial/ethnic mortality rates and rate ratios were examined at the MSA level. Findings illustrate substantial variations in environmental racism across the US, with MSAs in the Midwest and Northeast particularly severe. The ERI is positively associated with non-Hispanic (NH) White, NH Black, and Black mortality rates, as well as NH Black and Black to NH White mortality rate ratios at the MSA level. The ERI can be adapted for other geographic settings, time periods, and geographic scales to reveal patterns of environmental racism, measure its impacts on health inequities, and guide environmental and public health policy interventions to address these inequities.

title: Adult temporal mobility (2002-2010) in material wealth and physical health, self-perceived health, sociality, and use of addictive substances: Insights from an observational exploratory panel study among Tsimane’ Indigenous People in the Bolivian Amazon
abstract: Changes in relative socioeconomic rank during adulthood (intragenerational mobility) are increasingly recognized as important determinants of health and other well-being indicators. Quantitative studies in high-income countries find that mobility in rank generally correlates with these outcomes, but the direction and mechanisms remain unclear. Evidence from small-scale societies is scarcer due to limited panel data. We examine the correlation between mobility and well-being indicators among 350 Tsimane' adults (age≥16y: women = 184; men = 166) in the Bolivian Amazon, using nine consecutive years of panel data (2002-2010). Guided by four theories (dissociation [any mobility harms], socialization [people adapt to any new rank], "falling from grace" [extreme downward mobility harms], and set-point ["effects" are temporary]) we assess how changes in quintile rank of material wealth correlate with four aspects of well-being in 2010: physical health, perceived health, sociality, and use of addictive substances. Results showed partial support for each theory and revealed that upward and downward mobility each correlated with a mix of favorable (e.g., lower likelihood of being overweight, greater food satisfaction) and unfavorable (e.g., increased anger) indicators. Importantly, mobility was not associated with most outcomes, lending support to set-point theory and highlighting that any mobility could correlate with tradeoffs in health and other well-being indicators. In sum, as in high-income countries, our findings reveal heterogeneity and ambiguities, and the need for a new theory that acknowledges the simultaneous gains and losses that correlate with socioeconomic mobility.

title: How is family functioning associated with depressive symptoms among women living with HIV in China? Findings from a 4-year longitudinal study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Women living with HIV (WLWH) experience often poorer mental health. Family plays a central role in Chinese society and family influence would be particularly salient for Chinese WLWH. Current literature predominantly focuses on how family influences on mental health. Little is known about how mental health affects family functioning, and specifically, this reciprocal dynamic within this population. AIMS: To examine the reciprocal relationship between family functioning and depressive symptoms among Chinese WLWH over a 4-year period. METHODS: A three-wave longitudinal study was conducted among Chinese WLWH, at baseline, 2-year, and 4-year follow-up. Data were collected via individual face-to-face interviews, using structured questionnaires. Cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) was performed in data analysis. RESULTS: A total of 382 participants (Mean age: 36.77 years) were included at baseline; 379 (99.2%) and 372 (97.4%) completed the 2-year and 4-year follow-ups, respectively. Bivariate correlations indicated that family functioning and depressive symptoms were significantly and negatively correlated at each wave. Results from CLPMs revealed a consistent unidirectional relationship: higher family functioning at both baseline and the 2-year follow-up significantly predicted reduced depressive symptoms at the subsequent time point (β = -0.13, p < .05) among WLWH. Conversely, neither depression at baseline nor 2-year follow-up were significant in predicting subsequent family functioning. CONCLUSION: The findings highlight the protective role of family functioning in reducing depressive symptoms among Chinese WLWH over time, suggesting that family support can serve as a buffer against depression. The development of tailored family-based interventions to enhance family dynamics is strongly warranted for this population.

title: Obituary: Robert J. Earickson (1934 -2026)
Treading a fine line in equitable breastfeeding support: balancing breastfeeding promotion while avoiding pressure to breastfeed – a realist evaluation
abstract: Background Breastfeeding support is most effective when delivered face-to-face, yet professionals must balance tensions between promotion, maternal autonomy, and rapport across diverse families. The contextual mechanisms shaping this support, particularly motherhood norms, remain underexplored. Drawing on cultural health capital theory, this study unfolds the relational dynamics of breastfeeding support, exploring how health visitors in a Danish breastfeeding intervention balanced adherence to professional recommendations without provoking feelings of breastfeeding pressure equitably among mothers in different socioeconomic positions. Methods Applying a realist evaluation approach, data consisted of 35 home visit observations, 6 focus groups with 34 health visitors and 16 individual interviews with mothers. This study was part of a comprehensive evaluation of the Danish Breastfeeding - a good start together intervention. Results In seeking to promote breastfeeding in line with professional recommendations while avoiding pressure on mothers in lower socioeconomic positions, health visitors sometimes undermined their support by downplaying their expertise. Health visitors' reticence in offering explicit breastfeeding support - intended to protect mothers from feeling pressured - was perceived by mothers as a lack of support and professionalism. Conclusion In breastfeeding support, professionals' efforts to avoid pressure and reliance on tacit assumptions about families' feeding decisions may reduce proactive support and reinforce breastfeeding inequities. This highlights the need for professional reflexivity in a field often marked by guilt and shame.

title: Mandated supporting, not reporting: Reimagining maternal health care for women who use drugs
abstract: This study examines how carceral logics shape maternal healthcare for pregnant women who use drugs. Through qualitative interviews with 21 women and 14 providers in Florida, we explore how punitive surveillance, via mandatory reporting and child welfare investigations, disrupts prenatal care and exacerbates stigma. We find that actual and anticipated involvement of child welfare services (CWS) inadvertently operates as an extension of poverty governance. Participants described deep fear of CWS, particularly newborn removal, as a central reason for avoiding prenatal care. Many reported dehumanizing clinical encounters shaped by stigma. To overcome structural barriers, women identified the need for trauma-informed, nonjudgmental care models, including expanded access to medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD), harm reduction services, peer service navigation, and parenting support. Providers echoed these calls and critiqued abstinence-oriented mandates. Instead, "mandated supporting", a relational, harm reduction-based approach, emerged as an alternative to punitive reporting. The study demonstrates how punitive state policies, while well-intended, exacerbate trauma, disrupt recovery, and intensify health inequities. Findings underscore how reproductive justice frameworks can inform more compassionate and effective responses to maternal substance use.

title: HIV medication adherence in the migration and settlement journey: Experiences and perspectives of migrant women living with HIV
abstract: Medication adherence is the cornerstone of HIV care and management and involves taking HIV medication as prescribed. Though barriers to adherence are well-documented, little research to date has examined the everyday experiences of medication adherence of people living with HIV. As migrant women living with HIV (mWLWH) are disproportionately impacted by HIV in Canada, it is pertinent to better understand their unique experiences of medication adherence. This study examined the processes by which mWLWH engage with medication adherence and how these processes are influenced by their socio-structural context throughout their migration and settlement experiences. In this interpretive description study, we draw on 1) semi-structured interviews with mWLWH (n = 10) and service providers (n = 14) as a primary data sources, and 2) document review as a secondary data source. Through reflexive thematic analysis, we constructed four themes: 1) The context of everyday and long-term work of medication adherence; 2) Demonstrating medication adherence to prove you are not a threat nor a burden; 3) Anticipating future barriers to medication adherence in Canada by stockpiling HIV medications; and 4) Managing medication adherence in the context of housing insecurity. Overall, we demonstrate how mWLWH manage their everyday experiences of medication adherence, while navigating the complexities of migration and settlement. Further, our findings demonstrate that HIV remains a complex health condition, where medication adherence is highly regulated and scrutinized.

title: Compounding stigma: An experimental study comparing perceptions of an individual using Ozempic, bariatric surgery, or behavior modification
abstract: Weight loss is a billion-dollar industry; methods of weight loss influence weight stigma and person perception. Prior research suggests individuals undergoing bariatric surgery face compounding prejudice from both their physical condition and the surgery itself. Bariatric surgery is often viewed as “taking the easy way out.” Emerging evidence reveals similar sentiments regarding weight loss drugs. To date, no research has directly tested whether attitudes about a person differ if they underwent bariatric surgery compared to weight loss drugs. Thus, the present study empirically tests whether perceptions of a person vary as a function of their chosen weight loss strategy. A sample of 297 participants (78.8% women, M age = 20.2, 42.4% BMI > 25.0 kg/m 2 ) were randomly assigned to view one of three vignettes describing a woman (“Alex”) who lost weight (and then regained it later) through either bariatric surgery, a common weight loss medication (i.e., Ozempic), or behavioral modification (i.e., diet/exercise alone). Participants were presented questionnaires regarding their beliefs/attitudes toward Alex, weight, and weight loss strategies. Results demonstrate that Alex was viewed more negatively and assumed to be less healthy if she lost weight through Ozempic compared to diet and exercise alone. There were no differences if Alex lost weight through bariatric surgery compared to the other methods. Further, it was clear participants underestimate the prevalence of weight regain and misjudge the efficacy of various weight management strategies. This work highlights the need for empirically informed information on body weight in public health and mitigation strategies for weight stigma.

title: The biopolitics of “previving”: Femininity, labor, and reproduction
abstract: "Previvors"-individuals who develop an identity around cancer-related genetic mutations they carry and come together in biosocial community-challenge conventional notions of illness by inhabiting a unique pre-diagnosis space. This study seeks to understand how previvors navigate their new biomedicalized identities and their relationships to gender, family, and reproduction while they undergo genetic testing, counseling, and preventative surgeries. By analyzing 41 semi-structured in-depth interviews with previvors, we explore their liminal pre-disease status. Gendered labor, reproductive imperatives, and care strategies are discussed in relation to previvors' experiences with family planning and prophylactic treatment. Critically engaging with broader healthcare and socioeconomic disparities that impact previvors' lives, this study amplifies previvors' voices-while simultaneously considering how this biopolitical population is shaped by stratified reproduction, technologized regimes for self-optimization, and white women's wellness cultures under neoliberalism.

title: Understanding how green space accessibility and utilisation relate to common mental health difficulties: A cross-sectional study in North West England
abstract: Green space exposure is associated with better mental health, but the independent contributions of accessibility and utilisation, and whether utilisation mediates the effects of accessibility and mental health, remain unclear. The objectives of this study were to (i) quantify the independent associations of green space accessibility and utilisation with common mental health difficulties (CMD) prevalence; (ii) test whether utilisation mediates the effect of accessibility; and (iii) investigate whether accessibility and utilisation moderate one another's associations with CMD. We integrated novel small-area anonymised mobile phone data, high-resolution environmental metrics, and primary care records for 2.6 million people across Cheshire and Merseyside, England to quantify these pathways in 2024. Results showed that accessibility and utilisation were independently associated with lower CMD prevalence. Residential tree exposure showed the most consistent association among accessibility measures (RR = 0.936), while walking time in green space showed the strongest association among utilisation measures (RR = 0.900). Mediation analyses provided no evidence that utilisation mediated the association between accessibility and CMD. However, moderation models identified a compensatory interaction, whereby associations between active green space engagement and lower CMD prevalence were strongest in areas with poorer environmental access. Our findings demonstrate that accessibility and utilisation have distinct but interacting associations with population mental health, supporting urban policies that promote both locally accessible green environments and opportunities for their active use.

title: Silence beneath the surface: Examining intersectional sexual violence among Asian immigrant women
abstract: Asian women experience high levels of sexual violence, yet are less likely to disclose or formally report compared to any other racial/ethnic group. The objective of this study is to examine the intersectional factors that contribute to sexual violence and silence among Asian immigrant women. Guided by intersectionality and using community-based participatory research methods, we conducted 62 life history interviews with Chinese, Korean, Indian, and Filipino immigrant women in Los Angeles, California and Atlanta, Georgia of varying legal statuses. This study fills important gaps in the literature by examining how silence surrounding sexual violence is produced, maintained, and reinforced through intersecting factors among Asian immigrants. The study found that silence regarding sexual violence was produced by: 1) childhood experience of violence and migration; 2) learning silence through early socialization; 3) gendered norms; and 4) normalization of sexual violence. Once participants disclosed to family, friends, or formally reported, silence was often maintained and reinforced through: 1) familial encouragement to maintain silence; 2) inadequate healthcare systems; and 3) inadequate institutional response. Our findings suggest that sexual violence was extremely common, even normalized, yet only a small fraction disclosed to anyone, and an even smaller number formally reported the incident to authorities. Healthcare and policy implications are discussed including the need for immigration-informed care, trauma-informed education and safe reporting mechanisms.

title: Temporal aspects of walking in the neighbourhood for people living with dementia
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: A supportive neighbourhood environment can play an important role in fostering people with dementia in their independent mobility, everyday functioning, and social participation. Their lived experiences of walking in the neighbourhood can provide contextualised knowledge and understanding, which can inform policies and programs to support people with dementia to remain active, engaged and age in their homes and communities. This paper focuses on exploring the temporal aspects of the walking experiences of people with dementia in neighbourhoods and their strategies and approaches regarding the challenges and issues encountered. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: This study adopted qualitative methods with 26 participants in Metro Vancouver, Canada. Each participant with dementia (or dyad with care partner) took part in four interview sessions guided by multiple data collection methods: semi-structured sit-down interviews and walk-along interviews with concurrent photo and video documentation. Data analysis was conducted using reflexive thematic data analysis. RESULTS: Four themes were generated: 1) Recognizing Age Related Changes, 2) The Changed Reality of Walking while living with Dementia, 3) Social Changes in the Neighbourhood, and 4) Walking as Connecting with the Past. DISCUSSION AND IMPLICATIONS: The findings illustrate the processes in which the participants enacted physical and cognitive strategies to address the cognitive and functional changes taking place over time in their journey of living with dementia. Additionally, they demonstrate the value of recognition and association of places in the neighbourhood that contribute to a sense of belonging and comfort in the community.

title: Structural stigma and intersectional inequality in schizophrenia: A systematic review and qualitative meta-synthesis
abstract: Schizophrenia is unequally distributed across social hierarchies and is associated with stratified pathways of care, coercion, and recovery. Although stigma has been widely studied, existing scholarship has predominantly emphasized interpersonal attitudes and individual behavior, leaving structural stigma embedded in policy regimes, institutional practices, and epistemic hierarchies insufficiently synthesized. Guided by PRISMA 2020, this systematic review and qualitative meta-synthesis examined 29 sources, comprising 17 core empirical studies and 12 contextual or theoretical sources, addressing schizophrenia or psychosis in relation to at least one additional marginalized social position. Five overlapping structural mechanisms were identified: economic/policy exclusion; spatial/environmental marginalization; institutional care inequities/cultural unsafety; coercive/carceral pathways; and epistemic injustice/diagnostic bias. Across settings, these mechanisms interacted to shape access to services, pathways into care, the credibility accorded to lived experience, autonomy, and opportunities for recovery. Their effects were most pronounced where schizophrenia-related stigma intersected with racialization, socioeconomic disadvantage, migration status, homelessness, sexual or gender minority status, Indigenous identity, criminal justice involvement, or HIV-related vulnerability. The findings support conceptualizing structural stigma as an upstream determinant of inequality in schizophrenia, operating through both material resource allocation and symbolic recognition within mental health systems. Reducing these inequalities requires coordinated, intersectionality-informed reform across policy, institutional, community, and epistemic domains rather than relying solely on individual-level interventions.

title: Retraction notice to “Masculinity under pressure: How gender norms shape men's mental health help-seeking in the post-pandemic era” [Soc. Sci. Med. 404 (2026) 119468]
Plain language in healthcare interpreting. Reflections from interpreter-mediated consultations
abstract: Current models of care emphasise patient participation, which depends on patients' understanding of specialised medical knowledge and their ability to navigate complex healthcare systems. In this context, plain language has been promoted to enhance comprehension, but it has been mainly examined in written communication and its role in interpreter-mediated healthcare interactions remains underexplored. This study addresses this gap by analysing healthcare interpreting practices through the lens of plain language, conceptualised here as a form of epistemic mediation within structurally unequal healthcare systems. Drawing on 101 interpreter-mediated consultations collected in 2017 in a hospital in Madrid (Spain) and analysed through a secondary qualitative approach, 106 interpreter interventions were identified and classified using thematic analysis. As a result, we identified four interrelated categories that shape how medical knowledge is communicated and understood in interaction: making specialised knowledge accessible, managing information and epistemic boundaries, negotiating understanding, and reconfiguring meaning across sociocultural frameworks. Although these practices may enhance patient understanding and support navigation across institutional and sociocultural contexts, they also raise questions concerning accuracy, professional boundaries and paternalism. Therefore, the study reveals the tension between promoting accessibility and maintaining precision, and between supporting patients respectfully and enabling their autonomy within asymmetrical healthcare encounters. In light of these findings, the study proposes understanding healthcare interpreting as an epistemic process through which specialised knowledge is negotiated, redistributed and, at times, transformed.

title: Physical and sensory disabilities and displacement: A systematic review
abstract: In this paper, we provide the first systematic scoping review of English-language research on physical and sensory-related disabilities amongst displaced people of all age groups around the globe. While disability and displacement individually generate distinctive social, health, and accessibility challenges, their confluence can compound these challenges and heighten vulnerability in ways that have not received adequate scholarly attention. Following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, our systematic scoping review summarizes peer-reviewed literature - encompassing empirical and theoretical approaches, but excluding meta-analyses and reviews - on the intersection of disability and displacement, takes stock of current research findings, identifies persistent gaps in knowledge as well as biases and blind spots in the research, and provides systematic data analysis on some of the core questions that have animated the field. Our analysis finds a sharp increase in research on the conjunction of displacement and disability over the last decade. However, such work remains largely siloed within disciplinary boundaries and inordinately focused on South-North migration patterns and resettled refugees, limiting the scope of the field and our understanding of more common migration statuses and displacement patterns. We call for future research to traverse disciplinary divides, center the experiences of affected individuals, and investigate more fully the causal impact of physical and sensory disabilities on migratory mobility.

title: Navigating a syndemic: Caregiving, dual identities, and child-headed households in rural Lesotho
abstract: Child-headed households (CHHs) have become a salient feature of family life in parts of Southern Africa where HIV/AIDS, poverty, labour migration, and, more recently, COVID-19 have interacted to produce a syndemic that has eroded adult caregiving capacity. These intersecting structural pressures have contributed to sustained orphanhood, household instability, and the reorganisation of caregiving responsibilities within families. This article examines how children in CHHs in rural Lesotho navigate the intersecting effects of HIV/AIDS and COVID-19, negotiate caregiving responsibilities, and construct dual identities as both students and household heads. The study was conducted in Mafeteng district, Lesotho, and draws on qualitative data generated between March and June 2023 from 28 participants aged 12-18 years, with an analytical focus on 20 children in primary caregiving roles. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, participant diaries, non-participant observation, and participatory visual methods, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings demonstrate that resilience and vulnerability coexist within CHHs and caution against romanticising children's coping capacities in contexts of structural neglect. By adopting a syndemic lens, the article argues that overlapping epidemics do not merely intensify vulnerability but actively reorganise family systems and reshape childhood. The study underscores the need for coordinated social protection, education, and child-welfare responses that recognise children's agency without relying on it as a substitute for institutional responsibility, while addressing the structural conditions that compel them to assume adult caregiving roles.

title: What is (not) distinct about asylum seekers’ violence exposures? New insights from a novel network-based survey
abstract: Violence is a substantial public health concern because it can portend both immediate and longer-term physical and mental health consequences. To date, most research assessing migrants' violence exposures before migrating has focused on asylum-seekers or refugees alone, leaving open important questions about exposures among those who leave violent contexts but do not seek these statuses. To that end, we conducted a network-based survey to recruit a novel sample of migrants in need of international protection (MNP) in Costa Rica (N = 400) who migrated away from the same countries in the same years but only some of whom applied for asylum. This study offers one of the first accounts of (dis)similarities in the amount and types of pre-migration violence exposures between those who sought asylum and those who did not. Results reveal three key takeaways: (1) the majority of both groups report violence exposures the year before migrating, although the probability is higher among asylum-seekers; (2) differences between asylum-seekers and non-are concentrated among select demographic groups, especially women, young adults, and the least educated; and (3) asylum-seekers are more likely to report primary victimization, greater numbers of perpetrators and persecution types, and victimization by political actors than are non-asylum-seekers. Focusing on asylum-seekers alone thus likely underestimates the size of violence-affected migrant populations and heterogeneity within them. Our findings underscore the importance of screening for violence among all migrants who left violent contexts, regardless of immigration status, and of applying more inclusive sampling methods to extend our scientific lens beyond asylum-seekers alone.

title: Normative values for paid and unpaid work productivity for estimating productivity-adjusted life expectancy in Finland
abstract: BACKGROUND: Normative regional estimates of productivity are essential for deriving reliable predictions of productivity-adjusted life expectancy (PALE). This study aimed to establish Finnish population norms for health-related productivity by estimating age- and sex-specific norms for paid and unpaid work productivity indices, as well as combined weighted productivity index. Using national life expectancy data, corresponding PALE values were also estimated. METHODS: Data were derived from a digital survey of a geographically and demographically representative sample of the Finnish adult population aged 18-79 years between June and August 2024 (n = 3644). Population-level productivity indices were estimated using the WPAI General Health Questionnaire for five-year age groups by sex with values ranging from 0 (completely unproductive) to 1 (completely productive). PALEs were estimated by multiplying weighted productivity indices with life expectancy estimates obtained from the Statistics Finland. Undiscounted, 1.5% and 3% discounted PALEs were produced. RESULTS: The weighted productivity index for the total population was 0.770 (male 0.780; female 0.760). At age 20, PALE for males was 42.9 years (undiscounted), 29.3 years (1.5% discount), and 21.3 years (3% discount). For female, corresponding PALE values were 46.1 years (undiscounted), 30.4 years (1.5% discount), and 21.6 years (3% discount). CONCLUSIONS: This study provides the first population-level normative estimates of health-related productivity in Finland, covering both paid and unpaid work. These norms offer an important benchmark for burden-of-disease analyses and support evaluation of productivity impacts across demographic subgroups. Continued refinement is warranted as more detailed data on unpaid work and productivity losses become available.

title: Association between early-life food insecurity and depressive symptom trajectories in middle-aged and older adults: The mediating role of educational attainment
abstract: Background While the long-term impact of childhood adversity on mental health in middle and old age is receiving increasing attention, the association between food insecurity at different early-life stages and the dynamic trajectories of depressive symptoms remains unclear. The potential mediating role of educational attainment in this relationship also warrants investigation. Methods Utilizing data from the nationally representative China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), this study included 4546 participants aged 45 and above with complete information. Based on retrospective data, early-life food insecurity was categorized into distinct periods: Early Childhood (0-5 years), Middle Childhood (6-12 years), Adolescence (13-17 years), and Multiple periods. Group-based trajectory modeling was employed to identify developmental trajectories of depressive symptoms from 2011 to 2020. A counterfactual framework-based mediation model was used to analyze the mediating effect of educational attainment. Stratified analyses were conducted by gender and residence. Results Five distinct depressive symptom trajectories were identified. Early-life food insecurity, particularly exposure during Middle Childhood (OR range: 1.34-2.03) and Multiple periods (OR range: 1.51-2.81), significantly increased the risk of belonging to non-stable, high-risk depressive trajectories. Mediation analysis revealed that educational attainment played a significant mediating role in the association between food insecurity during Middle Childhood, Adolescence, Multiple periods, and the risk of adverse depressive trajectories. The indirect effect values were 0.009, 0.007, and 0.010, accounting for 9.83%, 10.82%, and 7.14% of the total effect, respectively. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested that these associations were more pronounced among females and rural residents. Conclusion Early-life food insecurity, especially during middle childhood or across multiple developmental periods, was associated with less favorable depressive symptom trajectories in later life. Education explained only a modest share of these associations, suggesting multiple life-course pathways linking childhood deprivation to later-life mental health.

title: From crisis to cuffs: The impacts of police involvement in mental health emergencies among racialized children, youth, and families in Toronto
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Evaluation of mental health emergency response is primarily police informed. Whether service users feel supported by police-based crisis interventions is overlooked. OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study is to explore the impact of policing on racialized children, youth, and families during mental health emergencies. METHODS: Through detailed narratives and testimonies from 11 racialized service users, the harms of police involvement in mental health emergencies are uncovered. Intervention experiences and help-seeking behaviours were discussed. Participants shared their impressions of police knowledge on mental health, racial bias, and effectiveness in reducing symptoms. RESULTS: Four themes were developed: (1) Incongruity of involving police in mental health crisis response, (2) Intersectional biases of police, (3) Criminalization of children and youth, and (4) Replacing control with collective care in mental health response systems. CONCLUSION: The consensus among racialized service users was that police response to mental health crises is unhelpful and deters them from seeking future assistance. They advocated for community-led support for mental health emergencies.

title: From exposure to composition: Market and household adjustments under Singapore's mandatory nutri-grade labeling policy
abstract: Mandatory front-of-pack (FOP) labeling influences diets through consumer substitution, firm portfolio responses, and pricing. This study examined the market and household purchase implications of Singapore's Nutri-Grade (NG) policy - mandatory graded FOP label for pre-packaged beverages (A = most healthy to D = least healthy), analyzing market adjustments and household purchase composition around its implementation. Using representative household scanner data, we constructed a product-month panel to estimate difference-in-differences models of purchase volume and price for products classified as NG C/D versus A/B. We assessed supply-side responses using Poisson models of product entry/exit and decomposed market-level nutrient density changes into reformulation, entry/exit, and consumer switching. Finally, household fixed-effects interrupted time-series models evaluated nutrient density changes relative to counterfactual trends. Post-policy, the differential changes in purchase volume and price for NG C/D relative to A/B were statistically insignificant. However, new-product introductions shifted strongly toward NG A/B and product discontinuation rates did not differ between NG C/D and A/B. Decomposition indicated that market-level nutrient density improvements were driven predominantly by product entry and exit rather than consumer switching or reformulation. In contrast, household purchase-weighted sugar and energy density increased relative to counterfactual trends, while purchase-weighted Nutri-Score, a measure of the overall nutritional quality of beverages, improved. These findings highlight that mandatory graded labelling reshapes beverage markets primarily through firm portfolio adjustments rather than immediate consumer substitution. Notably, reductions in total sugar exposure at the household level need not coincide with improvements in the nutrient density of the household purchase basket, underscoring the importance of jointly tracking both exposure and composition metrics in evaluating the nutritional impact of FOP labelling policies.

title: Using a fire-horse cohort to estimate mortality associated with dual inheritance stress
abstract: Dual Inheritance theory posits that persons reaching reproductive age must allocate their time, energy, and resources, at least temporarily, to either producing offspring or attaining social status. Ill health (including mortality) is hypothesized to arise from the stress induced by striving to reconcile these competing imperatives. Using data from the Human Mortality Database, we test predictions made by dual inheritance theory for population health. Our test exploits the 1966 episode of the Japanese superstition that stigmatizes women born in "Fire-Horse" years. This superstition reduced not only births by 25% in 1966 but also the marriage prospects of women born in that year. We applied Box-Jenkins time-series modeling to data describing mortality in 50 Japanese birth cohorts (i.e., 1945 through 1994) to test the hypothesis that sex specific death rates at ages 20-24 and 25-29 for both sexes of the 1966 cohort would exceed those expected from rates exhibited by cohorts born before and after. Contrary to the dual inheritance hypothesis, the 1966 cohort exhibited lower than expected mortality at ages 20-24 and 25-29 for both sexes. Our findings suggest that the socioeconomic advantages of being born into a small cohort may buffer the pathogenic effects of dual inheritance stress. These findings should improve forecasts of the health effects of strategies societies can choose from to influence, and adapt to, the ongoing decline in fertility in much of the developed world.

title: Corrigendum to “Educational inequalities are associated with distinct metabolomic and gut microbiome patterns in adults” [Soc. Sci. Med. 403 (2026) 119454]
Artificial intelligence in population breast cancer screening: A two-year cost-effectiveness analysis
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To investigate the cost-effectiveness of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into breast cancer screening in Australia. METHODS: Standard screening practice (independent assessment of mammograms by two radiologists, with a third resolving discordance) was compared with three AI-human screen reading strategies: 1)Integrated (one radiologist and AI independently assess mammograms, with a second radiologist for discordance); 2)Triage Single (AI classifies mammograms as 'low-risk' or 'not low-risk' before human review, with standard reading for 'not low-risk' mammograms, single-radiologist reading for 'low-risk' mammograms); and 3)Triage Only (AI used to classify mammograms as 'low-risk' or 'not low-risk', standard reading for 'not low-risk' mammograms, no human reading for 'low-risk' mammograms). A two-year decision-analytic model was developed using a retrospective cohort of 108,970 mammograms from Australian women aged 50-74 (2015-2016). The model incorporated cancer detection and recall outcomes from an Australian health system perspective. Deterministic one-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses assessed uncertainty. Scenario analyses incorporated cancer detection and recall estimates from a prospective randomized controlled trial to explore how base-case results may differ using an alternative screening workflow. RESULTS: In the base-case analysis, Triage Only was the most efficient strategy, saving an average of $4 per person screened but detecting 0.521 fewer cancers per 1000 people screened compared to standard practice (ICER $8206 per additional cancer detected). Integrated and Triage Single were dominated. Sensitivity analyses indicated Triage Only is unlikely to be cost-effective (cost-effective in <1% of simulations). Scenario analyses showed AI-supported screening was more effective, though more costly, than standard practice (ICER $1123 per additional cancer detected) and may be cost-effective. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings highlight that potential efficiency gains from AI may not necessarily translate into cost-effectiveness in breast cancer screening. Prospective evaluation incorporating real-world AI-assisted screening workflow and longer-term patient outcomes will be critical to determining the value of AI in population breast screening programs.

title: Neighborhood amenities, health services, and built infrastructure and epigenetic aging
abstract: BACKGROUND: Epigenetic aging has been proposed as an important biological pathway linking neighborhood environments to health. Yet, few studies have examined the effect of neighborhood resources on epigenetic aging. To fill this gap, this study aims to examine the effects of neighborhood amenities, health services, and built infrastructure on epigenetic aging. METHODS: Data were from 3786 participants in the Health and Retirement Study 2016 Venus Blood Study. Epigenetic aging was determined using Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge2, and DunedinPACE, which were linked to 13 Census-tract indicators reflecting the availability of local amenities, health services, and built infrastructure from the National Neighborhood Data Archive. RESULTS: Greater availability of amenities, health services, and built infrastructure was associated with slower epigenetic age acceleration, though these relationships were significant only for Horvath and Hannum clocks. These associations were largely similar across sex, race, and ethnicity. In addition, built infrastructure was indirectly associated with slower epigenetic age acceleration, as indexed by PhenoAge, GrimAge2, and DunedinPACE, through increased physical activity. CONCLUSION: Greater availability of local resources may slow down epigenetic aging. Given the effect of decelerated biological aging on reduced morbidity and mortality risk, our findings suggest that place-based interventions to boost local amenities, health services, and built infrastructure could be a promising strategy for promoting healthy aging.

title: Between-school socioeconomic segregation and adolescent bullying: A cross-national multilevel study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Bullying is a major public health concern among adolescents. Ecological frameworks suggest that bullying is shaped not only by individual characteristics but also by broader school, institutional, and macro-level contexts. We examined whether country-level between-school socioeconomic segregation helps explain differences in bullying perpetration and victimization. METHODS: We analyzed nationally representative data from 101,287 adolescents aged 11-15 years in 21 countries and regions across Europe and Canada participating in the 2017-2018 Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study. Between-school socioeconomic segregation was measured at the country level using the bias-adjusted Duncan dissimilarity index based on family socioeconomic position. Multilevel logistic regression models examined associations with bullying perpetration and victimization, adjusting for individual characteristics, GDP per capita, and Gini index. RESULTS: Each one percentage-point increase in between-school socioeconomic segregation was significantly associated with 5-6% higher odds of bullying perpetration (odds ratio [OR] = 1.05, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.03-1.07) and victimization (OR = 1.06, 95% CI = 1.04-1.09). Segregation accounted for roughly half of the between-country variation in bullying perpetration (49.6%) and victimization (56.3%), although the absolute magnitudes were modest. However, it did not significantly modify socioeconomic differences in these behaviors (P-interaction > 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Between-school socioeconomic segregation is an important contextual factor associated with adolescent bullying. Because the association between segregation and bullying was observed across the socioeconomic spectrum, policy responses should, in addition to targeting disadvantaged groups, be more universal and structural. Reducing socioeconomic segregation between schools may promote more socially cohesive educational environments and help reduce bullying.

title: Double jeopardy: Health-protective effects of educational attainment are stronger in deprived neighbourhoods
abstract: This study quantifies the relative contributions of educational attainment and the immediate social and physical environment to self-reported health. Using mixed-effects ordered logistic regression models applied to the Understanding Society dataset (2010-2023), we find that both educational attainment and neighbourhood deprivation levels are strongly and independently associated with self-reported health. The interaction analysis suggests that the health returns to education are greatest in more deprived neighbourhoods and that individual-level and neighbourhood-level resources can compensate for the absence of one another. These findings underscore the importance of addressing both individual-level and neighbourhood-level socioeconomic factors to reduce health inequalities.

title: Living the work: Internal and identity challenges of adolescent peer navigators living with HIV
abstract: Introduction Adolescent peer navigators living with HIV play a vital role in linking clients to care, supporting adherence, and humanizing HIV services. Their value stems from lived experience-an identity that both empowers and leaves them vulnerable. While research highlights their contributions, less is known about how navigators experience the personal and emotional demands of their work. This study explores how they make sense of supporting adolescents while managing their own HIV-related vulnerabilities. Methods Through the AMPATH Kenya research network, we conducted in-depth interviews with 30 participants: 11 current peer navigators (55% female, median age 25), 6 former peers (33% female, median age 31), and 13 supervising healthcare workers (100% female) at two adolescent HIV clinics. Interviews explored role identity, emotional labor, stigma, and wellbeing. Data were analyzed using Interpretive Phenomenological Analysis to capture participants' meaning-making around supporting adolescents while negotiating their own identities and life trajectories. Results Peer navigators described a continuous balancing act between personal HIV experience and professional responsibilities. Three interconnected themes emerged: (1) "living openly, living carefully"-strategically managing disclosure to build trust while minimizing stigma; (2) "you can't pour from an empty cup"-absorbing adolescents' crises while suppressing personal distress; and (3) "I am proof that life goes on"-deriving empowerment and affirming resilience through helping others. Healthcare workers highlighted the emotional demands of the role and the expectation that peers model stability. Conclusion Peer navigation relies on relational labor and lived experience, not just training. Sustaining this workforce requires mentorship, emotional support, and clear professional pathways to help peers manage personal vulnerability while supporting adolescents effectively.

title: “I want what the white lady gets…”: Deconstructing racial disparities in gynecological cancer
abstract: Despite decades of diversity and inclusion initiatives in healthcare, racial disparities in gynecological cancer diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes persist and, in some cases, are worsening. Black women continue to experience later-stage diagnoses, diminished provider communication, and poorer survivorship outcomes. This paper presents findings from five focus groups conducted with individuals (n = 26) diagnosed with gynecologic cancers, guided by an intersectional lens rooted in Black feminist theory. Using thematic analysis, four recurring themes emerged: (1) diagnostic delays and dismissal, (2) medical racism and epistemic violence, (3) systems not designed for us (4) knowledge gaps and the need for patient-centered education. These findings reveal that the persistent disparities in gynecological cancer outcomes cannot solely be addressed by implicit bias training or access-based interventions. Instead, they require a transformation of the epistemological and structural foundations of gynecologic care, which continue to be shaped by values that do not consider Black patients. The integration of Black feminist frameworks into gynecologic oncology research offers a critical intervention, one that centers lived experience, challenges the medical-industrial complex, and prioritizes patient dignity. Our findings contribute to a greater understanding of the lived experience of gynecological cancer patients and reveal implications for praxis, including culturally rooted patient education, trauma-informed survivorship care, and the need for structural accountability within oncology practice and research.

title: Living with persistent illness and uncertainty: Patient narratives on Lyme disease in Nova Scotia, Canada
abstract: Persistent, unexplained symptoms attributed by patients to Lyme disease present significant challenges within healthcare systems where diagnostic uncertainty and contested legitimacy shape clinical and institutional responses. This qualitative study draws on in-depth interviews with individuals in Nova Scotia who experience persistent symptoms following suspected or confirmed Lyme disease. Using an interpretive phenomenological approach informed by the embodied health movement framework, the analysis examines how participants interpreted their experiences and navigated interactions with healthcare and public health systems. Participants described complex diagnostic and treatment trajectories shaped by perceived testing limitations, inconsistent clinical interpretations, and limited recognition of persistent symptoms. These dynamics contributed to feelings of dismissal and uncertainty, prompting many to seek additional opinions, pursue alternative care, or engage in self-advocacy. As these struggles unfolded, participants reported broader disruptions to daily life, including shifts in family roles, relationship strain, and reduced functional capacity. Institutional messaging and jurisdictional constraints further shaped their sense of legitimacy within the healthcare system, while community networks and peer support offered crucial validation and interpretive resources. For some, these engagements extended into advocacy and public education aimed at improving recognition and care. The findings illustrate how individuals navigate the intersecting domains of embodied experience, biomedical uncertainty, and institutional structures, and how experiential knowledge becomes a resource in the absence of clear clinical consensus.
