In this study, we leverage a real life social interactional setting to investigate the link between the genetic burden of depression and behaviors that may evoke negative evaluations from others. We analyze observations about survey participants made by interviewers who were not privy to participants' genetic risk. Analysis of approximately 18,000 unique participants across two US datasets of older adults shows that a higher polygenic index (PGI) of depressive symptoms increased the probability of being perceived as experiencing cognitive struggle and discomfort, and being unhealthy, but not of being seen as untrustworthy or disengaged. These effects seem to be accounted for by stable differences in average depressive symptoms between individuals rather than elevated depressive symptoms during particular interactions. Specific evaluations were to some degree explained by the genetic correlation of depression with certain other traits, including ADHD, neuroticism, and self-rated health. Our findings suggest that the process of rGE in depression involves micro behaviors that are interpreted by others as signals of low competence and that create awkwardness during social interactions.

title: The challenged conscience: Moral predicaments of hospital frontline administrators in China's medical disputes
abstract: Although medical disputes have become a pervasive challenge in global healthcare systems, the role of hospital organizations in this process has received limited scholarly attention. In the Chinese context, existing research on medical disputes often treats hospitals as the background or monolithic actors, neglecting internal organizational dynamics. This article addresses this gap by examining hospital frontline administrators (HFAs), a pivotal group in resolving medical disputes. Drawing on the theory of street-level bureaucracy and ethnographic fieldwork, the study demonstrates how structural and working conditions, including conflicting institutional goals, resource constraints, and information asymmetry, generate acute moral predicaments for HFAs. These predicaments manifest as severe role conflicts, institutional suppression of empathy, and the normalization of habitual misrepresentation. The article further highlights that HFAs actively develop coping strategies to navigate these challenges, exercising different forms of agency within institutional constraints. By centering on HFAs, this study reexamines the complex role of hospitals in China's medical dispute resolution and provides broader sociological insights into the intersection of healthcare governance, moral ambiguity, and frontline administration.

title: Cost-Effectiveness of a Digital Parenting Intervention for Reducing Violence and Related Health Burden Among Adolescents in Tanzania
abstract: Background Violence against children is a major global public health concern associated with substantial physical and mental health burden across the life course. Parenting interventions are effective in preventing violence against children, yet evidence on their cost-effectiveness, particularly for digitally delivered programmes in low-resource settings, remains limited. We evaluated the cost-effectiveness of a blended-digital parenting intervention in Tanzania. Methods We conducted cost-effectiveness and cost–benefit analyses alongside a cluster-randomised controlled trial of ParentApp for Teens delivered to caregivers and adolescents aged 10–17 years. Trial outcomes were combined with programme cost data to estimate delivery costs at scale. Cost-effectiveness ratios (CERs) were calculated as cost per incident averted using incidence risk ratios from 14-month follow-up data. A discounted CER approach proportionally allocated intervention costs across multiple outcomes. Cost–benefit analysis compared prevention costs with immediate public-sector labour costs associated with formal case response. Results The intervention achieved significant reductions in multiple violence outcomes, including adolescent sexual violence victimisation, child maltreatment, and caregiver intimate partner violence—forms of violence associated with substantial health consequences. Using observed RCT implementation expenditure of US$69.02 per enrolled dyad, estimated costs per incident averted were US$30.83 for adolescent sexual violence, US$5.43 for child maltreatment and US$12.03 for caregiver IPV. Under a prospective routine-delivery scenario of just under US$6 per dyad at n=10,000, corresponding CERs were US$2.67, US$0.47 and US$1.04, respectively. At scale, routine delivery was estimated at approximately US$6 per caregiver–adolescent dyad, compared with an estimated US$121.10 in immediate labour costs for a reported case entering formal response. Conclusions ParentApp is a cost-effective preventive intervention with potential to reduce violence-related health burden at scale. Blended-digital parenting programmes can reduce violence against children at low cost and may generate short-term public-sector savings where prevented cases would otherwise require formal response.

title: Understanding inter-city travelers’ weekend daily mobilities, noise, and psycho-physiological stress: Evidence from residents with cross-city work-residence arrangements
abstract: Noise is an important environmental stressor, yet how noise-related stress unfolds across everyday mobility contexts remains insufficiently understood. Existing mobility-based studies have focused largely on intra-city movement and self-reported psychological stress, with less attention to physiological stress in real-life settings and to inter-city mobility under regional integration. This exploratory study examines how weekend mobility contexts are associated with objective noise exposure, subjective noise perception, and physiological and psychological stress responses among inter-city travelers with cross-city work-residence arrangements. Integrating real-time noise sensing, activity-travel diaries, self-reported measures, and wearable physiological data, we analyzed 945 weekend observations nested within 44 participants living in Zhongshan and working in Zhuhai, a specific subgroup of inter-city travelers in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, China. Path analysis with cluster-robust standard errors showed that higher-than-usual objective noise exposure was directly associated with physiological stress, while its association with psychological stress was mediated by perceived noise. Weekend mobility contexts were also important. Travel episodes, especially non-leisure-oriented travel, were more strongly associated with elevated stress-related outcomes than most activity episodes. No statistically significant stress-related association was detected for inter-city leisure activities, whereas inter-city non-leisure activities were linked to stronger perceived noise and higher indirect associations with physiological and psychological stress. These findings provide preliminary evidence that noise-related stress is context-dependent and pathway-specific. By integrating wearable physiological sensing with real-time noise measurement and activity-travel diaries, this study advances a contextualized understanding of how regional integration may reshape everyday environmental stress and health-related outcomes. Public health interventions should address mobile noise exposure and related stress beyond residential environments, particularly in contexts of regional integration.

title: Swallowed silence, strategic silence, and safe disclosure: A multi-level framework for understanding non-disclosure among internally displaced women experiencing gender-based violence
abstract: Despite decades of investment in gender-based violence (GBV) services, a substantial proportion of survivors in humanitarian settings never disclose their experiences or seek formal help. Existing frameworks have largely conceptualized this silence as a product of access barriers, overlooking its social rationality as deliberate, strategic non-disclosure. This paper proposes the Silence-Disclosure Framework, integrating two original constructs: Swallowed Silence (the phenomenological experience of deliberate suppression) and Strategic Silence (the social-rational calculus underlying non-disclosure). The framework is developed through secondary analysis of two qualitative studies: 33 internally displaced women (IDWs) in Douala, Cameroon, and 352 internally displaced persons (IDPs) and 28 service providers in Kaya, Burkina Faso, both employing intersectional analytical frameworks. Silence operates at three interdependent levels: structural (the social conditions that make disclosure costly), analytical (a deliberate cost-benefit calculus, Strategic Silence), and phenomenological (the embodied burden of sustaining that silence over time, Swallowed Silence). The framework reconceptualizes silence as constrained agency rather than a deficit of knowledge or access, with direct implications for programming that targets the social conditions of disclosure rather than solely service availability.

title: Does menstrual cycle tracking enhance female athlete health and performance? Evaluating five implicit assumptions of an emerging paradigm
abstract: According to an emerging paradigm in the field of sports science and medicine, women athletes can optimize performance and minimize injury by syncing their training to their menstrual cycles. This paradigm links specific cycle phases to performance, perceived exertion, and injury risk. Some researchers, training staff, and coaches have started to apply the paradigm, embracing digital surveillance and prediction of menstrual cycle phase as a strategy to track and optimize athlete performance, promote health, and understand and minimize injury risk. Many see digital menstrual cycle tracking as empowering to female athletes at all levels, from the elite to the recreational. In this article, we identify five often implicit assumptions underpinning the menstrual cycle tracking model of female athlete health and performance. We find the evidence for these assumptions to be unconvincing, warranting skepticism about their efficacy and caution about implementing digital cycle tracking in sport.

title: Racially motivated hate crime exposure and birth outcomes: Analysis of US vital statistics data 1995-2020
abstract: Exposure to racially motivated hate crime represents a salient form of structural and interpersonal racism that is associated with detrimental mental and physical health. Although prior research shows that stress during pregnancy can influence birth outcomes, empirical evidence linking hate crime exposure to adverse birth outcomes remains limited. Using National Vital Statistics Birth Data from 1995 to 2020 linked to county-level hate crime data, we use linear probability models and leverage variation in the timing of hate crimes in the county to examine the association between maternal exposure to a hate crime targeting her own race during pregnancy and the likelihood of preterm birth or low birth weight among Black, Asian, and Hispanic mothers, compared with White mothers as the reference group. Hate crime exposure is associated with a higher likelihood of preterm birth, though not with low birth weight; this association is stronger among Black and Asian than White mothers. When stratified by maternal education, the relationship between hate crime exposure and the likelihood of preterm birth is significantly larger among Black and Hispanic mothers with at least some college education than similar White mothers. Hate crime, as a marker of the racialized social environment, may contribute to racial disparities in birth outcomes. Policies reducing hate crime and its health effects may improve maternal and infant health and narrow inequities at birth.

title: Impact of prenatal sex selection on intimate partner violence against women: Evidence from India
abstract: A reduction in unwanted births may have significant implications for intra-household dynamics and women's welfare. In recent decades, India has seen a sharp rise in sex-selective abortions following the diffusion of prenatal sex detection technology, leading to fewer unwanted female births. This paper studies the impact of prenatal sex selection on intimate partner violence (IPV) against women in India. We measure prenatal sex selection by interacting the state-level sex ratio at birth with the firstborn's sex, a proxy for a household's propensity to practice sex selection. Because sex-selective abortions are rare for first births, the firstborn's sex can be treated as quasi-random. We include state-survey round fixed effects to control for evolving state-level preferences. We show that this measure is positively associated with ultrasound use during pregnancy, terminated pregnancies, and the likelihood of male births, indicating higher incidence of sex-selective abortion. Using nationally representative National Family Health Survey data, we find that greater prenatal sex selection reduces women's exposure to IPV. This effect is not driven by reduced fertility, changes in women's bargaining power, or female labor supply. Instead, we find that it operates through a reduction in the gap between the desired and actual male-female sex ratio within households, bringing actual composition closer to desired composition.

title: Gender differences in trusted sources of information and preventive health behaviors among Hispanic immigrants: The case of COVID-19
abstract: With recent changes to the health information landscape, understanding how sources of health information are associated with preventive health behaviors (PHBs) remains an important area for research. In particular, understanding where structurally marginalized populations like Hispanic immigrants receive trusted health information- and how this information is associated with PHBs-is critical, given their more limited access to formal information sources. Further, how gender patterns the association between trust in information sources and PHBs is often overlooked in research on structurally marginalized groups. In this study, we examine how Hispanic immigrants' trusted sources of information are associated with PHBs protecting against COVID-19, focusing on how this association varies by gender. We leverage data from the VidaSana Study, a survey of Hispanic immigrants in Indiana, and its extension, the Hispanic COVID-19 Rapid Response Study. We first identify characteristics associated with trusting sources on COVID-19 before predicting the number of PHBs as a function of trusted information sources and gender. Results indicate that participants who trust the radio as a source of information about COVID-19 are more likely to engage in PHBs. However, interaction models show that men who do not trust radio or TV about COVID-19 are driving this association, as they are less likely to engage in PHBs. We suggest that traditional health communications sources focus on fostering trust among Hispanic men as a way to disseminate accurate and timely information about health concerns.

title: Safety prioritization beyond efficiency: The role of age, health status, and ingroup preferences
abstract: A key challenge for policymakers is allocating limited resources to improve safety. One approach is to compare the cost-per-life-saved against a metric such as the Value of Statistical Life (VSL), an approach that prioritizes efficiency - i.e., the number of lives saved. But public preferences may reflect concerns beyond efficiency. In two experiments conducted in May and June 2020, we examine how people trade efficiency against distributive principles (equity in distribution and saving those most at risk), and beneficiary characteristics (age and health status). Self-interest was also considered by randomly assigning respondents to adopt either an impartial or socially inclusive personal perspective. Across both experiments, efficiency was the dominant concern, with equity and self-interest also valued. In the experiment focused on age (N = 314), saving younger lives received greater weight than saving older lives, but the effect was small and heterogeneous. It was driven primarily by younger respondents - older respondents showed no comparable prioritization. In contrast, the experiment focused on health (N = 316) revealed no aggregate preference for prioritizing people in good health over those in poor health. Ingroup preferences among respondents in good or poor health offset one another. Self-interest framing did not amplify ingroup preferences. Overall, the findings indicate limited consensus for adjusting VSLs based on age or health status. Some age-related weighting emerges without cross-group agreement, and there is no overall support for health-based adjustment. Recognizing how ingroup preferences shape public views is important for informing safety policy.

title: “Beggars can't be choosers”: Exploring service users' perspectives on charitable meal services while experiencing homelessness
abstract: Charitable meal services are an essential source of nourishment for many people experiencing homelessness (PEH), yet little research has examined how everyday organizational practices shape experiences of power, dignity, and participation within these settings. Guided by the work of Paulo Freire, this critical ethnography explored how power is enacted and experienced within charitable meal services for PEH in two mid-sized Canadian cities. Data were collected through participant observation and semi-structured interviews conducted between September 2023 and April 2024. Participants described charitable meal services as essential for meeting immediate needs while highlighting how organizational practices, provider discretion, and interpersonal relationships shaped experiences of autonomy, dignity, and belonging. Three interconnected themes were identified: 1) being deprived of choice; 2) treated as "less than"; and 3) making it work. Our findings suggest that charitable meal services are more than sites of food provision but provide relational environments in which everyday organizational practices shape experiences of care, dignity, and power. While respectful, participatory practices can foster more positive experiences, lasting reductions in food insecurity require broader structural responses addressing poverty, housing affordability, and income security. By centering lived experiences of PEH, this work highlights the limitations of charity-based models and offers research, policy, and practice recommendations aimed to support more equitable and rights-based approaches.

title: Chronicling Care: Ethnographic Case Dossiers and Charts to Investigate a Safe Motherhood Intervention in Northern India
abstract: Ethnographic research has demonstrated how clinical practice is shaped by institutional, social, and material conditions, yet it is seldom integrated into the evaluative frameworks used to assess health system performance. In maternal health, reliance on documentation and indicator-based audits can obscure how risk develops and is managed within everyday clinical work. This paper advances a methodological approach—ethnographic case reconstruction—that brings qualitative inquiry into direct analytic relation with clinical processes and reporting systems. The study drew on fieldwork conducted alongside a Safe Motherhood intervention in select public hospitals of Uttar Pradesh, India. Combining sustained observation, case-specific interviews, and analysis of medical and administrative records, the research assembled detailed case dossiers and temporally structured charts mapping sequences of care. These reconstructions were compared with the ways that cases were later represented in hospital records and audit systems. A reconstructed case of postpartum hemorrhage illustrates how clinically significant deterioration can take shape through successive gaps in monitoring, interpretation, and response, while remaining only partially reflected in formal documentation. By tracing care as a temporally extended and distributed process, the method reveals how evaluation systems may misrecognize clinical realities and produce administratively coherent but incomplete accounts. Ethnographic case reconstruction offers a complementary approach to audit-based evaluation, generating context-sensitive evidence that can inform clinical oversight, strengthen intervention design, and expand the evidentiary basis of global health assessment.

title: Discrimination and risk of spontaneous abortion in a preconception cohort study
abstract: Discrimination may increase risk of spontaneous abortion (SAB, pregnancy loss <20 weeks' gestation) through physiological responses and limited access to resources. We examined associations between self-reported experiences of discrimination and SAB incidence among 7359 participants in Pregnancy Study Online (PRESTO), a preconception cohort study (2013-2025), of whom 80% identify as non-Hispanic White. Eligible participants were 21-45 years, assigned female at birth, and U.S. or Canadian residents. Participants completed the Williams' Everyday Discrimination and Major Experiences of Discrimination scales. We derived summary variables for frequency of everyday discrimination (range: 0 to ≥7) and number of lifetime discrimination events (range: 0 to ≥3), with higher values indicating greater discrimination. We collected SAB data on follow-up questionnaires during preconception, early and late pregnancy. We used Cox models to estimate adjusted hazard ratios (HR) and 95% CIs. Relative to no everyday discrimination, HRs for low, medium, high, and very high scores were 1.12 (95% CI: 0.95-1.31), 0.96 (95% CI: 0.81-1.12), 1.07 (95% CI: 0.91-1.27), and 1.15 (95% CI: 0.96-1.37), respectively. HRs for 1, 2, and ≥3 events of lifetime discrimination (vs. none) were 0.98 (95% CI: 0.86-1.12), 1.21 (95% CI: 1.04-1.42), and 1.19 (0.99-1.43), respectively. Lifetime experiences showing the strongest associations with SAB incidence were discrimination by police (HR = 1.24, 95% CI: 1.01-1.53), in housing (HR = 1.19, 95% CI: 0.96-1.48), and medical care (HR = 1.19, 95% CI: 1.03-1.37). SAB incidence varied by type and timing of discrimination exposure, suggesting interventions aimed at reducing the harmful effects of discrimination during preconception are warranted.

title: Heat, home-based assault and domestic and family violence injuries: Evidence from hospital emergency department presentations
abstract: BACKGROUND: Elevated temperatures have been associated with increased interpersonal violence, yet evidence from hospital, health-sector data remains limited. Guided by theories linking environmental conditions, social interactions and violence-related harm, this study examines home-based assault injuries, including domestic and family violence (DFV) related injuries, presenting to emergency departments (ED) in Victoria, the only state in Australia with mandatory recording of rich data on injuries enabling assessment of the relationship with heat exposure. METHODS: A retrospective analysis of the Victorian Emergency Minimum Dataset identified home-based assault injury presentations (2009-2024) and DFV-related injury presentations (2016-2024). Daily temperature and heat-stress metrics were derived from Australian Gridded Climate Data and time and place aligned with ED presentations. Associations between heat exposure and injury presentations were examined using generalized linear mixed models. RESULTS: A total of 28,637 home-based assault injuries and 10,194 DFV-related injuries were identified. Home-based assault injuries occurred more frequently during summer, weekends and holiday periods. After adjustment for temporal and contextual factors, unusually hot days were associated with a 5.7% increase in home-based assault injury presentations, while days exceeding 30°C were associated with a 6.7% increase. DFV-related injuries demonstrated similar temporal patterns, although associations with heat exposure were not statistically significant after adjustment for season. CONCLUSIONS: Higher temperatures were associated with increased presentations for home-based assault injuries. The findings indicate that environmental conditions are relevant to understanding violence-related injury in residential settings across metropolitan and rural communities in high-income countries and suggest that climate-related factors warrant consideration in violence prevention strategies, injury prevention initiatives and health service planning. By using robust ED data that is unlikely to be influenced by external factors, this study extends existing evidence beyond police-reported and recorded incidents, and provides insight into violence-related injuries requiring acute healthcare.

title: Editorial Board
Unbundling social protection: Sex-specific pathways between social grant receipt and adolescent sexual violence in South Africa
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Social protection is a central component of violence prevention among adolescents, however, the mechanisms through which it may reduce the risk of sexual violence (SV) and transactional sex remain understudied, particularly in observational real-world contexts. METHODS: Based on a theory-informed a priori framework, we used mixed effect models and GSEM to examine pathways linking grant receipt and hypothesised familial, economic and schooling mediators at Wave1 to reduced odds of outcome at Wave2. Data are drawn from a South African prospective cohort of 1353 adolescents aged 10-24, 69% living with HIV (2014-2017). RESULTS: Past-year prevalence of contact/non-contact SV was comparable between males and females, ranging 2% to 9%. Transactional sex was higher among females than males only at baseline (11.2%vs1.5%). Baseline grant receipt (90%), schooling (95%), positive parenting (56%) and parental supervision (55%), and household necessities (58%) did not differ by sex. Food security (77%) was higher among males. Among females, grant receipt was associated with a lower likelihood of contact/non-contact SV and transactional sex through household necessities. Household necessities were associated with higher likelihood of schooling, and in turn, schooling was associated with lower likelihood of transactional sex. Among males, no indirect pathways were identified, although grant receipt was associated with a lower likelihood of contact/non-contact SV. Parental supervision was associated with lower likelihood of contact/non-contact SV among females and transactional sex among males. CONCLUSION: Social grants may reduce SV and transactional sex among adolescents through sex-specific economic and schooling pathways. Among females, integrating social protection with schooling and parental supervision may strengthen prevention efforts of contact/non-contact, while the mechanisms for males need further investigation.

title: Retraction notice to “Beyond preferences: Rethinking shared decision-making through the lens of care’ [Soc. Sci. Med. 390 (2026) 118801]
Mediating hospital attendance: Invisible administrative work and structural vulnerability in outpatient care
abstract: Non-attendance at outpatient appointments is commonly understood as a problem of patient behaviour. However, this perspective overlooks how organisational arrangements shape patients' opportunities to attend care. This study examines non-attendance as an organisationally mediated outcome, focusing on how administrative practices influence access to outpatient services. Using an institutional ethnographic approach, we conducted observations and interviews with medical secretaries in two outpatient surgical departments in Denmark and analysed relevant policy documents. The analysis was informed by the concepts of structural vulnerability and invisible work. Findings show that non-attendance emerged through the interaction of organisational conditions and patients' capacities to navigate them. Long waiting times, complex communication systems, and monolingual administrative infrastructures created barriers to attendance, particularly for patients facing linguistic, social, or practical challenges. Although both departments operated within the same regulatory framework, they differed in how these challenges were managed. One department relied on flexible, relational practices, whereas the other followed a more standardised and procedural approach, resulting in different forms of support, follow-up, and discharge. Medical secretaries played a central mediating role by coordinating communication, compensating for infrastructural gaps, and adapting organisational routines to patients' circumstances. The study demonstrates that non-attendance is not solely the result of individual behaviour but is shaped by how healthcare systems organise the conditions for participation. Efforts to reduce non-attendance should therefore address organisational and communicative barriers.

title: Social network exposures, political party affiliation, and perceived health risk
abstract: Why do people perceive risk differently during the same public health crisis? Using longitudinal, nationally representative panel data from the Understanding America Study spanning two years of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States (March 2020--February 2022), we show risk perception can be a result of both social experience and social construction. Specifically, we examine how risk exposure within close social networks and political party affiliation jointly shape perceived risks of infection, hospitalization, and death. Results indicate that each additional social network member's infection, hospitalization, or death predicts higher perceived risk of the corresponding outcome (all p ≤ .01). Republicans report lower perceived risks than Democrats on average, but the association between social network infections and perceived infection risk is steeper among Republicans (p < .05), which suggests that risk exposure and political identity also interact in creating risk perception. Party-stratified models corroborate that within-person increases in network exposures are followed by higher perceived risks. Phase-specific analyses reveal shifting salience of network experiences and partisan identity across the pandemic. Risk exposure in social networks and political identity (partisanship) appear to operate jointly in shaping health risk perceptions, highlighting the need for tailored risk communication strategies to support effective preparedness for future pandemics.

title: Responsibility beyond accountability: Navigating trust and control in Swedish primary care purchasing
abstract: In the wake of critiques of New Public Management and evidence-based medicine, alongside concerns about welfare fraud, demands for trust, control, and evidence risk being framed as existential either-or choices. This paper rethinks healthcare governance beyond such polarisation by combining Antje Vetterlein's concepts of responsibility and responsibilisation with Guido Möllering's distinction between the duality and dualism of trust and control. Using abductive document analysis, we examine contract documents regulating purchaser-provider relations in all twenty-one Swedish regions (2025), focusing empirically on improving continuity of care. We show how contracts articulate moral and causal responsibility and how follow-up arrangements specify who judges responsibility and on what grounds. From this analysis, we derive three ideal-type governance modes: delegated (centring moral responsibility and professional discretion), formalised (defining causal responsibilities with codified metrics and consequences), and negotiated (processing responsibility through dialogue and mutual adjustment). Across modes, trust and control are typically interdependent (duality) and can be mutually reinforcing. When positive expectations break down (e.g., suspected welfare fraud), they flip into opposing forces (dualism). We conclude that governance choices are ultimately choices about responsibility. Different configurations of responsibility not only organise trust and control in distinct ways but also shape what it means to act as a responsible provider. Navigating governance is therefore not about choosing trust or control, but about deciding how responsibility should be organised and cultivated. A key finding is that dialogic arrangements can cultivate moral responsibility without displacing causal responsibilities.

title: “If I want to tap into a cord blood bank later, I felt that I should do my part and donate”: Mutualism in women's accounts of umbilical cord blood donation
abstract: Umbilical cord blood, the blood remaining in the umbilical cord and placenta after birth, is rich in hematopoietic, or blood, stem cells. Since 1989, cord blood has been used clinically to treat various conditions. including leukemia, lymphoma, and aplastic anemia. Given these potential uses of cord blood, birthing persons can opt to save cord blood in a private bank for a fee or donate it to a public cord blood bank. In this paper, we draw on qualitative interviews with 76 women who donated or wanted to donate to Canada's public cord blood bank to explore their reasons for cord blood donation and the meanings they ascribe to cord blood donation. Using mutualism as a theoretical lens, our analysis illuminates how decisions to donate cord blood are informed by complex considerations of the benefits to both unknown recipients and birthing donors and their child-to-be, both of whom are constructed as donors whose contributions to the public bank position them as worthy and deserving of future withdrawals. We further suggest that women's accounts of their decisions to donate cord blood enact a community characterized by an ethic of mutual care. Our analysis provides insight into the ways in which donating brings cord blood donors into relations with other social actors, including their child-to-be, unknown cord blood recipients, and a broader social body or community of imagined donors.

title: “Authority Brokerage in Mental Health Self-diagnosis”
Prenatal exposure to maternal stress during the 2024 floods in Valencia, Spain, and risk of prematurity
abstract: Pregnancy is a period of heightened susceptibility to external insults. In October 2024, an unprecedented torrential rain (DANA) struck South-East Spain. Concentrated in just a few hours and specific areas, it triggered severe flooding that caused 238 casualties and extensive property damage -the most devastating natural disaster in Europe so far in the 21st century. Using a Difference-in-Differences framework and administrative microdata on pre- and post-disaster births, in this study we analyse whether pregnant mothers who were exposed to the floods were more likely than those unexposed to deliver babies with poorer health outcomes. We also analyse dose-response patterns and test whether mothers in more exposed areas experienced heightened risks. Focusing on prematurity as an indicator of perinatal health that captures key social and physiological mechanisms at work, particularly stress, we find that babies exposed to the floods in utero at the final stages of gestation experienced significantly worse outcomes. These results provide new evidence of the intergenerational consequences of maternal stress triggered by acute natural disasters.

title: Diagnosing employability: neurodiversity and the expansion of diagnosis into the workplace
abstract: This paper analyses the workplace as a critical site where overdiagnosis is institutionally reconfigured. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in three workspaces hosting technology startups and creative agencies in Lisbon, Portugal, including participant observation and in-depth interviews with twelve neurodivergent employees and three HR managers, the paper traces how the neurodiversity movement's ethos of "difference, not deficit" is absorbed into organisational governance. It explores how initiatives framed as inclusive often intensify institutional demands for formal diagnosis as a prerequisite for accommodations, recognition, and employability itself. For employees, diagnosis operates ambivalently as both a gateway to support and a mechanism of surveillance tying legitimacy to a medical label; for HR managers, diagnostic categories function as managerial tools that render difference legible, predictable, and optimisable. The paper identifies two institutional logics driving this expansion: a gatekeeping logic, in which diagnosis is still required to access protection, and a celebratory logic, largely absent from existing accounts of institutional diagnosis, in which certified difference is marketed as a productive organisational value, intensifying rather than easing diagnostic demand. Together, these logics extend theories of institutional classification to the workplace as a distinctive site and show that norms of able-bodiedness operate through incorporation as much as exclusion. Overdiagnosis thus emerges less as a matter of clinical excess than as a socio-institutional phenomenon. The Portuguese case offers a Southern European perspective on dynamics of diagnostic expansion examined primarily in Anglo-American contexts, with implications for identity, governance, and the definition of the legitimate worker.

title: Rethinking health in later life: A six-dimensional model based on the European SHARE survey
abstract: The accelerating global aging population requires updated conceptualizations and measurements of health in later life. While traditionally framed around physical, mental, and social dimensions, recent research suggests that additional dimensions may form part of the broader health construct in older adults. However, empirical validation of such multidimensional health constructs using population-based data remains limited. We analyzed data from 46,317 participants aged 50-104 years (M = 71.33, SD = 9.34; 42.6 % men, 57.4 % women) from Wave 8 of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). To examine the structure of health in later life, we applied a theory-informed data-driven psychometric approach. Candidate variables were first identified through a review of theoretical health frameworks and mapped onto SHARE indicators. We conducted Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA), Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), and second-order Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The second-order SEM model supported a multidimensional structure of health comprising six dimensions: Physical Health, Functional Ability, Cognitive Function, Psychological Wellbeing, Financial Autonomy, and Social Engagement. Standardized factor loadings ranged from 0.579 to 0.832. Model fit indices were: RMSEA = 0.054, 90 % CI [0.053, 0.054]; CFI = 0.904; SRMR = 0.050. These findings suggest that health in later life is best conceptualized as a multidimensional system of capacities and resources encompassing physical, functional, cognitive, psychological, social, and financial dimensions. By empirically deriving this structure from large-scale data, this study bridges theoretical frameworks of healthy aging with their operational measurement. Future research should examine longitudinal interplay among these dimensions and validate this structure beyond Europe.

title: Sexual orientation, food insecurity, and barriers to food-bank use in the UK: Longitudinal evidence from Understanding Society
abstract: Background Food insecurity has increased in the UK, yet little is known about disparities by sexual orientation or whether food-insecure sexual minority adults face distinct barriers to food-bank access. Methods We used the 2011-2025 UK Household Longitudinal Study to examine sexual orientation disparities in food insecurity, food-related financial pressure, food-bank use, and reasons for food-bank non-use. Food insecurity was measured using the eight-item Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES). A high food-spending-burden measure, calibrated against FIES-defined food insecurity, was applied across Waves 3-15. We estimated logistic and population-averaged longitudinal logistic regression models. Results Compared with heterosexual adults, bisexual adults, adults in the "other" sexual orientation category, and adults who preferred not to disclose their sexual orientation had 23%, 66%, and 23% higher adjusted odds of food insecurity, respectively. No significant disparity was observed among gay/lesbian adults. Disparities were particularly pronounced among bisexual women, women in the "other" category, and non-disclosing women. Longitudinal analyses showed persistent food-related financial pressure among "other" and non-disclosing respondents, with disparities during and after the COVID pandemic. Among food-insecure respondents, adults in the "other" and non-disclosing categories had higher odds of food-bank use. Among food-insecure non-users, bisexual and non-disclosing adults were more likely to report not wanting to use food banks, while gay/lesbian adults were more likely to report being unable to use them. Conclusions This study provides, to our knowledge, the first nationally representative longitudinal UK evidence linking sexual orientation with both food insecurity and food-bank access. Findings support sexual-orientation-disaggregated monitoring and more inclusive food-support systems.

title: Measuring the biological embedding of chronic stress: Allostatic load algorithms and cancer risk in a prospective cohort
abstract: BACKGROUND: Epidemiological studies on chronic stress and cancer risk have produced inconsistent findings, likely due to challenges in measuring stress exposure. The allostatic load model offers an alternative biomarker-based framework by capturing the biological embedding of chronic stress. OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between allostatic load and cancer risk, compare alternative operationalizations of the allostatic load construct, and assess whether biomarker patterns underlying cancer risk are consistent with the allostatic load model's premise of multisystem dysregulation. METHODS: We conducted a nested case-control study within the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC)-Granada cohort, including 955 incident cancer cases and 955 matched controls. Pre-diagnostic allostatic load was estimated using 16 biomarkers reflecting neuroendocrine, cardiometabolic, renal, hepatic, and immune system function, measured on average 15 years before diagnosis. Four alternative allostatic load indices were calculated using clinical vs. distributional cut-offs and biomarker vs. system-weighting. Conditional logistic regression estimated associations with cancer risk adjusted for known risk factors. Biomarker contributions were further investigated using machine learning and mixture modelling. RESULTS: Higher allostatic load was associated with increased cancer risk, with better model fit for indices based on clinical cut-offs (OR = 1.30, 95% CI: 1.18-1.42 per 1-unit increase for an equal-system-weighted clinical index), showing a dose-response relationship (OR = 2.24, 95% CI: 1.68-2.99 for Q4 vs. Q1; p-trend < 0.001). Machine learning and mixture analyses supported the role of multisystem physiological dysregulation, with contributions from most biomarkers and particularly strong influence of neuroendocrine and metabolic components. CONCLUSIONS: Findings support allostatic load as a measure relevant to cancer risk and are consistent with the model's premise that disease risk reflects coordinated physiological dysregulation. An allostatic load index based on pre-specified clinical cut-offs can detect cancer risk years before diagnosis, offering a reproducible option to increase comparability across studies and populations.

title: Change in the association between financial hardship and mental health before and during the cost-of-living crisis in Australia
abstract: There is growing concern that the current cost-of-living (COL) crisis may have exacerbated the adverse experience of financial hardship and its effect on mental health, but no study has provided evidence on this using longitudinal data. We aimed to address this knowledge gap to inform policy responses. We analysed 13 annual waves (2012‒24) of nationally representative data from the longitudinal Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey to examine change in the prevalence of financial hardship and the association between hardship and mental health from the pre-crisis period (2012‒19) to the COVID-19 (2020‒21) and the COL crisis periods (2022‒24). Fixed effects models were used to examine the within-person changes in working-age individuals. Mental health was assessed using the Mental Health Inventory. The analysis sample comprised 148,419 observations from 18,759 individuals between 2012 and 2024. Our results showed that the prevalences of hardship increased during the COL crisis period and the deterioration in mental health associated with financial hardship was greater during this period, compared to the pre-crisis period (interaction effect: -0.84; 95% CI -1.22, -0.46). A much greater decline in mental health during the COL crisis period was observed for individuals experiencing mortgage hardship, but only for those with large mortgage repayments (-2.57; 95% CI -5.00, -0.41). These differences were not seen during the COVID-19 period. These findings underscore the need for immediate interventions to alleviate financial stress to prevent mental health problems.

title: Treating the incumbent patient in triage: An analysis of “first come, first served” as a procedural rule
abstract: Allocating scarce intensive care resources requires decisions about both which patients should receive priority and which rules should guide those choices. We investigate how the procedural allocation rule "first come, first served" (FCFS) shapes triage decisions. Using experimental ICU bed allocation scenarios, we examine how 8227 scientists across disciplines, surveyed in April and May 2020, make life-and-death allocation decisions when patients differ in clinical and social characteristics and arrive simultaneously or sequentially. Many respondents prioritize the earlier-arriving incumbent patient even when the alternative has stronger survival-relevant claims, indicating a robust arrival-priority pattern. At the same time, the incumbent frame is associated with lower decision avoidance, suggesting that FCFS can function as a morally and organizationally "safe" shortcut in high-stakes settings. Reliance on FCFS varies across expert communities in ways consistent with disciplinary training. Health economists, whose work emphasizes trade-offs and policy evaluation, exhibit lower average adherence to FCFS than other health-related scientists, although substantial reliance on FCFS persists even within this group. The findings highlight a tension between procedural legitimacy and benefit-based triage criteria and suggest that guidelines should anticipate default-preserving tendencies and omission concerns when designing equitable and clinically grounded allocation procedures.

title: Longitudinal associations between U.S. state/local government policing and social service expenditures and Black adolescent and young adult suicide deaths
abstract: Recent evidence points to an alarming increase in Black youth suicides over the past decade; yet little research has examined structural impacts on this disparity. The present longitudinal study examined 1-year and 5-year lagged associations between state and local police and social services expenditures and years of potential life lost (YPLL) to suicide among Black adolescents (10-17) and young adults (18-25) from 2010 to 2020. Using a Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling (DSEM) approach with U.S. Census of Governments and CDC data, results revealed that per 100,000 Black adolescents, every $100 per capita annual increase in the previous-year police expenditure was associated with 135 more YPLL to suicide (γ = 1.35, 95% CI: 0.27, 2.15). Per 100,000 Black young adults, every $100 per capita increase 5-years prior in K-12 education expenditure was associated with 30 fewer YPLL to suicide (γ 10 = -0.30, 95% CI: -0.59, -0.06), housing and community development expenditure was associated with 128 fewer YPLL (γ 10 = -1.28, 95% CI: -2.07, -0.38), and health expenditure was associated with 112 fewer YPLL (γ 10 = -1.12, 95% CI: -1.84, -0.25). Findings suggest that the reallocation of police expenditure toward K-12 education, housing and community development, and health expenditures may be promising in reducing Black young adult suicide. Policymakers committed to reducing Black adolescent and young adult suicide must consider reexamining state and local budgets through an evidence-based approach, ensuring the long-term investment in social services that are upstream drivers of suicide prevention.

title: From listening to verification: PDMP risk governance and the transformation of pain credibility in healthcare
abstract: The 2022 revision of the CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids acknowledged that recent opioid governance has produced chronic pain patient dismissal and abandonment, yet the institutional mechanisms that generate such outcomes remain insufficiently theorized within health communication scholarship. This paper examines how the textual infrastructure of risk governance restructures the conditions under which chronic pain is believed in clinical settings. Drawing on a text-based institutional ethnography of Georgia's Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) and the NarxCare risk-scoring system, the analysis traces how legal, technical, and interface-level texts coordinate clinical action across regulatory, administrative, and algorithmic sites. Three findings follow. First, PDMP texts reorganize the cognitive starting point of the clinical encounter by placing algorithmic risk representations at its visual apex. Second, an intertextual chain tethers prescribing legitimacy to documentary procedures unrelated to the patient's medical condition. Third, this reconfiguration redistributes the burden of credibility work along gendered lines through a policy framework that collects gender as data while declining to analyze it, an algorithm that encodes gender as a weighted risk input, and an interface whose threshold logic is more likely to be triggered by the diagnostic trajectories that gendered patterns of pain recognition themselves produce. The paper theorizes the distinction between narrative credibility and documentable credibility as infrastructural determinants of communicative conditions.

title: Conceptual ambiguities, systemic barriers and emotional labour: Healthcare professionals’ perspectives on navigating ethnicity in genomic medicine
abstract: The increasing integration of genomics across multiple clinical specialties has necessitated a better understanding of how ethnicity information is understood, prioritised, and recorded. In many areas of medicine, ethnicity data is routinely collected to monitor access to services and to support aspects of clinical decision-making. In genomic medicine, ethnicity information is additionally drawn upon as a proxy for biological ancestry, to support the interpretation of genomic data. However, ethnicity is a socially constructed and politically charged category and rarely aligns with the biological specificity demanded by genomic analysis, complicating its operationalisation in clinical practice. Drawing on qualitative interviews with healthcare professionals involved in genomic medicine (n = 23), including clinical geneticists, genetic counsellors, clinical scientists, and nursing teams, this study examines how ethnicity is interpreted and used in everyday clinical work. Using reflexive thematic analysis informed by an interpretivist epistemology, we identify widespread uncertainty about the meaning, purpose, and downstream use of ethnicity data, alongside concerns about discomfort, miscommunication, and the emotional labour involved in ascertaining patients' ethnicity. Participants described particular inconsistencies in data collection following the introduction of genomic testing across various clinical disciplines, limited visibility of how ethnicity information is used beyond the clinic, and tensions between routine data collection and more targeted, context-specific approaches. These findings underscore the need for greater attention to the social and ethical dimensions of recording ethnicity in genomic medicine, including clearer workforce support, and more nuanced approaches to when and how ethnicity-related information is sought.

title: Surveillance, violence, and assistance: Distinct typologies of police contact and prospective health outcomes among people who use drugs
abstract: Policing is increasingly understood as a structural determinant of health, yet the social epidemiology of police contact remains limited by limitations to variable-centered measurement which may not capture the complexity of exposure. We aim to address this gap in a cohort of people who use drugs, a population facing disproportionate and consequential police contact, using person-centered methods to examine qualitatively distinct exposure profiles. We applied latent class analysis to 11 police contact indicators among a longitudinal cohort of people who use drugs in Baltimore, Maryland (N = 486) and estimated associations between baseline police-contact class and health outcomes at 6-month follow-up using BCH-weighted logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors. We identified three classes: minimal contact (64%), routine enforcement (25%), and violent enforcement (11%), the latter characterized by high surveillance alongside violence, coercion, and paradoxically, police assistance. After adjustment, those in the violent enforcement class had increased odds of nonfatal overdose at follow-up (aOR 3.23, 95% CI 1.78-5.87), while those in the routine enforcement class had higher odds of injection drug use (aOR 2.85, 95% CI 1.56-5.23) and lower odds of HIV testing (aOR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39-0.85). These findings demonstrate that police contact comprises qualitatively distinct typologies associated with distinct downstream health consequences among people who use drugs, and point to a need for longitudinal research to elucidate the mechanisms through which each operates. Implications of the co-occurrence of severe enforcement and police assistance among the most impacted individuals for reforms which aim to mitigate harmful police contact on population health are discussed.

title: Pregnancy termination outside the formal healthcare system before Dobbs: Consideration and attempts among abortion seekers in Mississippi
abstract: Research on abortion outside formal healthcare has focused primarily on self-sourced medication abortion (mifepristone and misoprostol or misoprostol alone). Less is known about how abortion seekers understand other pregnancy-ending practices, including non-evidence-based methods such as herbs, vitamins, alcohol, or physical stress. We examine how abortion seekers in pre-Dobbs Mississippi learned about, evaluated, attempted, or rejected these methods before obtaining clinic-based abortion care. Between December 2021 and August 2022, we conducted semi-structured telephone interviews with 24 abortion seekers recruited through Mississippi's only outpatient abortion clinic and analyzed transcripts using inductive thematic analysis. Interest in pregnancy termination outside formal healthcare was shaped by cost, travel, scheduling demands, and privacy and disclosure concerns. Respondents' language did not map neatly onto distinctions between evidence-based self-sourced medication abortion and non-evidence-based methods; instead, they described "at-home abortion," home remedies, or efforts to induce a period or miscarriage. They relied primarily on informal information sources, including online searches, friends, and personal or professional networks. Concerns about safety, effectiveness, bodily harm, and future fertility led some to reject or stop attempts to end pregnancies on their own. Six respondents attempted pregnancy termination before presenting for clinic-based care using non-evidence-based methods; none succeeded. These findings show how structural barriers, limited reliable information, and uncertainty shaped abortion-seeking before Dobbs, even when clinic-based care remained legally available. These accounts illuminate informational gaps and risk perceptions that may be especially consequential after Dobbs, as access to clinic-based care becomes more restricted.

title: Corrigendum to “How is family functioning associated with depressive symptoms among women living with HIV in China? Findings from a 4-year longitudinal study” [Soc. Sci. Med. 407 (2026) 119705]
Commercial opposition and the politics of proof: Institutional design for regulatory durability in food and nutrition policy
abstract: The commercial determinants of health literature has documented how corporations shape policy environments, including by exploiting the norms of evidence-based governance to demand proof that cannot exist on policymaking timelines. But policy must still be made, so how is evidence-based policy made when the most policy-relevant evidence does not yet exist, and who gets to decide what counts as sufficient evidence for action in the face of organized industry opposition? This article addresses these questions through a case study of Chile's pioneering food labeling and marketing law. Drawing on elite interviews (N = 17) and document analysis, including legislative history, regulatory decrees, consultation records, and implementation materials, I examine how regulatory authority was constructed despite the systematic contestation of the scientific and legal basis for regulation by industry actors. Results show that policymakers built institutional arrangements through which evidence could be produced, interpreted, and defended through three mechanisms: (1) strategic delegation from legislation to rulemaking, (2) anticipatory coordination between legal and scientific expertise during rulemaking, and (3) bureaucratic embedding of monitoring and interpretation during implementation. These arrangements helped generate a cumulative evidentiary record that has withstood industry opposition, legal and trade challenge, and political turnover. Results extend commercial determinants of health research by showing how states might respond to the weaponization of evidentiary uncertainty by creating institutions that could continue producing and defending evidence.

title: Competing institutional logics in public-private hospital arrangements in England
abstract: There has been an increase in partnership working between the NHS and the private healthcare sector in recent years, particularly for elective surgical care. The private sector now delivers a increasing share of NHS-funded services and alongside this privately funded healthcare has continued to grow. As consultants increasingly work across the NHS and the private sector, they must deal with complex and sometimes conflicting institutional demands. This paper explores how competing priorities, pressures and incentives are negotiated across and within the NHS and the private sector, using institutional logics theory to consider the interaction between the different logics of professionalism, bureaucracy and markets. We conducted 84 interviews between 2023 and 2025 with medical consultants, senior leaders and governance leads working across NHS and private healthcare providers in England. We identify three institutional logic dualities: professionalism and market, professionalism and bureaucracy, and bureaucracy and market. We show how these dualities shape opportunities for private work, clinical decision-making, professional identity, oversight mechanisms and governance structures. Our analysis highlights how institutional logics are merged, contested and managed in clinical and organisational practice and we consider the implications for accountability, transparency and professional autonomy. Our study contributes to institutional logics theory by considering how consultants' decisions and practices are constantly renegotiated as professional values, bureaucracy and markets interact.

title: Pragmatic sensemaking: Mapping the cultural work of people living with dementia and their care-partners
abstract: RATIONALE: Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) affect over 100 million people living with dementia (PLWD) and care-partners worldwide, creating intersecting challenges of brain change, social identity, and everyday routines. By examining how physiological and social dimensions intertwine, we chart implications for social scientific models and medical framings of ADRD and complex biosocial conditions more broadly. OBJECTIVE: We examine how people living with dementia (PLWD) and family care-partners make sense of, and respond to, life with dementia. METHODS: We completed a team-based multi-site ethnography across three U.S. states: 314 site visits, 117 interviews, and four years of longitudinal observation. In addition to in-depth analysis of cases and accounts, we used network visualizations to map shared understandings (cultural schema) in respondent narratives. RESULTS: Participants engaged in pragmatic sensemaking: adapting available meanings to make sense of shifting challenges, rather than holding to a singular narrative of life with dementia. Four schemas were empirically central in dementia narratives: health and medicine, social cognition, social roles, and change over time. Case analyses show how people combine and reconfigure these understandings as their circumstances shift. Participants understand ADRD not as solely 'loss' or 'journey,' medical challenge or social circumstance, but as a phenomenon involving all of these, and requiring adaptive responses. CONCLUSIONS: Although life with dementia can vary with wealth, biography, disease type and stage, people across divergent circumstances relied on pragmatic sensemaking, adapting available meanings to address practical and existential challenges of life alongside ADRD. Pairing computational analysis with ethnography makes this interpretive work visible and reveals patterns conventional accounts overlook, with implications for scholarship on how people respond to complex conditions like ADRD that resist reduction to purely medical or social elements.

title: Adjudicating medical uncertainty in public settings: How police officers, health workers, and people who use drugs exercise discretion when assessing overdose risk
abstract: Overdose continues to cause a significant number of deaths in the United States each year. In recent years, naloxone, a medication used to reverse the effects of overdose, has become more accessible to professionals and lay people outside formal healthcare institutions. Existing research has demonstrated the life-saving benefits of naloxone, yet less attention has been paid to how responders decide whether and how to administer it. In this article, I draw on over 300 h of ethnographic fieldwork in Kensington, Philadelphia to demonstrate how police officers, health workers, and people who use drugs (PWUD) exercise discretion in overdose risk incidents in response to institutional mandates, organizational pressures, and relationally embedded situational knowledge. I show how responders navigate medical uncertainty surrounding naloxone and other overdose technologies through three dominant, and at times overlapping, orientations: weaponization among police, as a moral imperative to save lives among health workers, and through relational negotiation among PWUD. This study contributes to research on urban poverty governance, medical uncertainty, and science and technology studies by demonstrating how medical technologies are mobilized differently in uncertain, public, high-risk overdose incidents and how discretion is shaped by responders' institutional positions and relationships to PWUD.

title: Labour, capital, and the Nordic health paradox
abstract: While Nordic countries are associated with comparatively low levels of economic inequality, their social mortality gradient is comparable in magnitude to that found in far less egalitarian societies, a phenomenon commonly referred to as 'the Nordic health paradox'. This paper argues that much of this apparent paradox may stem from an overly narrow conception of economic inequality, which tends to be centred around the distribution of labour market earnings at the expense of other sources of inequality. Using administrative data covering the Norwegian working-age population between 2006 and 2024, we chart the all-cause mortality gradient not only by labour income, but also by capital income and wealth. We find that returns to wealth are associated with mortality above and beyond labour income, net of key sociodemographic controls, and that the resulting gradient is markedly steeper for wealth than for labour income alone. These findings suggest that traditional, labour-income-centred measures of economic inequality incompletely capture the resources that shape survival, and that incorporating wealth in particular can help make sense of the persistence of health inequalities in Norway. More broadly, the results point to the importance of considering dimensions of inequality beyond those emerging from labour-market institutions alone. Because our analysis is confined to a single country, it does not permit a direct cross-national comparison, but it offers a template for revisiting the Nordic health paradox elsewhere using more comprehensive measures of economic resources.

title: Loneliness in migrants: Are there differences compared to non-migrants? A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background A migrant is any person who moves across an international border or within a State, away from their habitual place of residence. Migrants may be at greater risk of experiencing loneliness. However, no comprehensive meta-analysis has examined this association. This study aimed to explore the levels of loneliness among migrants compared to non-migrants based on quantitative studies. Methods The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases were searched from inception to March 2025. Methodological quality of studies was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute Checklist for cross-sectional and cohort studies. A random-effect model was used to estimate the pooled effect size. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Q and I 2 statistics. Publication bias and potential moderators (sex, age, and loneliness scale used), were also examined. Results Initially, the literature search yielded 2196 records. Forty studies were included in the systematic review, of which 30 were eligible for the meta-analysis, comprising 258,387 participants (18.6% migrants). After controlling for moderators, the random-effects model indicated a significant positive association between migration and loneliness ( g = 0.21; 95% CI [0.13, 0.30], z = 4.92, p < .01), with migrants reporting higher levels of loneliness than non-migrants. Substantial between-study heterogeneity was observed. Moderator analyses revealed no statistically significant effects. Conclusion The present meta-analysis provides evidence of a positive association between migration and loneliness. Understanding how migration processes shape experiences of loneliness is essential for policies that promote social integration and well-being among the migrant population.

title: The influence of disease label, disease signs and levels of contact on the stigmatization of inflammatory bowel disease: A vignette experiment
abstract: Inflammatory Bowel Diseases (IBD) are chronic bowel conditions with socially taboo symptoms, often resulting in individuals with IBD anticipating or experiencing stigmatization. Research indicates that the public tends to avoid medical conditions like IBD due to disease signs triggering feelings of disgust and perceived contamination risk, which is the premise of the disease avoidance model. Further, greater avoidance often occurs at higher levels of contact. Our study explored the influence of disease label (disclosed IBD label vs no disease label), disease signs (IBD symptoms) and levels of contact (short, long, and sustained) on public stigmatization of IBD. Participants (N = 450) read vignettes of a hypothetical individual with IBD exhibiting symptoms in a workplace context. Participants were randomly allocated to disclosure of the IBD label or no disease label conditions and completed ratings of avoidance and emotional reactions, and a measure of disgust sensitivity. Findings indicated that there was greater avoidance of IBD: (1) in the no disease label condition; (2) for sustained and closer contact; and (3) for more observable and disgust-eliciting disease signs. Additionally, emotional reactions did not differ according to the presence or absence of the IBD label, and higher disgust sensitivity was associated with avoidance of IBD (i.e., only for the no disease label condition). The public appear less avoidant of IBD for circumstances involving shorter contact and less disgust-eliciting symptoms. However, disclosing one's IBD label does not appear to be protective in mitigating avoidance towards the condition in situations involving prolonged contact.

title: The Intersectional Discrimination Index – Revised: Refinement and further psychometric assessment
abstract: The Intersectional Discrimination Index (InDI) includes three measures of anticipated, day-to-day, and major discrimination for intercategorical intersectionality research. Previous studies found that the measures are unidimensional with high loadings, good test-retest reliability, predictive validity, and measurement invariance between Canadian and United States (US) samples. Gaps included the need for cognitive interviewing, reassessing stability of the measures' configural and metric structures in a diverse US sample and identifying ways to protect participant well-being. From 2021 through 2025 we conducted cognitive interviews, revised, and then psychometrically assessed the InDI-Revised (InDI-R) in English and Spanish among US adults, including a community-engaged sub-study with people living with HIV. We conducted 75 cognitive interviews and modified the measures to clarify that the InDI-Anticipated assesses future expectations, address ambiguity, add items about social distancing and mistreatment by family, and simplify response options. Next, we examined the internal validity of the English InDI-R in an online survey of Black, Latino/a/e, and White adults (n = 2,763, half sexual/gender minority). Confirmatory factor analyses indicated the InDI-R measures are unidimensional with high item loadings, consistent with the original InDI. Inter-item residual correlations indicated potential redundancies, which may be addressed by merging items in future studies. We also tested whether strengths-focused questions would protect respondent affect. Participants were happier and less upset when administered strengths-focused questions after the InDI-R. These results provide support for internal validity of the InDI-R measures and inclusion of strengths-focused items in discrimination studies.

title: Workplace discrimination in relation to mental well-being and suicidal ideation
abstract: Despite many individuals experiencing discrimination at work, research elucidating the implications of workplace discrimination for mental health is limited. We aimed to estimate the hypothesised dose-response relationships of frequency and number of types of discrimination at work with poor mental well-being and suicidal ideation. We analysed cross-sectional data from 2594 participants (57% male, mean age: 42.3 years, response rate 14.3%) of the 2021 wave of a study examining job quality and well-being in Luxembourg. Participants were asked how often they were exposed to discrimination due to sex, age, ethnicity, religion/worldview, nationality, disability or sexual orientation at work within the last year. They were also asked for suicidal ideation during the last year. Poor mental well-being was measured via the WHO-5 Well-being Index. Logistic regression estimated the associations of reported frequency and number of types of discrimination with poor mental well-being and suicidal ideation. We observed increasing odds of both outcomes in association with increments in the frequency and number of types of discrimination. Compared to participants reporting no experience of discrimination, individuals exposed to discrimination weekly or daily had elevated odds of poor mental well-being (Odds Ratio (OR): 1.73, 95% Confidence Interval (CI): 1.04- 2.90) and suicidal ideation (OR: 2.38, 95% CI: 1.21-4.71). Exposure to three types of discrimination was also associated with poor mental well-being (OR: 1.65, 95% CI: 1.02 - 2.66) and suicidal ideation (OR: 2.33, 95% CI: 1.17-4.64). Even though the design of our analysis does not allow causal conclusions, its results point towards a dose-response relationship between workplace discrimination and poor mental well-being as well as suicidal ideation.

title: Corrigendum to “Are you sexually active?”: Unilateral informing patterns in communicating the sexual impact of prostate cancer treatment” [Soc. Sci. Med. 404 (2026) 119528]
Community social environment in relation to opioid use disorder across an urban-rural spectrum
abstract: BACKGROUND: Addressing the opioid epidemic requires understanding environmental factors influencing population-level risk of opioid use disorder (OUD). To elucidate the role of social environmental conditions on opioid-related risk environments, we assessed two community-level measures-social disorganization and social capital-in relation to OUD across an urban-rural spectrum. METHODS: In a case-control study using medical records (2012-2020) from a Pennsylvania health system, 14,674 OUD cases were frequency matched (on age, sex, year, medical record duration) to 58,696 controls. Study individuals were geocoded using residential addresses and assigned to community-level measures created from secondary data. Using logistic regression, we analyzed associations of social environmental measures with OUD in non-stratified models and models stratified by community type, adjusting for individual-level socio-demographic characteristics and community socioeconomic deprivation. Sub-scales of social capital (bonding, bridging, linking) were assessed. RESULTS: Higher social disorganization was associated (odds ratio [95% CI]) with increasing OUD odds with an exposure-effect relationship (quartile [Q] 2: 1.21 [1.10, 1.32]; Q3: 1.42 [1.28, 1.59]; Q4: 1.77 [1.59, 1.98]; vs Q1). Higher social capital was associated with decreasing OUD odds, with an exposure-effect relationship (Q2: 0.89 [0.82, 0.96]; Q3: 0.85 [0.78, 0.93]; Q4: 0.80 [0.72, 0.89]; vs Q1). Bonding social capital accounted for most of this association. Results for social environmental measures remained consistent when adjusting for socioeconomic deprivation but differed by community type. CONCLUSIONS: Findings add to prior evidence suggesting an influence of the social environment on opioid-related risk. To respond to the opioid epidemic, structural responses should address social environments to improve conditions.

title: “Being safe and being yourself is two different things”: a scoping review on the violence faced by sexual and gender minority adolescents living in low- and middle-income countries
abstract: PURPOSE: Sexual and gender minority (SGM) adolescents are at risk for interpersonal violence, however, much of the research to date has focused on SGM adolescents in high-income countries. This review describes the current research on SGM adolescents' experiences of violence in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). METHODS: In January 2024 and July 2025, a scoping review with single-reviewer screening was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute's methodological framework. Peer-reviewed publications in English or Spanish were included if interpersonal violence, defined as all acts of harm, threatened or actualized, against another person, was explored as an outcome among SGM adolescents living in LMICs. RESULTS: A total of 76 articles were identified for inclusion. SGM adolescents reported experiencing physical, psychological, and sexual violence in multiple settings. School was the most referenced setting (n = 51), and both classmates and school staff were identified as perpetrators. Violence also occurred in the home (n = 30), the larger community (n = 25), and in other institutional settings (n = 11). Frequently, SGM adolescents described experiencing forms of violence specific to their SGM identity, such as physical or verbal punishment for not conforming to gender or sexuality norms or threatening to be outed. No peer-reviewed publications describing or evaluating violence prevention interventions targeting SGM adolescents in LMICs were identified. CONCLUSION: SGM adolescents reported frequent accounts of physical, psychological, and sexual interpersonal violence, indicating a grave public health problem. To promote the health of SGM youth globally, it is imperative that research on this topic progresses from detecting and understanding violence to intervening and evaluating violence prevention efforts.

title: Exploring the therapeutic benefits of a community garden and nature-based project designed for people experiencing homelessness: A qualitative study
abstract: People experiencing homelessness face profound health inequalities, including high rates of mental and physical illness, problematic substance use, injury and reduced life expectancy. While the therapeutic benefits of greenspace are established, research on nature-based interventions for this population remains limited. This study explores how a tailored green social prescribing programme delivered through a supervised community garden and nature-based activity project can improve wellbeing amongst people experiencing homelessness. The research was conducted at a primary care centre in Scotland. Semi-structured interviews with centre clients (n = 11) and programme staff (n = 3) captured experiences and perceived therapeutic processes. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis and informed by an existing greenspace programme theory model. Five themes are presented in relation to nature, the individual-self, and the social-self. Findings suggest that greenspace interventions accessed through tailored green social prescribing have the potential to be therapeutic for people experiencing homelessness. To realise these benefits, interventions must accommodate individuals' capacities and circumstances, which may differ from other populations.

title: Editorial Board
Keeping the distance: An ethnographic study of professional autonomy and boundary work among hospital surgeons
abstract: Interprofessional collaboration is essential to hospital care, yet ward-level nurse-surgeon relations often appear strained.
