This ethnography follows 16 surgeons over six months in a Norwegian university hospital to examine how spatial, organisational, and interactional practices shape surgeons' professional autonomy and jurisdictional boundaries, and under what conditions they contribute to professional distance in ward-based collaboration. Bringing together Abbott, Freidson, and Strauss, we treat episodes of interprofessional coordination, including paging, corridor consultations, and ward encounters, as sites where logistical control is negotiated, constrained, or redistributed. The findings show that surgical work was often reactive in its initiation, even when surgeons exercised considerable authority within bounded clinical arenas. Ward co-presence generated ad hoc enlistment and interruptions that disrupted planned work trajectories, making availability both clinically necessary and difficult to sustain. Surgeons responded through spatiotemporal tactics, including avoiding wards, triaging calls, and deflecting nonurgent tasks, to protect logistical control. We reframe apparent 'uncooperativeness' as organisationally conditioned boundary work that protects logistical control while also reproducing professional asymmetries, shifting coordination burdens towards nurses, and generating professional distance. By linking Abbott's concept of jurisdiction, Freidson's theory of professional autonomy, and Strauss's analysis of negotiated order, the study shows how the spatial organisation of hospital work shapes professional relations through uneven distributions of mobility, access, exposure to interruptions, and control over work.

title: Intergenerational education and late-life cognitive performance: A comparison between rural Mexico and South Africa
abstract: Educational trajectories across the lifecourse have been associated with late-life cognitive outcomes; however, studies in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are limited. This study examines the relationship between intergenerational educational mobility and cognitive performance among older adults living in rural areas of Mexico and South Africa. Data from the Mexican Health and Aging Study (MHAS), the Health and Aging in Africa: Longitudinal Studies of an INDEPTH community in South Africa (HAALSI), and their harmonized cognitive aging ancillary studies, Mex-Cog and HAALSI-Dementia, were analyzed using linear regression models to assess cognitive performance (i.e., global cognition, executive function, language, memory, and orientation domains) based on educational mobility. The study included 482 Mex-Cog rural participants and 607 HAALSI-Dementia participants. Mex-Cog rural participants were younger, had slightly more schooling, and were more likely than HAALSI-Dementia participants to have formal education in both generations. In study-stratified models, upward educational mobility and formal education in both generations were positively associated with cognitive performance across domains relative to neither generation having formal education; however, upwardly mobile participants generally had lower cognitive scores than those with formal education in both generations. Our findings underscore the importance of considering lifecourse and contextual social determinants - including historical reforms, education quality, and rural-urban differences - when evaluating the associations between education and cognitive aging in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Experiencing medical desertification: A care-seeker-centered qualitative comparison across rural and urban sites in France and Slovenia
abstract: "Medical desert," referring to conditions of unequal access to medical care, remains contested in its definition and measurement. Predominantly supply-focused, most studies rely on quantitative indicators and few examine how care-seekers perceive and navigate shortages, nor do they address desertification as a dynamic, policy-driven process. None, to our knowledge, compare these experiences across rural and urban settings or countries. We conducted a qualitative comparative investigation during the COVID-19 pandemic among people experiencing health and social vulnerabilities in France and Slovenia, employing the WHO Availability, Accessibility, Acceptability, and Quality (AAAQ) framework. From January to July 2021, we interviewed 156 participants in one urban (Paris-Seine-Saint-Dénis) and one rural (Vendôme territory) site in France and 214 participants in one urban (Ljubljana) and one rural (Pomurje) site in Slovenia. Thematic analysis revealed shared patterns across sites and countries. Participants in all sites reported insufficient availability of services and personnel; urban residents experienced shortages despite nominally abundant resources. Accessibility barriers extended beyond spatial distance to encompass cost, time poverty, informational gaps, digital exclusion, language barriers, and clientelism. Dissatisfaction with care quality (claims of dismissive providers, absent holistic diagnosis, eroded trust) was pervasive although invisible to standard medical desert metrics. Social vulnerabilities compounded these barriers, producing uneven experiences of desertification. These findings demonstrate that care-seeker-centered approaches can foreground processes of medical desertification that transcend the rural-urban divide. By illuminating perceived shortages that supply-side indicators miss, they suggest that desertification may reflect a broader austerity-driven erosion of public healthcare whose consequences surfaced during the pandemic.

title: Home as workplace: Employment conditions, employer relationships, and mental health among migrant domestic workers in Macao, China
abstract: Background Employment conditions are important social determinants of health among migrant domestic workers (MDW), yet most studies examine individual employment characteristics rather than multidimensional employment environments. This study examined how employment condition profiles and employer-employee relationships were associated with depressive and anxiety symptoms among MDWs in Macao, China. Methods Cross-sectional data were drawn from 1769 completed surveys using respondent driven sampling and an analytic sample of 1743 female MDWs (Filipino, n = 1376; Indonesian, n = 367) were included in the analysis (2016-2017). Latent class analysis identified employment condition profiles across three domains: working environment, living environment, and compensation. Multivariable hierarchical linear regression models, stratified by nationality, examined associations between employment profiles, employer-employee relationship measures, and depressive and anxiety symptoms. Results Two working environment profiles, three living environment profiles, and two compensation profiles were identified. Living environment profiles were most consistently associated with depressive and anxiety symptoms across both nationality groups. Compared with the favorable living environment profile, profiles characterized by living outside the employer's home and noisy residential conditions were associated with poorer mental health among Filipino MDWs. Working environment showed fewer adjusted associations, and compensation profiles were not independently associated with either mental health outcome. Fear of contract termination remained independently associated with poorer mental health, particularly among Filipino MDWs. Conclusion Living environment and perceived employment insecurity were the employment dimensions most consistently associated with MDW mental health. Policies that improve housing quality and protection against arbitrary contract termination may promote the mental health of MDWs.

title: Insurance is not enough: Access barriers, usual source of care, and reliance on the emergency department
abstract: BACKGROUND: Emergency department (ED) overuse for non-urgent conditions is a persistent driver of rising health care costs in the United States. Federal and state policy has focused primarily on expanding insurance coverage as the principal lever for redirecting patients to primary care, yet coverage expansion may be insufficient when structural barriers, including provider shortages, network gaps, and insurance non-acceptance, constrain patients' ability to establish a usual source of care (USC). Racial and ethnic minority populations face these barriers disproportionately. METHODS: Using 2021-2022 California Health Interview Survey data (46,810 interviews; 8.6% response rate), we estimated survey-weighted multivariable logistic models guided by the Andersen-Newman Behavioral Model of Health Service Use. The analytic sample comprised adults self-identifying as Asian, Black, Hispanic, White, or other race/ethnic groups (up to 45,916 observations). Two outcomes were examined: using the ED as a USC and having no-USC. Key enabling variables included three measures of provider access barriers (provider not accepting new patients, difficulty finding a general physician, and provider not accepting insurance), insurance status, employment, and family income. FINDINGS: Approximately 1% of adults reported using the ED as their USC and 16% of adults reported having no-USC at all. All three measures of access barriers are associated with higher odds of using the ED as their USC or not having a USC. Difficulty finding a general doctor is associated with 3.13 times higher odds of ED as a USC (SE: .533). Having private insurance is negatively correlated with relying on the ED as a USC (OR: .22 to .41, SE: .083 to .101) and having no-USC (OR: .18 to .84, SE: .013 to .045). Poor self-reported health is associated with higher odds of ED reliance (OR: 1.82 to 2.50, SE: .509 to .851). CONCLUSIONS: Insurance coverage is an important but insufficient enabling resource. Structural barriers to primary care were associated with higher odds of ED reliance by an amount large enough to substantially offset coverage-related gains. Policy must extend beyond insurance expansion to address provider capacity, network adequacy, and continuity of care, particularly for Black and marginalized populations.

title: Growing up with ADHD: How diagnosis shapes socioeconomic trajectories
abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is the most prevalent mental health disorder diagnosed in childhood in the United States, and evidence on its long-term economic consequences has largely been established using diagnosis-based measures. This paper examines how a childhood ADHD diagnosis affects adult labor market outcomes, focusing on disentangling employment effects from earnings effects and addressing sources of bias in self-reported diagnoses. Using data from Wave IV (2008-2009) of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), comprising 8570 participants, we implement a framework that simultaneously accounts for non-random selection into employment and measurement error arising from self-reported ADHD. Our results show that childhood ADHD substantially reduces employment probabilities in early adulthood. In contrast, once both endogeneity and selection are properly addressed, the estimated effect of ADHD on earnings conditional on employment is substantially attenuated and precisely estimated near zero. Moreover, the employment penalties in early adulthood appear less pronounced later in the life course, suggesting that the economic costs of ADHD are concentrated at labor market entry rather than persisting throughout adulthood. These findings highlight the importance of accurately measuring mental health conditions when estimating their long-term economic impact. They further suggest that policies aimed at early and systematic detection, access to care, and targeted labor-market support may yield substantial economic benefits by mitigating employment disadvantages that emerge at the transition from education to work.

title: Health system barriers to care for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex populations in Nepal: A qualitative multi-stakeholder study
abstract: Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex (LGBTI) individuals face persistent barriers to healthcare in many settings. However, little is known about how health-system factors shape inequities in Nepal. This study aimed to examine the experiences of care, barriers to inclusive services, and opportunities to strengthen the health system for LGBTI individuals in Nepal. We conducted in-depth qualitative interviews using an interview guide with 28 participants-LGBTI community members, healthcare providers, leaders of LGBTI-led organizations, and policy stakeholders-in Nepal. Data were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. Three themes emerged: where the health system breaks down, how LGBTI individuals adapt, and what health system strengthening could look like. Participants described limited availability, affordability, and accessibility of LGBTI-relevant services; exclusion at registration and admission; and clinical encounters shaped by limited provider knowledge and binary assumptions. In response, LGBTI individuals reported concealing their identities, relying on non-governmental organization (NGO)-run services, self-managing health needs and often placing trust in individual providers rather than the healthcare system. Participants emphasized that strengthening care requires moving from legal recognition to implementation through affordable services, trained clinical and non-clinical staff, privacy protections, respectful facility practices, curriculum reform, and institutionalization of LGBTI-inclusive care beyond NGO-run services. The findings show that access to healthcare for LGBTI populations in Nepal is shaped by routine health-system practices, even when services are not explicitly denied. Improving equity will require embedding LGBTI-inclusive care within routine public health services, with clear policy implementation, provider education, facility-level accountability, and sustainable government-community partnerships.

title: Bridging divides: The role of social science in operationalising transdisciplinarity for epidemic preparedness in sub-Saharan Africa, 2012–2023
abstract: This paper investigates the role of transdisciplinarity, social science, and communities' knowledge in epidemic and pandemic preparedness and response in sub-Saharan Africa. It addresses how social science contributions have evolved over the past decade, explores the ways in which transdisciplinary approaches have been implemented and developed and analyses how social science can help to operationalise transdisciplinarity. The research applies a conceptual framework focusing on the intersection of power, knowledge, and crisis, and adopts a definition of transdisciplinarity that emphasises multi-actor collaboration and the integration and bridging of academic and non-academic knowledge. Three empirical case studies are presented: neglected zoonoses (2012-2014), the West Africa Ebola outbreak (2014-2016), and the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2023). This paper argues that attention to the politics of knowledge and power dynamics in research and policy implementation is key to understanding how social science and transdiciplinarity can be a catalyst for knowledge integration and bridging into effective epidemic preparedness and response systems. The paper identifies three main areas of social science contribution. The first of these is how social science serves as a catalyst, translating, bonding, and connecting diverse disciplinary perspectives. Secondly, social science functions as a nexus, facilitating connections and collaboration across academic and societal boundaries to address complex challenges. Thirdly, the operationalisation of innovative social science methods, such as transdisciplinary modelling, participatory research, rapid response studies, and social media analysis, offers opportunities for generating actionable, context-specific knowledge that bridges science, policy, and practice. The findings advance theoretical and empirical understanding of transdisciplinary approaches, and assess progress towards more contextually-responsive, integrative and bridging strategies.

title: Biodiversity and well-being: A systematic review and meta-analytic structural equation modeling analysis
abstract: The relationship between biodiversity and human well-being is a critical area of interdisciplinary research, representing a fundamental interlinkage between environment and society. However, existing evidence remains fragmented regarding whether measured biodiversity (i.e., objectively assessed biodiversity attributes; e.g., Shannon diversity index and species richness) and perceived biodiversity (i.e., individuals' subjective perceptions of biodiversity-related features) are differentially associated with well-being, and whether and how perceived restorativeness explains this relationship. We thus conducted a systematic review (pre-registered on the Open Science Framework) and utilized one-stage meta-analytic structural equation modeling to construct integrated models guided by the attention restoration theory, which posits that environments perceived as restorative can help individuals recover from attentional fatigue. Following PRISMA 2020, 102 studies were finally included from Web of Science, Scopus, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure, covering records indexed up to October 2025. Results showed that measured biodiversity was significantly and positively associated with perceived biodiversity, and indirectly with self-reported well-being via perceived biodiversity and perceived restorativeness. In addition, among the different restorativeness dimensions (i.e., being away, extent, fascination, and compatibility), being away and fascination exhibited the most robust mediation roles. Study location did not significantly moderate any path, although a relatively stronger positive effect was observed in Asian samples than in non-Asian populations, suggesting a broadly consistent biodiversity-well-being relationship across geographic regions. Risk of bias was assessed using the study quality assessment tools developed by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute. Findings support integrated policies and practices that jointly promote biodiversity conservation and human well-being.

title: The long-term health consequence of the 1958-61 Great Leap Forward and famine in China: Life-stage exposure and later-life frailty
abstract: This paper examines the long-term health consequences of exposure to the 1958-61 Great Leap Forward movement and famine in China among individuals born between 1910 and 68 (n = 19,426). We used a cross-sectional Difference-in-Differences approach to compare cohorts exposed to the GLF at different life stages, while accounting for several types of selection bias. The results show that compared with unexposed individuals, exposure to the GLF at ages 0-3 and 4-11 was associated with a 0.021 and 0.042, respectively, increase in later-life frailty. In contrast, no significant adverse effects were observed among individuals exposed during adolescence or adulthood. The results further revealed that only significant adverse effects were observed among men. These findings highlight the importance of the early-life experience of extreme external events in shaping long-term health outcomes.

title: War comes home: Conflict exposure and intimate partner violence in Ethiopia
abstract: Armed conflict can increase risks of violence within households, including intimate partner violence (IPV), that is, physical, sexual, or psychological harm inflicted by a current or former partner. Existing evidence links conflict exposure to IPV, but little is known about how IPV risk scales with the intensity of nearby violence, whether conflict exacerbates pre-existing IPV, contributes to new IPV, or both, and the household-level mechanisms that may underlie these associations. We examine these questions in Ethiopia, a country affected by recent large-scale conflict. We link geolocated conflict events from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) to six waves of household panel data collected across five regions between 2016 and 2021, and estimate individual fixed-effects models. A one standard deviation increase in local conflict events is associated with a 1.6 percentage point (pp) increase in the probability of reporting any IPV, a 1.1 pp increase in the probability of physical IPV, and a 1.1 pp increase in the probability of sexual IPV, corresponding to 7%, 11%, and 33% of the respective outcome means. The association rises with conflict intensity: each additional conflict event predicts higher IPV, whereas the presence of an isolated event does not. Associations are concentrated among women reporting no lifetime IPV at baseline. Conflict exposure predicts higher psychological distress in both partners, reduced working hours, lower husband income, and greater acceptance of wife-beating. The findings suggest that IPV prevention, integrated with mental health and livelihood support, belongs in the core of responses to escalating conflict.

title: Help-seeking behavior and its determinants among gender-based violence survivor women in Africa: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background Gender-based violence is a pervasive public health and human rights problem that disproportionately affects women in Africa, resulting in profound physical, psychological, and social consequences. Despite these impacts, many survivors do not seek formal help due to stigma, fear, and limited access to resources. This study aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence of help-seeking behavior and identify its determinants among gender-based violence survivor women in Africa. Method A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following standard methodological guidelines, using studies identified from African Journals Online, PubMed/MEDLINE, PsycINFO, EMBASE, and Google Scholar. Data were extracted and analyzed using a random-effects model to estimate the pooled prevalence and associated factors. Statistical heterogeneity and publication bias were assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression test. Result Thirteen studies involving 31,061 women were included. The pooled prevalence of help-seeking behavior among women who experienced gender-based violence in Africa was 33.86% (95% CI: 28.23, 39.49). Help-seeking behavior was significantly more likely among women with access to fuel sources (aOR = 2.26; 95% CI: 1.54, 3.32), women from rich households (aOR = 2.57; 95% CI: 1.12, 5.90), and women with independent land ownership (aOR = 1.85; 95% CI: 1.30, 2.64). Conclusion and recommendation Only one-third of women survivors of gender-based violence in Africa reported help-seeking behavior, highlighting a substantial unmet need for support services. Economic empowerment and access to productive resources, including land ownership and household assets, play a critical role in enabling help-seeking behavior. Interventions aimed at improving women's economic independence and access to essential resources should be integrated into gender-based violence prevention and response strategies across African settings.

title: Embodied harm, normalised suffering: experiences of unpaid care and domestic work among women across the life course in sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Unpaid care and domestic work (UCDW) is an important determinant of women's health and wellbeing in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). While its gendered burden and health consequences are increasingly documented, less is understood about how women interpret these consequences and how the unequal responsibility for UCDW becomes normalised as ordinary, unavoidable, or morally valued. Guided by necrosocial incorporation, a framework we develop by bringing ecosocial theory into conversation with necropolitics, we examine these processes across the life course in Kenya and Uganda. We conducted a reflexive thematic analysis of 36 in-depth interviews with women aged 18 to 59 and 30 oral histories with women aged 60 and above. Our analysis identified five interconnected pathways linking UCDW to poor health and diminished wellbeing. These involved persistent stress around household survival, cumulative physical strain from repetitive labour, time poverty from competing responsibilities, curtailed sleep and recovery from extended working days, and deprioritisation of women's own health and care needs. Participants' accounts also reflected three configurations through which unequal responsibility for UCDW became normalised: (1) constrained recognition, (2) resigned acceptance, and (3) joy, duty, and fulfilment through UCDW. Across these configurations, normalisation lay in women's continued primary accountability for ensuring that UCDW was completed, including where they recognised harm, desired support, or experienced care as meaningful. Read through necrosocial incorporation, these findings show how structurally produced harm becomes embodied and entwined with gendered understandings of care, duty, and moral worth. Addressing these harms requires public investment that reduces the demands of UCDW and redistributes responsibility within and beyond households.

title: Overcoming the corporate playbook in international treaty negotiations: Insights from the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control
abstract: International health-related treaty negotiations are often subject to outsized influence from transnational corporations and states that protect economic interests at the expense of developing and implementing strong, health-promoting obligations. In the early 2000s, proponents of global tobacco control faced these conditions when negotiating the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control. Indeed, the tobacco industry and major states, including the United States and China, exerted continual pressured to abandon or weaken the Convention. Even more challenging, World Health Organization officials and health ministry representatives on state delegations were inexperienced with treatymaking. Despite these circumstances, the Convention contains a markedly strong set of obligations. Existing theories centered on major state power and domestic politics cannot explain this outcome. Drawing on a document analysis, this paper argues that the Convention's unexpected strength is explained by the distribution and uses of institutional, principled, and expert authority by a diverse coalition of state and non-state actors that shared a vision, evidence basis, and moral claims for the treaty. As international health-related treaties can help advance progress on pressing transnational health issues, and contemporary negotiations face resistance from industry opponents, this work offers important insight on how multistakeholder coalitions can negotiate strong obligations under the most challenging conditions.

title: Empowered yet accountable? Digitalisation and the shifting boundaries of responsibility in healthcare; A qualitative investigation with patients and healthcare professionals
abstract: Responsibility for illness management is being reconfigured changing professional practices and increasing expectations of patient self-management, e.g. through digitalisation. This article examines how responsibility is produced, distributed and enacted between patients, healthcare professionals and healthcare institutions. This study draws upon 54 qualitative interviews with 38 patients and 16 healthcare professionals in Danish hospital settings. The work utilizes abductive thematic analysis informed by perspectives on governmentality and responsibilisation (Foucault, Lupton) and Bourdieu's concepts of capital and habitus. The findings show that digitalisation redistributes not only access to health information, but also the interpretive and coordinative work required to manage illness. Patients are increasingly expected to monitor, interpret and act upon information, while professional authority over legitimate knowledge and treatment largely remains intact. This produces an important tension between roles and responsibilities. Moreover, patients' capacity to act responsibly is shaped by their social positions and available economic, cultural, health and digital capital. We conceptualise responsibility as an organisational and relational effect emerging at the intersection of patients, professionals and digital healthcare infrastructures. Digitalisation may consequently enable participation and agency while simultaneously intensifying burdens and reproducing existing social inequalities.

title: Migrant labour and antimicrobial resistance in two Nepali factories: A biosocial analysis
abstract: Occupational environments contribute to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) through pollutants, injuries and the everyday use of medicines. This mixed-method study, conducted in 2023 and 2024, explores the biosocial dynamics linking working conditions and antibiotic resistance among migrant and local workers in a cement factory and a steel factory in Nepal. Combining ethnographic observation, survey data and microbiological testing, we compare labour organisation, occupational hazards, antibiotic use and Escherichia coli (E. coli) susceptibility across the two sites. Hazards and injuries were structured differently between the factories. In the steel factory, migrant workers used more antibiotics to treat work-related illness. Reduced E. coli susceptibility was more common among migrant workers in the steel factory, and among local workers in the cement factory. The organisation of industrial work and labour migration contribute to the multifactorial development of AMR, alongside clinical and agricultural antibiotic use. Combining ethnography, pharmacology and microbiology, our biosocial analysis identifies the workplace as an under-recognised site in the production of AMR and points to the need for occupationally grounded approaches to AMR prevention.

title: “Dr. TikTok”: How algorithms suggest ADHD and autism diagnoses
abstract: The internet allows patients to take a more active role in the diagnostic process, as the interactivity of "Dr. Google" and other online symptom-checkers demonstrates. Social media has emerged as a locus where (self-)diagnoses can be made through social interaction with others who identify as holding diagnostic identities. This paper builds on a foundation of research analyzing TikToks about ADHD and autism and the platform's content recommendation algorithm to examine how users are served content that implies that they occupy a given diagnosis, representing a distinct iteration of Dr. Google. The algorithm, not the user, could trigger the diagnostic process by labeling the user with a diagnosis or other pathologizing characteristics. I analyze how the TikTok algorithm encourages content themes and forms that may alter public perception of the boundaries, characteristics, and prevalence of ADHD and autism, as well as their entanglement with each other and the label of neurodivergence. I engage with the TikTok algorithm using digital ethnographic and discourse analysis approaches to understand "Dr. TikTok" as an example of how diagnostic pathways may be becoming increasingly mediated by AI systems. I find that the TikTok algorithm shapes TikToks about ADHD and autism by encouraging creators to engage in practices like speaking in second-person to the viewer and positioning relatable experiences as a form of subjective diagnostic expertise, situating these videos as paradoxically hyperpersonalized, yet inclusive. This study contributes to the sociology of medicine by showing how AI systems could intervene in and reorder the traditional diagnostic process.

title: Violence exposure across the life-course and allostatic load: Applying the structural life course modeling approach to examine violence temporal patterns and the promotive and protective role of adolescent social connectedness
abstract: Exposure to violence is a major public health concern whose physiological consequences accumulate across the life-course in ways that are not yet fully understood. Although violence exposure has been linked to elevated allostatic load markers (AL), no study has directly compared whether developmental timing, cumulative burden or recency of exposure most strongly drives this relationship, nor whether adolescent social connectedness operates through promotive effects, protective effects, or both to mitigate these physiological consequences. Using data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), and the Structured Life Course Modeling Approach (SLCMA), this study addressed both gaps by simultaneously testing three competing temporal hypotheses and examining whether peer, school, and parent connectedness during adolescence operated through promotive or protective pathways. Results revealed that cumulative violence exposure across development showed the strongest association with adult AL, outperforming both developmental timing-specific and recency-based hypotheses. Of the three social connectedness domains examined, only peer connectedness demonstrated significant promotive effects on reducing AL, while no domain buffered the relationship between cumulative violence exposure and adult AL. These findings suggest that the cumulative burden of violence across development, not when it occurs, drives physiological dysregulation, and that peer relationships during adolescence may represent a unique and lasting pathway to promote physiological health. Given that elevated AL is a strong risk factor for chronic disease and premature mortality, sustained efforts to reduce violence exposure across the life course and strengthen adolescent peer relationships are warranted as complementary public health priorities.

title: Paraprofessionals as liminal professionals: The case of physician associates / assistants in the UK NHS hospitals
abstract: We examine how paraprofessional physician associates/assistants (PAs) experience and navigate their everyday work, drawing on 126 interviews and one focus group across five NHS hospitals in England and Scotland. PAs described sustained ambiguity around their professional regulation and scope of practice, their ambiguous positioning between doctors and nurses, and organisationally being physically embedded within medical teams but governed under non-medical frameworks. We explain PAs' experiences of liminal enduring status drawing on Söderlund and Borg's (2018) conceptualisation of liminal process, position, and place. Moreover, to analyse this ongoing liminality, we introduce the concept of liminal markers - the material, symbolic, and organisational features, such as human resource classification, pay bands, governance arrangements, uniforms and everyday artefact - through which liminality is made visible and stabilised. We explain how PAs respond to enduring liminality with collective identity work oriented towards local legitimacy, relational continuity, and narrowing temporal focus to immediate clinical practice. We also conceptually reframe paraprofessional PAs' liminality as structurally embedded and collectively sustained, rather than temporary transitionary experience.

title: Which good practice exists for policymaking under uncertainty? An interdisciplinary review with relevance for health technology assessment (HTA)
abstract: Appropriate policymaking under uncertainty can lead to better decisions around how constrained resources are used. Although approaches from the technical sciences can provide robust, generalisable uncertainty estimations, they cannot account for the varying social, economic, and cultural contexts in which policies are made and implemented. We evaluated current health technology assessment (HTA) practice, finding limited consideration of social science perspectives, which may be inadequate for policies that influence behaviour, cross jurisdictions, or deal with multiple vested interests. To identify approaches that could address this gap, we conducted an interdisciplinary review of frameworks for policymaking under uncertainty, using an iterative approach for cross-disciplinary learning. We applied a comprehensive pearl growing search strategy and conducted inductive analysis combining grounded theory coding with pattern matching. We identified fourteen approaches to facilitate social science conceptualisations of uncertainty that are currently missing from HTA practice, alongside features of the decision problem and context that influence approach selection. Within the context of HTA, our analysis suggests that these approaches would be most applicable for interventions that change how care is delivered, highly contentious policy questions, and settings with poor implementation of HTA recommendations. We illustrate the applicability of our findings for three HTA challenges where conventional approaches are proving insufficient: reducing unnecessary caesarean section, reimbursement of locally manufactured products, and integrating patient voice in policymaking. We conclude that the policy questions reaching HTA agencies increasingly require a social science perspective, but that successfully doing so will require capacity building, philosophical alignment, and institutional adaptation.

title: Buy or rent? Mental health risk trade-offs from job loss between homeownership and mortgage debt
abstract: Housing wealth and homeownership are major determinants of health, with numerous studies pointing to long-term benefits. Many people consider homeownership an important, culturally normative and financially incentivised achievement in life. However, homeownership involves time-sensitive trade-offs: housing purchases are often mortgage-financed, which require regular payments and increase susceptibility to employment shocks. This article examines whether mortgage debt offsets a protective effect of homeownership on mental health after job loss in a quasi-causal staggered difference-in-differences design. We use large population-wide linked registry data from Finland between 2001 and 2019 to identify individuals who experienced long unemployment spells with and without mortgage-financed housing purchases in the three years before the job loss event. We then compare their trajectories of adverse mental health events and medication purchases against two separate control frames of homeowners and of tenants. Our results show that while mortgage strain impairs mental health primarily in the run-up to job loss in comparison to other homeowners, we find a longer-term advantage compared to tenants. However, when opportunities on the job market are scarce, the negative reaction may last longer. The results support the idea that wealth cushions economic shocks, and that debt primarily erodes these benefits in the short term.

title: Digital health literacy interventions for older adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of effects and intervention components
abstract: Although digital health literacy interventions for older adults have increased, it remains unclear which components are commonly used, and which may be linked to greater improvement. We conducted systematic review and meta-analysis and used the user- and task-oriented domains of the Transactional Model of eHealth Literacy to develop a theory-informed framework for mapping intervention targets and delivery features. English-language intervention studies published over the past two decades were identified through scientific databases. Twenty-three studies involving 3702 older adults were included, including seven randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Component mapping showed that most interventions targeted knowledge and technological skills, whereas task-oriented features varied in delivery channel, content or resource source, and instructional modality. Five RCTs contributed to the primary comparative meta-analysis, which showed a moderate improvement in digital health literacy favoring intervention groups over control conditions (SMD = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.08-0.86). A supplementary synthesis of uncontrolled within-group pre-post changes also indicated improvement, but these findings were exploratory. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested larger observed improvements in interventions integrating digital and health-related knowledge and skills than in those focusing on digital competencies alone. No clear subgroup differences were found by delivery channel, content or resource source, instructional modality, or relational support. Comparative evidence suggests that these interventions can improve older adults' digital health literacy, although the limited number of RCTs and substantial heterogeneity warrant caution. The component-level findings are exploratory and require confirmation in comparative studies. Interventions combining health-related knowledge with practical digital skills appear promising and warrant further evaluation in RCTs.

title: Ecological resilience and psychosocial utility among adolescents during societal instability: A utility-based economic evaluation
abstract: BACKGROUND: Adolescent psychosocial well-being has become a major global public health concern, particularly during periods of societal instability. Although ecological resilience systems within families, schools, and peer environments are recognized as important protective factors, little is known about their broader population-health and economic significance. This study examined whether ecological resilience is associated with psychosocial utility and explored its potential economic relevance using a utility-based evaluation framework. METHODS: Using data from 22,818 participants in the Israeli (2022-2023) Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) survey, we examined associations between ecological resilience and psychosocial utility. An Ecological Resilience Index (ERI) was constructed from family, school, and peer domains, and a Psychosocial Utility Index (PUI) was derived from mental well-being, life satisfaction, and psychosomatic functioning. Associations were evaluated using adjusted models, and utility differences were translated into exploratory economic valuation scenarios. RESULTS: Adolescents exposed to higher levels of ecological resilience demonstrated substantially greater psychosocial utility than those exposed to lower levels. The adjusted incremental utility difference was 0.2351. School and family resilience demonstrated the strongest associations with psychosocial utility. Scenario-based economic analyses suggested potentially substantial social value associated with resilience-related utility gains across a range of valuation assumptions. CONCLUSIONS: Ecological resilience systems embedded within family, school, and peer environments were strongly associated with adolescent psychosocial well-being. The findings suggest that resilience-promoting social environments may represent an important population-health resource and could have broader societal and economic relevance. Longitudinal research is needed to evaluate causal pathways and economic impacts.

title: Small area estimates of co-occurring health risk factors: A test of two synthetic population methodologies to estimate small-area prevalence of smoking, harmful alcohol consumption and obesity in England
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Small area estimates in health research currently capture single indicators but fail to reflect concurrent overlaps in health risk factors like smoking, increased alcohol consumption, and obesity. Local governments need detailed estimates of these risk factors to plan public health intervention strategies and tackle health inequalities. However, local data are often unavailable or highly restricted. This paper addresses this critical data gap by providing novel small area estimations of co-occurring health risk factors in England. METHODS: To generate the local estimates, we employ a spatial microsimulation approach for synthetic population generation using two alternative population synthesis algorithms: Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) and Simulated Annealing (SA). These approaches integrated individual microdata from Health Survey for England (HSE) data with small-area demographic constraints (sex, age, ethnicity, qualifications, partnership status and socioeconomic classifications) derived from the 2021 Office for National Statistics Census and was representative of a single year (2022). Small area estimates of three health risk factors: tobacco smoking, obesity, and harmful alcohol consumption, were modelled and validated against official independent aggregated benchmark data to Local Authority and/or Region level. RESULTS: Both methods produced small area estimates consistent with observed regional patterns. Analysis revealed smoking and obesity share similar spatial distributions, whereas alcohol consumption exhibits a distinct geographical profile. The resulting fine-grained analysis enabled the exploration of geographical areas of high estimated prevalence for co-occurring risk factors and overlaps between different sociodemographic characteristics. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates the utility of synthetic populations in estimating co-occurring health risk factors in small areas. Estimates from the synthetic populations can provide public health decision-makers and local governments with a vital tool for identifying local behaviour patterns, facilitating targeted, evidence-based public health interventions.

title: Tragedy normalised through inevitability: A culture of indifference in rural Malawi's maternity services
abstract: The systemic challenges confronting healthcare workers are often framed through individualistic concepts like burnout and moral injury, yet this obscures how these conditions produce a broader, collective transformation of the institutional care environment. The present study addresses this gap by investigating how the many challenges in rural Malawian district hospitals transform the broader work environment that ultimately impacts the quality of care. Employing an institutional ethnographic approach, the study drew on observation and in-depth interviews conducted in two district hospitals in rural Malawi. Our findings indicate that the many ongoing systemic challenges produced institutional-level collective behavioural responses that normalised detachment from patient care. We label this detachment as "culture of indifference," a sedimented, organisational-level orientation that is woven into the informal norms, unwritten rules, and taken-for-granted practices as the normalised way of functioning. The culture of indifference is a self-sustaining cycle composed of three mutually reinforcing elements: a systemic lack of effort to improve working conditions, a normalisation of dysfunction, and resigned passivity. For quality improvement initiatives to be effective in such settings, they must engage not only with individual behaviours but with the institutional culture that produces and reproduces them. This requires attending to what healthcare workers themselves identify as constraints on their practice and addressing the systemic signals that convey to those on the front lines that their work and their patients do not matter.

title: The impact of social safety net policies on mental health and suicide outcomes in the United States: A scoping review
abstract: Existing evidence indicates that there are reciprocal relationships between economic insecurity and poor mental health and suicidal behavior. In the United States, prior research shows that state and federal policies that increase social safety net program benefits or eligibility contribute to improved economic security. Thus, these policies may affect mental health and suicide outcomes. The aim of this scoping review was to synthesize the state of the evidence on the impact of state and federal social safety net policies on mental health, suicidal behavior, and suicide death. Of 64 identified studies, state or federal social safety net policies examined included those specific Earned Income Tax Credits (EITC; N = 14), minimum wage (N = 11), paid family or sick leave (N = 9), the 2021 Child Tax Credit (CTC; N = 8), the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP; N = 6), unemployment insurance benefits (N = 5), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF; N = 3), economic stimulus payments (N = 2) and eviction moratoriums (N = 2) during the COVID-19 pandemic, and multiple programs (N = 4). Most studies examined a single policy (N = 60), and more studies examined mental health outcomes (N = 53) than suicide outcomes (N = 15). Most studies that examined state or federal EITC, paid family or medical leave, the 2021 CTC, SNAP, TANF, unemployment insurance benefit, COVID-19 economic impact payment, and COVID-19 eviction moratorium policies found decreases in at least one measure of poor mental health, suicidal behavior, or suicide death. Studies that examined state minimum wage policies had mixed results. This body of research can be used to inform current policy debates and advance evidence-driven policymaking.

title: Stress in context: Social determinants, coping, and policy implications in a quota-matched Austrian sample
abstract: Stress is a near-universal experience with profound health implications, yet population-level data on its prevalence and effective coping strategies remain limited. This preregistered study examined the prevalence of stress, coping behaviours, and their associations with well-being in a quota-matched sample (N = 1099) from Austria, a high-income country with a robust social safety net. Using validated scales alongside novel stress and coping inventories, we found that 7.3% of participants reported extreme stress, with self-imposed pressure, commuting, and constant availability emerging as dominant stressors. Higher perceived support availability was associated with higher well-being but did not moderate the stress-well-being relationship. Self-selected coping (e.g., gardening, yoga) was associated with a weaker cross-sectional relationship between stress and well-being. Women reported higher stress than men descriptively, though this did not hold in covariate-adjusted models. Results suggest that in high-resource contexts, structural supports and individualized coping tools may play complementary roles.

title: Sailing between fate and control: Health systems resilience in the Caribbean Netherlands
abstract: Small, non-sovereign islands remain largely absent from the health policy and systems research literature, despite facing distinct governance challenges, rooted in logistical challenges, sociogeographical isolation, and post-colonial entanglements. We therefore studied how health system actors on Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, and Saba - three islands and 'special municipalities' of the Netherlands in the Caribbean - enact health systems resilience in everyday practice. We draw on multi-sited ethnographic research conducted between February and December 2024. We collected 44 interviews, 60 h of observations across disaster preparedness and crisis meetings, and analysed 109 policy documents. Our analysis followed an iterative, abductive approach, moving continuously between empirical data and a practice-based sociological health systems resilience framework. Our analysis identified three interrelated practices of health systems resilience: prioritising risks, building and mobilising alliances, and working with(in) double roles. Together, these practices reveal how health systems resilience on small islands works as an active process of mediating the space between managerial control and the recognition of fate; that is: uncertainties beyond full anticipation. We show that practices of health systems resilience may simultaneously reproduce structural vulnerabilities, mask governance deficits, and normalise conditions of persistent precarity. With our analysis, we contribute to theoretical debates about what health systems resilience means in practice and extend the limited empirical literature on health systems in non-sovereign small island geographies. We argue that the health policy and systems literature should engage more systematically with such peripheralised settings, where everyday ingenuity coexists with, and partly compensates for, structural inequalities.

title: Corrigendum to ‘Place and brain health: A community-led yarning study with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia’ [Soc. Sci. Med. 408 (2026) 119799]
Institutional maintenance of an elite profession: The case of performance-related pay in the English medical profession
abstract: This paper examines the medical profession's institutional work in maintaining its power in reward allocation committees. Although professionals can act as agents who create and disrupt institutions, this paper investigates their work in maintaining institutions by adhering to and reproducing the social processes and practices that support and enable their position of relative power. We elaborate and extend this theoretical focus through an empirical study of the performance-based reward system (our focal institution) for senior doctors in the English and Welsh National Health Service (NHS). We draw on empirical data from the observation of English national committees that allocated (national) Clinical Excellence Awards (CEAs), a form of pay for performance. We address the ways in which doctors were able to interpret the purpose of CEAs, to influence the way in which medical performance was assessed, and to navigate issues of self-interest and governance. Findings illuminate and elaborate the nuanced and often-hidden institutional work of elite members of the profession and extend prior analyses of institutional maintenance work by suggesting strategic invisibility as a previously overlooked element.

title: Recent Canadian immigration reforms and their consequences for migrant children and families’ health: the “globalization of indifference”?
abstract: Despite its reputation as a welcoming nation to refugees, Canada has enforced increasing restrictions on asylum, even in the face of evidence from the United States and around the world of the profound harm such restrictions cause. In this paper, we outline recent Canadian legal and policy reforms and their potential impacts on refugee health equity. Following Farmer's approach of ethnographic case narratives that aim to portray how current policy and legislation are embodied and felt in migrants' lives, we document avoidable harms to migrant children and families. Our data come from qualitative research with inadmissible asylum seekers and narrative pastiches from clinical encounters. We discuss the potential public health implications given the existing evidence on the social determinants of refugee mental and physical health. Given the global push towards increasing restrictions on migration and asylum, we ask what clinicians are to do when they are confronted by the social and political conditions that produce suffering for migrant children and families, but we also explore our clinical and political obligations to bring into view those who are rendered invisible by marginalizing policies. Ultimately, we call for a clinical ethics that resists the institutionalization and 'globalization of indifference'.

title: AI representations of mental health stigma: Quantifying the gap between AI estimations and human perceptions across gender groups using GPT-based LLMs
abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in mental health applications raises concerns about its potential to internalize and perpetuate societal biases. This research evaluates both disparities and misalignment in how large language models (LLMs), GPT-4 and GPT-5, represent perceptions of mental health across gender groups. The research comprises two studies. Study 1 applied widely adopted measures of Social Distance, Stereotypes, and Attitudes Toward Seeking Help to assess whether the AI models depict systematic gender differences. Study 2 compared AI estimations of Personal, Self, and Perceived Stigma with large-scale real-world human data from the Healthy Minds Study (N = 76,406) to evaluate alignment between AI estimations and human perceptions. Results from Study 1 showed the AI models consistently portrayed men as having the greatest desire for social distance from someone with mental health problems, relatively higher Stereotypes scores, and the least favorable attitudes toward help-seeking, compared with women and nonbinary individuals. Study 2 confirmed that this ordinal pattern partially aligned with human-reported data for Personal and Self Stigma. However, the AI models systematically underestimated Personal Stigma and Perceived Stigma while substantially overestimating Self Stigma for all gender groups. These findings reveal that, although the AI models have learned relative gender-based patterns reflecting human experiences to a certain extent, they function as distorted portrayals, highlighting the need for rigorous, context-specific validation against real-world data to ensure AI's safe and equitable deployment.

title: Positive emotions and credibility: Understanding how a community-engaged online campaign featuring clinician testimonials improved rural vaccine promotion
abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine hesitancy emerged as a public health challenge in the U.S., particularly affecting rural communities. This study examined the effectiveness of a community-engaged campaign, Communities Confronting COVID-19 (C3), in promoting COVID-19 vaccines among rural residents. Using a single-session four-arm randomized survey experiment involving N = 1364 rural residents, this study provided empirical evidence for the effectiveness of featuring clinicians serving rural communities as vaccine ambassadors and utilizing their personal testimonials in a community-engaged campaign. Results showed that, compared to non-testimonial clinician videos, rural clinician testimonials were rated as more effective by rural audiences. Rural clinician testimonials were associated with higher positive emotions and subsequently showed positive indirect associations with Perceived Message Effectiveness, perceived social benefits of COVID-19 vaccines, and general vaccine confidence. Furthermore, compared to rural community leaders, rural clinicians were associated with higher perceived social benefits of COVID-19 vaccines. Rural clinicians were also rated with higher credibility as vaccine advocates, which in turn was associated with higher Perceived Message Effectiveness, perceived social benefits of the vaccines, and general vaccine confidence. Neither condition significantly reduced vaccine misbeliefs nor provoked reactance. These findings highlight the key indirect roles of positive emotions and messenger credibility in promoting COVID-19 vaccines and rebuilding general vaccine confidence, offering actionable design insights for evidence-based campaigns to support vaccine confidence in underserved rural populations.

title: “I've got to believe in something”: Trust, cancer survivorship, and investing agency
abstract: The event of a life-limiting cancer diagnosis requires decisions from those diagnosed about the course of action they will take. In what can be an overwhelming event people tend to follow the normative route of using conventional medicine. But for some, this route might be rejected, and for others, it might be supplemented with other approaches. In this article we explore these matters through lens(es) of 'trust'. The study was undertaken with 81 participants diagnosed with life-limiting cancer. Participants' trust practices were variably associated with trust in self, individuals, organisations and systems. We consider the ways in which participants maintained trust, or how trust was disrupted and transformed, and what might influence these processes. We identify categories of trusting practices: dependent trusting, reflexive interdependent trusting in conventional medicine, reflexive interdependent trusting in other therapeutic systems, and mistrusting dependency. We then apply these categories of trust to the talk of our Māori participants to consider the similarities and the different realities of trusting practices for indigenous New Zealanders. We consider these trust practices conceptualised as the investment of one's agency and propose that this offers insights into the variable enactments of trust noted by our participants.

title: “Attention to the person who prepared the questionnaire”: Queer men's survey marginalia in HIV behavioural surveillance
abstract: Survey marginalia are the unsolicited annotations left by participants in the margins of questionnaires. Marginalia can offer valuable insight into how participants perceive study instruments and researchers, the meanings behind their responses, and add nuance to lived experiences that are otherwise obscured or unaccounted for in survey design. This paper presents a qualitative analysis of survey marginalia left by participants of a pen-and-paper HIV behavioural surveillance survey administered in person to sexual minority men at 2S/LGBTQ+ pride events across Canada. Using interpretive description and reflexive thematic analysis, we analyzed 671 unique data items contributed by 404 participants, representing 12% of the survey sample. Our analysis identified three overarching themes characterizing how participants engaged with the survey through marginalia: (1) Answer Unasked Questions, in which participants used marginalia to introduce identities and experiences that the survey otherwise did not account for; (2) Avoid Misclassification, in which participants provided contextual information to prevent misclassification of "risk behaviours"; and (3) Talk Back, in which participants engaged in critical dialogue with researchers, challenging assumptions, questioning the validity of survey items, and offering direct feedback. Drawing on queer theory and community-based research principles, we interpret these findings as evidence that participants actively resisted classificatory logics and asserted authority over how their lives and identities should be represented. We argue that survey marginalia are not methodological noise but a substantive resource for reflexivity and the co-production of knowledge in public health research. Practical recommendations for the design and administration of HIV behavioural surveillance surveys and research with queer people are offered.

title: Alternative visions: The strategic partial medicalization of ibogaine treatment
abstract: Ibogaine is a psychedelic substance classified as an illegal drug that has been found to have addiction interrupting properties. Over decades of uncontrolled experimentation, user groups in semi-clandestine networks have developed treatment protocols for substance abuse disorder using ibogaine. However, in the ongoing psychedelic renaissance, investors and startups are exploring the possibilities of using ibogaine or chemical analogs in mainstream therapy. This medicalization of ibogaine is viewed with ambivalence among ibogaine providers. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with providers, community organizers, medical professionals and venture capitalists, complemented with ethnographic observations of ibogaine conferences and clinics, we argue that a subset of the ibogaine community engage in a strategic partial medicalization, embracing some parts while rejecting others. Striving to legitimize their own healing practices, they embrace biomedical explanations of the substance's action but reject the idea of pharmaceuticalizing its administration. The case is illustrative of trade-offs that need to be made when alternative healing practices struggle for legitimacy. It provides a complementary perspective on the psychedelic renaissance that can inform ongoing debates about medicalization and pharmaceuticalization.

title: “It was so easy, it didn't feel real:” Positive abortion experiences post-Dobbs
abstract: Research on abortion has disproportionately focused on legal restrictions, barriers, and stigma, contributing to a "joy deficit" in scholarship and creating epistemic foreclosures on how researchers, professionals, and abortion seekers may envision an abortion seeking experience. This study explores the positive emotions and experiences that abortion seekers had while navigating a restrictive post-Dobbs context. We conducted 81 in-depth interviews with abortion seekers from Ohio, Kentucky, and West Virginia between July 2022 and June 2025 who experienced difficulties obtaining an abortion in their state. Despite multiple financial, logistical, and emotional challenges, most participants described positive dimensions of abortion seeking, including compassionate interactions with clinic staff, practical and financial support from abortion funds, feelings of relief and joy, and unexpectedly supportive responses from friends, family, and strangers. Many participants expressed surprise at the amount of support available and lack of judgment from staff and loved ones. Positive interactions often counteracted the burdens imposed by legal and logistical barriers and, in some cases, contributed to abortion destigmatization by encouraging disclosure and normalizing abortion within social relationships. While all participants experienced barriers obtaining an abortion, most did not have solely negative experiences. The findings from this study demonstrate that abortion is a multifaceted experience, and future research efforts should focus on analyzing positive aspects of abortion seeking in restrictive settings to increase accessibility and destigmatize abortion.

title: The hidden injuries of work: Institutional invisibility, precarity, and the recognition of occupational harm. A scoping review
abstract: Work-related injuries and occupational illnesses constitute a substantial but unevenly recognised burden on workers and health systems. While work can provide income, social protection, and social integration, it can also expose workers to physical, psychosocial, and organisational hazards, and the resulting harm remains unevenly documented within occupational health and safety (OHS) systems. Growing evidence indicates that official statistics and compensation and surveillance systems incompletely capture work-related harm, including among workers in precarious or temporary employment and migrant workers. This scoping review examines how work-related injuries and illnesses become institutionally invisible within systems of reporting, recognition, compensation, and surveillance. Drawing on 59 peer-reviewed publications conducted in or including middle- and high-income settings and published between 2015 and April 2026, the review synthesises evidence on the mechanisms through which occupational harm is underreported, misclassified, suppressed, or excluded from institutional records. The review followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with findings synthesised using a thematic, multilevel analytical approach. Across the literature, institutional invisibility may emerge through cumulative processes of invisibilisation rather than isolated reporting failures. These mechanisms include constraints on reporting, organisational practices such as claim suppression and incomplete recordkeeping, and institutional filters involving classification, compensation, surveillance, and regulation. They intersect with employment precarity and stratified protection, contributing to uneven institutional visibility among differently positioned groups of workers. Beyond surveillance bias, invisibility may also have downstream clinical and occupational consequences, including delayed access to care, compensation, rehabilitation, and return-to-work support. By proposing an integrative framework for understanding how occupational harm becomes institutionally invisible, this review contributes to debates in public health and health systems research on evidence production, risk governance, and health equity. It underscores the importance of incorporating occupational recognition into health equity agendas and addressing the institutional processes that shape whether work-related harm becomes visible and actionable.

title: Enacting the body multiple: Wellness strategies among younger adults under biopolitical health governance and accelerated study–labour regimes
abstract: Contemporary Chinese younger adults face a structural contradiction between the state-promoted biopolitics of 'Healthy China 2030' and accelerated work and study regimes. This study examines how young people enact and coordinate multiple bodily realities through everyday wellness practices and seek to maintain a workable body under these competing demands. Grounded in Annemarie Mol's theory of enactment, a reflexive thematic analysis of netnographic observations and 28 semi-structured interviews identifies four representative embodied strategies: punk wellness, modern medical wellness, traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) wellness, and hybrid wellness. These strategies reflect different modes and degrees of bodily coordination, ranging from low-integration bricolage to coordination within a dominant bodily reality and, finally, reflexive meta-coordination across modern medical and TCM-derived practices. The study introduces 'reflexive fluency' to capture hybrid wellness practitioners' embodied capacity to navigate heterogeneous health repertoires and bodily realities. As a form of embodied cultural capital, this fluency reveals emerging patterns of health stratification. By shifting the focus of 'coordination' from medical institutions to individuals, the study shows how mundane bodily practices become a means of managing structural constraints. These findings contribute to debates on biopolitics, embodiment, and health stratification in post-reform China.

title: “Their body is their territory”: Reproductive autonomy and governance by omission in Peru
abstract: Drawing on 22 in-depth interviews with government officials, civil society leaders, multilateral and community-based actors, we examine how reproductive autonomy is shaped, constrained, and contested within Peru's sexual and reproductive health (SRH) system. The findings point to a cascade of constraints across three levels. At the macro-level, political avoidance, conservative influence, and the enduring legacy of Fujimori-era forced sterilizations have produced sustained silence around SRH, limiting leadership, accountability, and investment. At the meso-level, this silence translates into institutional fragility, including supply shortages, uneven implementation, and weak oversight, which narrow contraceptive choice. At the micro-level, institutional weakness expands provider discretion, allowing moral reasoning, risk aversion, and gendered expectations to shape whether individuals can initiate, change, or discontinue contraception. These constraints are not experienced evenly: adolescents, rural populations, and low-income women are most affected, resulting in reproductive autonomy that is stratified. Participants described ongoing efforts to contest these constraints. Civil society organizations, youth networks, and community actors engage in rights-based education, institutional oversight, strategic litigation, and everyday advocacy. While these efforts do not resolve the underlying political and institutional conditions, they create spaces where reproductive rights can be asserted, defended, and monitored. We conceptualize these dynamics as governance by omission: a mode of reproductive governance in which reproductive autonomy is constrained and shaped through political silence, institutional drift, and expanded discretion, rather than through coercive policies, numerical targets, or formal prohibitions. This framework demonstrates how reproductive autonomy can be legally recognized yet unevenly realized. Furthermore, it highlights that without government presence, autonomy is fragile.

title: Work without a roadmap: A qualitative analysis of occupational and structural challenges among adolescent peer workers in HIV programs in Kenya
abstract: Background Peer navigator programs are central to adolescent HIV service delivery across sub-Saharan Africa, particularly within differentiated and community-based care models. While evidence demonstrates their effectiveness in improving engagement, retention, and psychosocial support, less attention has been paid to the labor conditions under which peer navigators operate. Drawing on feminist political economy, this study examines how peer navigation is organized, experienced, and sustained within resource-constrained health systems. Methods In-depth interviews were conducted with 30 participants at two HIV clinics in western Kenya: current peer navigators (n = 11, 55% female, median age 25), former peer navigators (n = 6, 33% female, median age 31), and healthcare workers (n = 13, 100% female). Interviews explored the structure, expectations, and lived experiences of peer navigation roles. Data were analyzed thematically, with attention to the temporal, economic, gendered, and professional dimensions of peer labor. Results Peer navigation was described as meaningful and impactful work structured by layered forms of precarity. Four key themes emerged. First, peer navigators experienced "boundary-less" work characterized by continuous availability and emotional labor extending beyond formal hours, absorbing gaps in under-resourced health systems. Second, compensation was stipend-based, producing financial insecurity, limited benefits, and constrained capacity for self-care, while moral narratives of "helping" obscured structural inequities. Third, female peer navigators described gendered vulnerabilities, including sexualized expectations, harassment, and safety risks, often without formal protections. Fourth, participants highlighted the absence of clear professional pathways, with limited opportunities for advancement or integration into the formal health workforce. Conclusions Peer navigation functions as undervalued care labor sustaining HIV services in resource-constrained settings. As peer-based models scale, sustainability must include fair compensation, formal protections, supervision, and structured career pathways.

title: Intersectional and territorial exclusion in Brazil's aging policy field: A critical analysis of access to bodily practices and inequalities
abstract: Brazil is aging rapidly, and deep social and territorial inequalities shape who can take part in the socially and culturally constituted forms of physical activity and leisure of later life (bodily practices). We asked how Brazil's aging policy documents frame active aging and access to these practices, and how they reproduce or challenge inequality. We analyzed 14 governmental, intergovernmental, and institutional documents published between 1994 and 2025, assembling and coding the corpus between January and June 2025. We combined reflexive thematic analysis with a critical, poststructural reading of policy discourse, guided by intersectional and decolonial perspectives. We identified four interconnected mechanisms: (1) under universalism and erasure, documents treat older adults as one neutral group; (2) under responsibilization and moralized autonomy, they ask people to manage their own aging even while naming structural conditions; (3) under territorialized implementation gaps, they leave pathways loosely specified across unequal municipalities; and (4) under metrics, recognition, and policy silence, they rarely disaggregate by race, gender, or territory, which limits what policy can see and address. Taken together, the findings suggest that universal rights-based commitments may leave intersecting inequities insufficiently addressed. Such commitments stay broad promises unless implementation and monitoring name the racialized, gendered, economic, and territorial conditions people live in. For critical gerontology and public health, the study shows how policy categories and silences shape who is recognized in later life, in Brazil and across Latin America and the wider Global South.

title: Editorial Board
Unequal returns to effort? Gender differences in health status and lifestyle
abstract: Equality of opportunity suggests that observed differences in an outcome of interest should only reflect factors within individuals' control, namely effort, and not circumstances beyond their control, such as their parent's level of education or longevity. In the health field, lifestyles are typically considered as individual effort and are viewed as legitimate sources of health inequality. However, it remains unclear to what extent these effort-related factors contribute to gender differences in health status. Using data from the Survey on Health Ageing and Retirement, we examine differences in health and lifestyles related to physical exercise and fruits and vegetables intake between men and women. We use a Shapley decomposition and generate a multidimensional health score based on a set of health-related outcomes. Interaction terms between gender and lifestyles suggest that insufficient physical activity is more strongly associated with poorer health in men than in women, whereas infrequent consumption of fruits and vegetables is more strongly associated with poorer health in women than in men. Finally, the decomposition shows that family socio-economic background is the main contribution of heath inequalities among women, while the frequency of physical exercise is the main contribution of health inequalities among men. Our results encourage gender-specific prevention policies to improve population health.

title: Medicines, ‘medication work’ and networks of support in the community following mental health hospital discharge: A qualitative interview study
abstract: 'Medication work' is routine medicine-taking tasks and strategies that individuals employ to ensure safe medicine use. 'Social networks' the social ties and connectedness that link people together, are considered important in people's health. This study explored the views of people with lived experience of mental illness, carers, and health professionals of medicines use following mental health hospital discharge to understand 'medication work' and social support. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with participants, recruited via social media and the research team's professional networks. To explore medication support a diagram of support networks was co-produced with participants. Analysis, informed by critical realism, explored personal holistic accounts and networks of support. Analysis of 34 interviews conducted with 10 people with lived experience, 7 carers and 17 healthcare professionals revealed extensive 'medication work' following discharge. Themes were mapped to a conceptualisation of 'medication work' and a construct of 'situated medicines work' added to reflect wider social and cultural contexts. Health professionals were valued within personal support networks, particularly for people with lived experience, by facilitating medication taking through advice and knowledge, Family, friends, and voluntary organisations played practical and emotional roles 'medication work' roles. Medication safety following mental health hospital discharge relies heavily on support networks and the 'medication work' of patients and carers.
