Health professionals play a central but variable and contextual, role within these networks. Greater recognition of social support networks and the situated nature of 'medication work' is needed to improve post-discharge medication safety and support in community mental health care.

title: Medical need or moral hazard? Public insurance transitions and healthcare utilization in South Korea
abstract: In South Korea's dual public insurance system, National Medical Aid (NMA) beneficiaries use more healthcare than National Health Insurance (NHI) enrollees, a pattern often attributed to moral hazard arising from low cost-sharing. Higher use may instead reflect greater medical need among a socially vulnerable population. We distinguish these explanations using both insurance status and eligibility transitions. Using longitudinal data from the Korea Health Panel 2019-2023 (analytic sample 2020-2023), we analyzed three outpatient outcomes-any use, visit days, and out-of-pocket expenditure-with individual random-effects panel models (utilization, visit days) and GEE-based two-part models (expenditure). Static models compared NHI and NMA beneficiaries; dynamic models compared four annual transition types defined by insurance status in consecutive years. We further tested insurance-by-health-status interactions. NMA beneficiaries did not differ significantly from NHI enrollees in the probability of any outpatient use but had significantly more annual outpatient visit days and lower out-of-pocket spending. We also observed elevated visit days among individuals who transitioned from NMA to NHI, although this estimate was based on a small transition group. Additional visit days associated with NMA were concentrated among beneficiaries reporting poorer self-rated health, a pattern that was broadly maintained when prior-year health status was used. These findings are more consistent with sustained medical need than with widespread moral hazard. The findings underscore NMA's role as a financial safety net for medically vulnerable populations. Policies to contain spending among low-income populations should account for underlying health needs to avoid restricting necessary care.

title: Bringing it home: Couple health behavior discordance and the physiological returns to social participation in China
abstract: Objective Social participation is assumed to benefit whoever engages in it. We ask whether that benefit survives a marriage in which spouses keep different health behaviors. Background The health implications of social participation outside the household may depend on circumstances within the marriage. Dyadic and stress perspectives suggest that behavioral differences between spouses may shape its associations with physiological health. Method Using data from the 2011 and 2015 waves of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (N = 1705 couples), we estimated Actor-Partner Interdependence Models linking formal and informal social participation to subsequent allostatic load. Models included lifestyle and substance-use discordance, their interactions with social participation, and couple means and differences for each behavior. Results Both lifestyle and substance-use discordance weakened the association between wives' formal participation and lower AL. Wives' informal participation was associated with higher AL at low lifestyle discordance, but this association weakened as discordance increased. For partner associations, husbands' formal participation was associated with lower AL in wives at high discordance. No interactions predicting husbands' AL were statistically significant. Implications The findings support a dyadic perspective on social engagement. Programs that promote community engagement for older adults reach wives whose households already run smoothly, and largely miss those whose households do not. Behavioral alignment between spouses is a precondition for those programs to work, not a separate health target.

title: Decentralized governance in tiered healthcare systems: Supporting equity with blockchain
abstract: Tiered healthcare systems seek to support equity by coordinating care across primary, secondary, and tertiary healthcare delivery organizations, yet fragmented cross-tier coordination and persistent differences in organizational capacity and authority can create avoidable disadvantages. Blockchain can distribute selected operational functions across organizations, but technical decentralization alone does not determine how such coordination is governed or how existing power asymmetries are affected. Drawing on 45 semi-structured interviews with key actor groups in China's tiered healthcare systems, supplemented by targeted follow-up clarification of selected operational changes and technical conditions, this article examines how decentralized governance is organized in blockchain-enabled healthcare systems. We identify three connected processes: on-chain governance, cross-organization decision-making, and cross-tier care coordination. Together, these processes show how operational decentralization may support specific equity-oriented aims in cross-tier care while authority and organizational capacity remain uneven.

title: Working-time patterns, job-related well-being, and turnover intentions among paid caregivers: a population-based longitudinal study
abstract: Paid care often involves long working hours and shift work schedules, yet national evidence on caregivers' working-time patterns and their associations with well-being and turnover intentions remains limited. Drawing on the effort-recovery framework, we compared care workers and home carers with other workers. This population-based longitudinal study used six waves of the UK Household Longitudinal Study (2012-2024). Five working-time exposures were modelled separately: usual weekly hours, total overtime, paid overtime, weekend work and nonstandard schedules. Covariate-adjusted generalised estimating equations examined associations with job-related anxiety and depression, measured with Warr's job-related affective well-being scale, and intentions to change employer or leave paid employment. Hours and schedule samples included 1476 and 1492 caregivers, respectively. At the first eligible hours observation, caregivers averaged 39.2 years and 82.8% were women. Caregivers reported fewer unadjusted usual weekly hours (30.0 versus 32.1), yet 2.00 more hours after adjustment (95% CI 1.54-2.46). They also had a 0.396-point higher weekend-work score (95% CI 0.360-0.431) and 3.82 times the odds of nonstandard work (95% CI 3.43-4.25). Within caregivers, longer usual hours, total overtime, weekend work and nonstandard schedules were associated with greater job-related anxiety and depression. Paid overtime showed no clear association with either outcome. Nonstandard work was associated with wanting a new employer (OR 1.46, 95% CI 1.21-1.78). Evidence for wanting to give up paid work was limited. These findings highlight schedule timing alongside work duration as a focus for supporting caregiver well-being and workforce retention.

title: 'The only way out is through': The flexibility and limits of trauma discourse in psychedelic contexts
abstract: "Trauma" has become a widely circulating cultural framework for making suffering intelligible. Sociological research has documented its institutional expansion but paid less attention to how people use it to organize experiences that disrupt orientation to body, self, and world. This article examines that situated process in non-clinical psychedelic contexts. Drawing on 48 in-depth interviews with people who defined their psychedelic experiences as challenging, we trace how participants mobilized trauma discourse in response to ontological rupture. The analysis identifies five configurations of therapeutic sense-making: somatic discovery of trauma, embodied re-experiencing, the experience as healing instruction, the recursive healing project, and the limits of therapeutic sense-making. Across the first four, trauma discourse condensed diverse suffering into an authoritative category and supplied vocabularies for sequencing experience and directing action; we use personalization to describe how this shared framework becomes biographically meaningful. The fifth captures the cases where personalization broke down: the framework felt imposed, became a performance for others, or disclosed memories and revelations participants could not hold as real. Our abductive analysis of these cases generated three dimensions of authenticity: subjective ownership, non-performance, and realness. The findings point to a structural tension: we suggest that circulating trauma discourse beyond credentialed clinical and ritual authorities both expands the framework's flexibility and leaves personalization vulnerable to social pressure, unaccountable authority, and unresolved epistemic uncertainty. This study extends sociological critiques of therapeutization by shifting attention from the diffusion of therapeutic frameworks to the conditions of their uptake.

title: From exploitation to emergency room: Health care discrimination, utilization, and health outcomes among youth who experienced commercial sexual exploitation
abstract: Discrimination in health care settings presents a significant barrier to accessing quality care, particularly for youth with experiences of commercial sexual exploitation of children (CSEC). This study examines how discrimination within primary care and emergency room (ER) settings mediates the relationship between CSEC victimization and negative health outcomes. Using data from a sample of 534 young people who experienced or are at high risk for experiencing CSEC, we employ structural equation modeling (SEM) to test three models: (1) the association between health care discrimination and negative health outcomes among CSEC survivors, (2) the mediating role of discrimination in primary care settings on health outcomes for CSEC survivors, and (3) the extent to which discrimination mediates the link between CSEC experiences and health outcomes through ER use. Findings indicate that CSEC experiences are significantly associated with poorer physical and mental health outcomes, both directly and indirectly through increased exposure to health care discrimination. Specifically, discrimination from health care providers fully mediated the relationship between CSEC and negative health outcomes in models including emergency room use, while discrimination was not a significant mediator in models focused on primary care utilization. This distinction is crucial because ER settings are often the first point of contact for CSEC survivors, making them a critical area for intervention. These results highlight the importance of addressing discrimination in ER settings to reduce barriers to care and improve health outcomes for CSEC survivors. The study underscores the need for trauma-informed, non-discriminatory health care approaches to ensure equitable access to care for vulnerable youth.

title: When filial duty exceeds capacity: How moral obligations become caregiver distress
abstract: Family caregiving is usually explained through burden, yet comparable demands can produce different moral and psychological consequences. We conducted a longitudinal qualitative study with 76 adult children who were primary caregivers for older parents with advanced cancer across nine provinces in China. Repeat interviews traced how filial responsibility changed as illness progressed and palliative care entered family decision-making. Four linked processes were identified: care became part of moral identity; endurance became the expected response to prolonged uncertainty; human limits were interpreted as moral failure; and good care was reconstructed without abandoning commitment. We define filial moral distress as suffering generated when the care a person believes a good child should provide exceeds what can be sustained, and that discrepancy is judged as evidence of moral inadequacy. Relational, clinical and structural conditions could intensify or interrupt this process. The findings show how valued obligations become psychologically harmful through self-evaluation rather than through demands alone.

title: The ethical labour of overdiagnosis research: Negotiating care in early detection
abstract: Particularly in relatively well-funded healthcare systems, medicine increasingly seeks to detect disease before it causes symptoms. Early detection can prevent suffering and premature death, but it can also diagnose conditions that will never become harmful. Although the existence of overdiagnosis is supported by clinical and epidemiological literature, its implications for practice remain contested. This paper examines how clinicians and researchers decide what evidence of overdiagnosis should mean for good care and how they act on it (or not). Drawing on three years of ethnographic fieldwork at conferences and seminars on overdiagnosis and early detection in the UK and internationally, supplemented by formal interviews with attendees and many informal conversations, I examine how evidence about the benefits and harms of intervention is interpreted, debated and translated into practice. Using Barrett's oesophagus as a central case, I seek to make a conceptual contribution to the literature by identifying two overlapping ethical orientations found in these fields. An "ethics of doing" treats intervention as a responsible response to the possibility of future disease. An "ethics of restraint" treats limiting intervention as a way of protecting people from harms produced by diagnosis and treatment. These are not fixed positions held by opposing groups: the same people may move between them as they respond to different forms of risk, responsibility and uncertainty. I argue that evidence alone does not determine how evidence of overdiagnosis should be acted upon. The same uncertainty can support intervention, because clinicians cannot know in advance who will develop serious disease, or restraint, because they cannot know who will benefit from intervention. What is at stake is therefore not simply whether overdiagnosis exists, but how harms and responsibilities are understood. By treating overdiagnosis as an ethnographic problem, the paper shows how competing responses to early detection are made consequential in practice and produce divergent notions of care.

title: Procedural justice in the deceased-donor pathway before computerised organ matching in China
abstract: Computerised organ-allocation systems are designed to standardise clinical criteria, reduce discretionary intervention, and improve traceability. However, matching begins only after potential donors have been identified, referred, authorised, medically maintained, routed through institutions, and entered into the allocation system. Drawing on seven months of multi-sited qualitative fieldwork in China (2017-2018), this article examines how organisational processes upstream of matching shaped allocation pathways during system-building. Participant observation, interviews with 17 professionals, field conversations and documents inform four proposed mechanisms: relational donor visibility, informal referral brokerage, monetised organisational routing, and potential loss of organisational provenance at formal system entry. These mechanisms concern which donations reach matching, through which institutions and jurisdictions, and whether their histories remain traceable; they need not alter algorithmic rankings. From this historical case, the article develops upstream pathway inequality and algorithmic input blindness, and proposes pathway justice as a framework linking entry conditions, routing and matching fairness. The contribution is a conditional proposition: consistent ranking alone cannot secure procedural fairness where upstream pathways remain opaque or unevenly governed. It does not establish the persistence of the reported practices.

title: Does pain dampen future outlooks? Examining daily and decadal time horizons
abstract: Background Positive future orientations are increasingly recognized as both a health-promoting resource and an intrinsic aspect of human well-being, while dampened outlooks represent a form of deprivation. This article considers whether pain-a defining corollary of contemporary collective despair-has implications for how people imagine their futures in the short- and longer-term. Methods We use daily diary and survey data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study to consider two distinct time horizons: expectations for tomorrow and decade-out life trajectories. Study 1 assesses whether number of daily pain sites is linked to expectations for positive and stressful next-day experiences, while Study 2 uses conventional survey data to examine how chronic pain interference relates to future expectations across multiple domains of life. Both studies employ hybrid between-within panel models to decompose within-person variance at each time scale alongside more stable between-person differences. Results Day-to-day occurrences of pain are associated with more pessimistic next-day anticipations, as reflected by within-person increases predicting higher odds of expected stress and lower odds of uplifts (Study 1). Chronic pain interference, meanwhile, modestly dampens decade-out expectations (Study 2), with work, financial, and health outlooks most discernibly susceptible. Conclusion Our two-study design provides novel evidence that pain does indeed "cast a shadow" over both short-term and longer-term future orientations. In this sense, pain constitutes not only a biopsychosocial clinical symptom but also a threat to how people are able to inhabit time.

title: Structural stigma in public discourse: Exposure to anti-transgender rhetoric and mental health among transgender women in the United States
Climate resilience through residential solar energy: Reducing health risks from extreme temperatures
abstract: Residential solar photovoltaic (PV) systems are widely recognized for their environmental benefits-reducing greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution. This study uncovers a previously undocumented role: solar PV adoption serves as a buffer against heat-related mortality. Rising extreme temperatures pose growing public health risks, yet households' ability to maintain safe indoor temperatures through cooling depends critically on energy affordability. As electricity prices increase due to supply disruptions and geopolitical shocks, vulnerable populations face heightened exposure to temperature-related mortality. We examine whether distributed renewable energy-specifically residential solar PV installations-can mitigate these risks by reducing households' reliance on grid electricity during extreme heat events. We exploit a natural experiment created by the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake, which triggered electricity price increases of up to 38 percent following nuclear plant shutdowns. Using prefecture-by-month mortality data from Japan (2009-2014), we employ an instrumental variable strategy leveraging exogenous spatial and temporal variations in solar radiation and electricity prices to identify the causal effect of solar PV adoption on temperature-related mortality. Solar PV adoption significantly reduces heat-related mortality, with effects concentrated among individuals aged 65 and older. Effects are more pronounced in warmer regions and in areas with more energy usage constraints. No comparable effects are observed at cold temperatures, consistent with solar PV's strong summer generation profile. These findings show that distributed renewable energy provides direct health protection during climate extremes. However, because adoption remains concentrated among higher-income households, associated health benefits may accrue unevenly, highlighting the need for targeted policies.

title: Comparing biomedical and psychosocial-cultural models in reducing public stigma toward schizophrenia: A holistic experimental study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Existing studies have primarily examined how biogenetic explanations for the causes of mental illness influence stigma, while largely neglecting the impact of presenting psychiatric medication or medical techniques as the primary solutions. The present study addresses this gap by experimentally investigating the effects of presenting the full biomedical model, including both explanations and treatments for the symptoms of schizophrenia, to the public on stigma. Furthermore, it compares these effects with those of a psychosocial-cultural model across nine experimental conditions. This study was exploratory in nature. METHOD: A total of 1067 participants from China were randomly assigned to one of nine groups: 1) Diverse Explanation + Diverse Solution, 2) Diverse Explanation + Biomedical Solution, 3) Diverse Explanation Only, 4) Biomedical Explanation + Biomedical Solution, 5) Biomedical Explanation + Diverse Solution, 6) Biomedical Explanation Only, 7) Diverse Solution Only, 8) Biomedical Solution Only, and 9) Control. Participants completed pre-experiment, post-experiment, and one-week follow-up assessments, and viewed a 4-min video manipulating the type of explanation and solution for schizophrenia in the experiment. This study was not pre-registered. RESULTS: Linear Mixed Models indicated no significant three-way interaction (Explanation x Solution x Time). However, explanations and solutions demonstrated differential effects on stigma and advocacy. Specifically, diverse solutions were more effective in reducing stigma, whereas diverse explanations were more effective in promoting private forms of collective action. CONCLUSION: These findings offered insights that future campaigns, educational programs, and advocacy initiatives should not only explain the diverse causes of schizophrenia but also highlight concrete examples of how individuals and communities can provide support and promote recovery.

title: Welfare regimes and the adoption of artificial intelligence in healthcare
abstract: This paper examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare through the analytical lens of the political determinants of health (PDOH), arguing that AI is not a politically neutral technological innovation but a domain in which longstanding distributive logics of welfare regimes are reproduced and potentially intensified. As a conceptual, theory-building contribution, this paper develops a set of testable propositions about how welfare-regime logics may condition the adoption, regulation, and distributive effects of AI in healthcare. While existing scholarship on AI in healthcare has largely centred on ethical risks, algorithmic bias, privacy, and data governance, these discussions often overlook how political systems shape both the speed and equity of AI adoption. Drawing on Navaro et al.'s typology of political regimes -social democratic, Christian democratic, liberal, and ex-dictatorship-the paper argues that welfare state traditions and power resource configurations may structure how AI is developed, regulated, and what are its distributive consequences. Social democratic regimes, with strong universalist commitments, are likely to adopt AI cautiously but equitably; Christian democratic systems may integrate AI through corporatist negotiation and regulated pluralism; liberal regimes may accelerate market-driven AI innovation at the cost of uneven access; and ex-dictatorship states may face the dual pressures of modernization and institutional fragility, leading to uneven but politically charged trajectories of adoption. The paper concludes by arguing that regulatory progress on AI must be conceptualized in light of the political frameworks it comes to operate within and therefore, for AI in healthcare to be inclusive it may require a reaffirmation of the values of universal access.

title: “Your health in your hands; doctor's order included”: A critical analysis of consumer-driven care and commodified expertise in marketing for direct-to-consumer laboratory testing
abstract: Direct-to-consumer laboratory testing is a rapidly proliferating service that extends tests previously only available in biomedical clinical settings to the consumer marketplace. This article presents a critical discourse analysis of DTC laboratory testing company websites and advertisements in order to understand how such companies situate laboratory testing as a useful consumer product. Like other direct-to-consumer biotechnologies such as genetic testing and wearable biometric monitors, it interpellates users through medical-neoliberal rhetorics of personal responsibility and risk management. Direct-to-consumer lab testing, however, occupies a unique niche that enables companies to both claim and subvert biomedical scientific authority. By appealing to both the biomedical-professional origins of laboratory testing and to culturally salient critiques of biomedicine, DTC testing companies detach biomedicine from its conventional institutional moorings while retaining its technoscientific appeal. In doing so, they advance a consumer-driven model of care in which medical expertise appears commodified. Considered alongside recent cultural and technological developments, I argue that DTC lab testing and adjacent services may represent the beginning of a broader technobiomedical transformation that challenges the dominant, institution-bound and expert-practitioner directed model of biomedical care.

title: Unemployment and mental health: Evidence of effect heterogeneity by social class in the UK
abstract: The causal effect of unemployment on mental health is well-documented, yet a given job loss episode likely does not harm everyone uniformly. Who is hurt, and how deeply, is contingent on an individual's position in the stratification structure, a dimension that has received little attention compared to gender and age. Drawing on Fundamental Cause Theory, we argue that social class shapes both exposure and vulnerability to unemployment and hypothesise a social gradient whereby the salariat is buffered against the mental health penalties of job loss relative to intermediate and working-class positions. We test this using UKHLS data (2009-2019) employing two mental health outcomes (MCS-12 and GHQ-12) and the ESEC social class scheme. Using a fixed effects individual slopes (FEIS) estimator, we retain all forms of unemployment rather than only exogenous forms to capture heterogeneity across the class structure. A consistent gradient emerged: (semi) routine workers and small employers & own account workers faced the strongest mental health penalties, whilst the salariat reported the lowest. This persisted after controlling for household income, pointing to non-monetary, psychosocial mechanisms. Job loss, as a critical life-course event, cannot be meaningfully abstracted from the unequal resources individuals are endowed with. In doing so, we bring a social class-analytic lens to a common causal question.

title: Augmenting workers and new technologies of care
abstract: Technology is increasingly seen as a viable option for 'solving' future (and present) crises of healthcare labour through the automation or augmentation of human labour. Exoskeletons are wearable robotic suits designed to augment care workers' strength and endurance and to protect them from injury. We frame our analysis of them within two impulses in feminist science studies: that care work reorients how technoscience is approached and assessed, and that technology demands careful attention to its entanglements with gendered and racialized labour and with militarization. Drawing on interviews with the designers of occupational exoskeletons, we first present their claims about the ways in which exoskeletons are a form of care for the bodies of healthcare workers; a means towards race and gender workplace equity; and a vehicle for revaluing care work. We then question these technoliberal claims, voicing concerns that exoskeletons can be a means of surveilling workers' bodies for the purpose of increasing productivity; potentially creating humanoid robots to replace them; extending life spans of work; and the hardening national borders against immigrant care workers. These speculations set an agenda for further localised study. We call for more grounded assessments of technoscience to understand what new care technologies are doing in the world and how these 'creeping' technologies may unsettle the relationship between care and technology. 23 semi-structured qualitative interviews were conducted in person and online from the United Kingdom and Canada between 2021 and 2026 with 13 exoskeleton companies and industry experts based in 8 countries. Observation and interviews were also conducted in person at 3 industry trade exhibitions.

title: From Anticipation to Reaction: Disability and the organisation of Emergency Department care.
abstract: In Emergency Departments (ED), adults living with disability (alwD) experience longer stays, higher admission rates, and poorer healthcare experiences and outcomes than people without disability. This paper examines how care for alwD is enacted in EDs, with particular attention to how disability-related needs are anticipated or addressed after difficulties emerge. Drawing on qualitative data and informed by the sociology of anticipation and complex adaptive systems theory, we examine how foreseeable needs were translated into action within the organisational conditions of ED care. Anticipatory care refers to identifying and responding to a person’s reasonably foreseeable needs before problems arise, while reactive care involves responding after difficulties have emerged. We conducted an experience-based codesign study across three Australian metropolitan EDs, including 75 interviews and one focus group with alwD, carers, key informants, and ED staff. Data were analysed inductively and abductively, with comparison across participant groups, data sources, and study sites. Findings showed that disability-related needs were frequently addressed reactively, amid time pressure and fragmented information which constrained anticipatory care. Anticipatory care was recognised as desirable but was rarely embedded within ED processes. Instead, anticipatory work was often displaced to carers and clinicians. From these findings, we developed an anticipatory-reactive care continuum comprising five patterns of care. The continuum illustrates how organisational conditions can enable, constrain or displace anticipation and provide a framework for examining how foreseeable needs are translated into action. These findings highlight opportunities to embed anticipatory capacity within ED practice to support equitable and person-centred care.

title: “I get anxious about looking anxious”: A qualitative study of anxiety, depression, and workplace productivity among professional workers
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Anxiety and depression are increasingly prevalent in working populations. This secondary analysis of qualitative workplace interviews develops a theoretical model of how these conditions interact with workplace structures to affect professional behaviour and productivity. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 189 professionals across multiple sectors in the United Kingdom between January 2023 and February 2025. Using reflexive thematic analysis, I identified 38 participants who, against pre-specified inclusion criteria, explicitly reported living with anxiety, depression, or both, and analysed their accounts in depth. RESULTS: Six interconnected themes emerged: (1) the disclosure dilemma, (2) identity-threat vigilance, (3) compensatory masking, (4) the productivity paradox, (5) managerial mediation, and (6) intersectional compounding. These themes are integrated into the Concealment-Disclosure-Adaptation (CDA) Model, which theorises that workers with anxiety and depression navigate a cyclical process of concealment, selective disclosure, and behavioural adaptation shaped by perceived psychological safety and intersecting identity characteristics. CONCLUSIONS: The CDA Model extends existing frameworks by foregrounding the dynamic, context-dependent nature of mental health management at work and its bidirectional relationship with productivity. The findings imply that encouraging openness about mental health at work is insufficient without managerial practices that favour practical flexibility over evaluative scrutiny, and without equity-informed support for workers facing compound stigma, for whom disclosure carries the greatest risk.

title: The mediating effect of loneliness in the relationship between disability and health-related quality of life
abstract: Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) captures an individual's wellbeing and is influenced by both mental and physical health. There is growing recognition of the role of wider health determinants, such as loneliness, which is strongly linked to both health and HRQoL and is now considered a critical public health priority. This study examines loneliness as mediator between disability and HRQoL. Data were analysed from wave 14 (2022-2024) of the Understanding Society UK Household Longitudinal Study with baseline predictions from waves 9, 12 and 13 to account for COVID-19 effects. Loneliness was measured using the 3-item UCLA scale, HRQoL by the 12-item Short Form Health Survey, and disability using single item questions on long-standing physical and mental illness, impairment, or disability. Analysis was based on complete case responses. Disability was associated to reduced physical HRQoL of -4.379 [95%CI:-4.632,-4.125], with 1.8% [95%CI: 0.9-2.7%] of this effect mediated by loneliness. The reduction on mental HRQoL was -2.661 [95%CI:-2.927,-2.394], with 23.7% [95%CI: 20.1-27.2%] mediated by loneliness. Having a diagnosed mental health condition was associated to poorer mental HRQoL of -4.128 [95%CI:-4.451,-3.804], of which 17.3% [95%CI:14.6-20.0%] was mediated by loneliness. Key findings remain consistent regardless of when baseline was measured. Disability has a greater effect on physical than mental HRQoL. Loneliness accounts for a larger share of the impact of disability on mental HRQoL than on physical HRQoL. Findings highlight the importance of addressing loneliness, especially among those with mental health conditions, to improve overall wellbeing. This requires research into effective interventions and greater recognition of loneliness as a key driver for HRQoL.

title: Adhering to the brief: Global health images as repeated icons
abstract: Scholars and practitioners of global health humanitarianism have increasingly reflected on acceptable visual representation in global health, employing a range of terms such as biases, tropes and stereotypes, with a focus on "white saviourism" and "suffering subjects". We introduce the term global health iconography to advance this discussion, arguing that global health has historically reproduced four main kinds of highly-controlled image types (the icons) mapped around two binary oppositions: gazing vs intervening, referring to observing a photographic subject with or without intervention taking place; and suffering vs empowerment, referring to the implied state of the photography subject. We drew on interviews with 29 photographers (conducted December 2023 - May 2024) and analysis of images pulled from 50 global health organizations' websites to understand how photographers approached the creation of stereotypical images requested by their employers, and the mundane arrangements needed for assembling such images in communities. We find that institutionalized global health photography is a collective system of icon production in which pre-defined symbolic forms are repeated and normalized, while alternative representations get discarded as photographers are pressured to create images aligning with a recognizable visual canon. The paper argues that global health visual culture has been moving from an iconography of gazing at suffering to gazing at empowerment, mediated by public criticism and arcs of redemption resulting in iterative paradigm shifts. We conclude that decolonizing the global health visual culture requires a form of iconoclasm and not merely offering supposedly better icons as well as wrestling with the uneasy rise of generative AI imagery.

title: Speaking up, stepping back: Expertise, authority and the social negotiation of overdiagnosis
abstract: The National Health Service Breast Screening Programme (NHSBSP) is a widely promoted public health intervention yet debates around overdiagnosis continue to shape discussions of its value. While prior research has examined health professional perspectives on breast screening, less is known about how those with healthcare related occupations mobilise and adjust their knowledge of overdiagnosis in different interactional contexts. This article draws on semi-structured interviews with twenty women who declined breast screening and/or breast cancer treatment following invitation to the NHSBSP. Most participants had health-related occupations, including general practitioners, medical writers, and patient advocates. Participants often drew on scientific literature to inform their decisions, with understandings of overdiagnosis and overtreatment playing a central role. This article examines how participants mobilised their expertise across different interactional contexts. Participants possessed significant expertise, but varied how much authority they claimed across interactions, so that knowledge and status were mobilised differently depending on context. In policy contexts, they challenged dominant narratives by raising concerns with those responsible for programme delivery and sharing alternative evidence. When interacting with clinicians, they adopted an authoritative stance, using their knowledge to contest prevailing assumptions about screening. In contrast, when engaging with lay audiences, they constrained their authority, signposting others to evidence rather than seeking to direct their decisions. These findings highlight that expertise and authority, are relational, shaped by audience reception, institutional recognition, and speakers' strategic restraint in how overdiagnosis is negotiated across policy, professional, and everyday settings.

title: Health citizenship, universalism, and unequal care: Brazil and Mozambique in comparative historical perspective
abstract: This article examines how formally recognised universal health rights become, or fail to become, substantive health citizenship in Brazil and Mozambique. Substantive health citizenship is defined here as the effective exercise of formally guaranteed health rights in practice. The analysis draws on an intentionally selected corpus of 71 documentary and bibliographic sources, updated through September 2026, using a historical, comparative, and interpretive documentary approach. Four analytical dimensions guide the interpretation: recognition, redistribution, institutional credibility, and territorial protection. Critical resonance is used as a heuristic strategy for relating connected but non-equivalent histories. The comparison shows that explicit racial recognition in Brazil can coexist with incomplete material and territorial repair, whereas constitutional universalism in Mozambique can coexist with linguistic and geographic barriers, as well as district-level implementation constraints. Cross-case analysis also refines the model itself: Mozambique broadens recognition towards the institutional intelligibility of linguistic and territorial difference, while Brazil broadens territorial protection beyond geographic reach by foregrounding dispossession, territorial rights, and differentiated public responsibility. The article therefore contributes a provisional model that separates substantive health citizenship, as the outcome to be explained, from the analytical dimensions used to interpret variation in its realisation.

title: Dutch policymakers’ views on what justifies involving children in health state valuation: A Q-methodology study
abstract: Economic evaluations of interventions aimed at younger populations often use health state values based on preferences of adults regarding children's health states. Although it has been argued that children should be involved in the process of valuing health states, it remains unclear which arguments are relevant to policymakers to justify such involvement. The aim of this Q-methodology study was to identify and examine viewpoints of Dutch policymakers regarding which arguments justify involving children in the health state valuation (HSV) process. Policymakers (n = 18) ranked 29 statements, based on two recent reviews, describing arguments potentially justifying the involvement of children in the HSV process, and explained their ranking. Interviews took place from February to April 2025. Four viewpoints were identified. Participants with viewpoint 1 maintain a contributory perspective and consider children's contributions a way to improve the accuracy of values. Those with viewpoint 2 hold a societal perspective, highlighting the inherent social value of children's involvement in the HSV process. Viewpoint 3 describes children's involvement from a moral perspective, with justifications based on moral arguments. Those with viewpoint 4 maintain an instrumental perspective in which involving children increases the legitimacy of decisions. Most policymakers supported involving children in the HSV process. Common methodological and ethical concerns about involving children in this process had limited support. The four viewpoints suggest that the support for involvement of children in the HSV process rests on different underlying rationales. Future research could investigate how to involve children in the HSV process, and how such involvement relates to the viewpoints identified in our paper.

title: Custody arrangements and the mental health of adolescents and their parents in the United Kingdom: A longitudinal analysis using understanding society
abstract: BACKGROUND: This study examines the association between custody arrangements and mental health among children aged 10-15 and their parents. It contributes to the literature by using individual fixed-effects models that account for observed and unobserved time-invariant individual and family characteristics. METHODS: We used longitudinal data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study (Understanding Society). Children's mental health was measured using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), and parents' mental health using the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-12). We compared two-parent families with sole and shared custody arrangements and distinguished between transitions into separation and stable post-separation arrangements. Analyses combined pooled regression with fixed-effects models. RESULTS: We found no differences in mental health among children and parents in sole vs shared custody arrangements. In contrast, adolescents in both sole-parent and shared-care arrangements showed more emotional and behavioural difficulties than those in two-parent families (0.28-0.31 SD). Fixed-effects models indicated similar within-child increases (∼0.33 SD). For parents, pooled models suggested worse mental health in separated families (0.24-0.30 SD higher GHQ scores). In contrast, In fixed-effects models, parents in separated arrangements had lower GHQ scores than when in two-parent arrangements, with reductions of 0.22-0.28 SD in GHQ-12 score. CONCLUSIONS: We found no mental health advantage of shared over sole custody for children or parents. However, the association between separation and mental health differed for children and parents after accounting for stable pre-separation characteristics.

title: Public preferences and willingness to pay for a net zero National Health Service: A discrete choice experiment in England and Scotland
abstract: Health services generate substantial greenhouse gas emissions and contribute to climate change, which is expected to increase pressure on those services. In response, health services have committed to reducing their emissions through net zero policies. Successful implementation of these policies depends on public support, yet little is known about public preferences for net zero policies for health services. This paper uses a discrete choice experiment fielded in February-April 2024 among 2050 adults (1018 in England and 1032 in Scotland) to elicit public preferences for net zero policies within the context of a publicly funded healthcare service. We find that respondents in England and Scotland are broadly supportive of net zero policies (net zero plans are chosen 88-93% of tasks), but support decreases if policies are financed by increased taxation (net zero plans are chosen in 76-79% of tasks). We find an average willingness to pay of £340-£358 per year, with significant preference heterogeneity across respondents based on income. 3-12% of respondents do not support any net zero policies and, based on debrief open-ended questions, most of them do not consider reducing greenhouse gas emissions a priority for the health service. Our results provide new and timely information about public preferences and trade-offs for net zero policies within health services. These results can inform net zero health and care policies that have public support.

title: What can the Independent Panel on Evidence for Action against Antimicrobial Resistance learn from science policy-interfaces in global environmental governance? A scoping review and conceptual framework
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a significant global health threat. To facilitate the generation and use of scientific evidence to support member states in their efforts to tackle AMR, the political declaration of the 2024 United Nations General Assembly High Level Meeting on AMR called for the establishment of an Independent Panel for Evidence on Action against Antimicrobial Resistance (IPEA). Translating evidence into action for complex problems like AMR is both technically difficult and inherently political, requiring the integration of multiple disciplines and sectors, and balancing diverse interests and priorities. In this scoping review, we synthesize the literature on the key normative and institutional design features and principles that underlie the effectiveness of Science-Policy Interfaces (SPIs) in global environmental governance, where SPIs have been operating for decades, to inform design choices for IPEA and other global SPIs. We found that the effectiveness of SPIs in environmental governance stems from their credibility, relevance, and legitimacy, which are driven by six normative governance principles (inclusiveness, accountability, transparency, communication, sustainability, and equity). These governance principles shape the effectiveness of SPI outputs through five process-related impact pathways: 1) trust building, 2) quality of knowledge, 3) clear roles and responsibilities for stakeholders, 4) SPI independence, and 5) contestability of evidence. These governance principles and pathways are interdependent; therefore, policymakers must carefully weigh trade-offs and make strategic choices. By moving from normative considerations of effectiveness to understand the impact of institutional features of SPIs, this synthesis can inform the practical design and evaluation of IPEA and other SPIs tackling complex health challenges.

title: Measuring social norms related to violent child discipline in Uganda: Mixed-methods scale development and validation
abstract: BACKGROUND: Norms-shifting interventions show promise in addressing violence against children (VAC), yet few culturally grounded quantitative measures of VAC-related norms exist, limiting norms change research and intervention evaluation. We aimed to document violent child discipline behaviors and norms in Uganda and develop psychometrically validated descriptive and injunctive norms measures. METHODS: Using a mixed-methods design, we interviewed young fathers and community members (n = 1044) in six regions of Uganda to identify VAC-related norms and inform survey item development. Items were included in surveys administered to three cohorts of young fathers (2023-2025) participating in the evaluation of REAL Fathers, a fatherhood mentorship intervention (ages 16-25; n = 2412; 752; and 440). We used exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis to evaluate the factor structure and reliability of the resulting measures. RESULTS: Qualitative data revealed strong social expectations supporting physical discipline, rooted in the belief that parents who love their children must discipline them firmly. Quantitative results indicated widespread agreement that VAC is commonly practiced and considered necessary for raising successful adults. Psychometric analyses supported a two-factor structure-harsh discipline and father engagement norms (F1) and gendered caregiving and household authority norms (F2)-with high internal consistency across all samples (F1:α = 0.90-0.94; F2:α = 0.78-0.90). CONCLUSIONS: By grounding scale development in qualitative exploration of fathers' normative environments, this study bridges gaps between qualitative norms research, quantitative measurement, and program evaluation, and provides validated measures to support the evaluation and design of interventions that address interconnected norms linking masculinity, gendered caregiving, household authority, and household violence.

title: Jurisdictional learning: When serious errors in healthcare trigger divergent responses in professional roles
abstract: Learning from serious errors in healthcare workplaces is crucial to prevent them from reoccurring. Typically, learning from errors implies convergence where healthcare professionals arrive at shared understanding and collaborate more closely. In this research, we study how doctors and nurses learn differently after they encountered the same serious errors. Drawing on three serious untoward incidents in an NHS Hospital Trust in England, we explain responses through "jurisdictional learning." We describe how errors prompt doctors and nurses to reinterpret their tasks, responsibilities, and authority from their existing jurisdictional positions. We find that doctors respond through jurisdictional encroachment, selectively extending oversight into tasks traditionally performed by nurses. Nurses, in contrast, respond through jurisdictional fortification where they reinforce their existing tasks and responsibilities through stronger reliance on policies, guidelines, and assertiveness. Our findings contrast the predominantly convergence-based logics of interprofessional learning by showing that professional roles interpret errors through the lens of their jurisdictional position and, in response, produce divergent role-based responses to redefine tasks, responsibilities, and authority.

title: Resilience as social practice: Negotiating long COVID at the intersection of illness and ageing
abstract: Resilience is often framed within neoliberal health discourses as an individual capacity for adaptation, obscuring how the ability to endure illness is socially organised. This article reconceptualises resilience as a biographically embedded social practice through a study of older and emerging older adults living with Long COVID, an uncertain chronic health condition that unsettles everyday life and expectations of ageing. Drawing on longitudinal qualitative data from a UK study comprising three phases of 23 interviews (2021-2023), this article presents four illustrative cases of participants aged over 50. Rather than a static attribute, resilience was a dynamic and often painful process in which participants situated the present in relation to past experiences and (un)imagined futures, while seeking to maintain a coherent sense of self amid disruption. This work was enacted through everyday practices such as adjusting routines, renegotiating roles and seeking recognition in healthcare and social relationships. These efforts were enabled or constrained by social conditions, including institutional acknowledgement, material resources and normative expectations of ageing, sometimes leading resilience to be performed rather than authentically experienced. A central finding is that resilience involved learning to live with ambiguity. An uncertain prognosis disrupted biographical continuity and required continual recalibration of temporal horizons, often producing experiences of accelerated or disjunct ageing. Resilience therefore emerged not as recovery but as the socially mediated maintenance of a liveable biography. Recognising resilience as social practice foregrounds the need to reorganise the institutional and relational conditions that make endurance possible.

title: The long-term and spillover effects of a radio drama on HIV knowledge, expressed stigma, willingness to disclose, and political priorities: Evidence from a cluster-randomized trial in Tanzania
abstract: Background Entertainment-education can influence public health knowledge and attitudes, but evidence on persistence and spillovers is limited. Methods We conducted a placebo-controlled, cluster-randomized trial in 30 villages in rural Tanzania. Within 15 matched ward pairs, we randomly assigned villages to a community screening of a radio drama modeling HIV disclosure and obtaining treatment or to a screening of an unrelated drama. Of 1205 respondents enrolled at baseline, 87% attended the screening and 97% completed the endline survey. Participants and enumerators were blinded to assignment. The primary outcomes at 18 months were preregistered indices of HIV knowledge, expressed stigma, willingness to disclose, and HIV policy prioritization. We also surveyed participants' partners, close friends, and teenage children to assess spillovers (secondary outcomes). The study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework. Results At 18 months, the HIV drama increased participants' knowledge (d = 0.14), willingness to disclose (d = 0.17), and prioritization of HIV policy (d = 0.17), but not expressed stigma (d = 0.07). These effects were about half as large as those measured two weeks after exposure. Willingness to disclose also increased among the partners (d = 0.16) and teenage children (d = 0.23) of screening attendees. The estimated effect on partners' policy prioritization was similar (d = 0.16) but less precisely estimated. We found no spillover in knowledge or stigma and no effects among friends. Conclusion A single group screening produced changes in HIV-related knowledge and attitudes that remained evident 18 months later. Spillover effects were evident but limited to household relationships.

title: In the streets “you must be hardened”: Gendered and structural drivers of violence against women and children among families in street situations in Kenya
abstract: PURPOSE: Violence against women (VAW) and children (VAC) are both causes and consequences of street life in Kenya. To inform violence prevention supports for families in street situations, this participatory research study sought to first understand what drives family VAW and VAC in the streets from the perspective of parents in street situations. METHODS: Guided by a Steering Committee and Parent Advisory Group (PAG), data collection included: (a) interviews with 20 mothers and 20 fathers; (b) eight consecutive focus group discussions (FGDs), including four with nine fathers, four with 10 mothers, and an additional FGD with past participants of a parenting programme (10 mothers); and (c) demographic surveys (40 mothers, 29 fathers). Five participatory co-analysis workshops were held with the PAG and community stakeholders to centre their voices in meaning-making, which informed an inductive reflexive thematic analysis using Gender Structure Theory as an analytic lens. RESULTS: The intersection of structural violence and patriarchy demanded gendered survival strategies (women's reliance on men for basic needs, men's exercise of power over women when denied power from society) that catalysed family VAW and VAC; violence which was further facilitated by substance use and the normalcy of corporal punishment. Family violence, in turn, entrenched a gendered order that perpetuated street life. CONCLUSIONS: To break the cycle of family violence and street life, family support initiatives should (a) target community-level gender norms and poverty reduction, and (b) include structural supports that promote the health, human rights, and physical safety of parents and their children.

title: Discursive constructions of uncertainty in chronic pain: Negotiating expertise and agency across diagnosis, treatment, and care trajectories
Early life adversity and alcohol misuse in mid and later life: The moderating role of adult residential characteristics
abstract: Alcohol misuse among mid- and later-life adults is a growing public health concern. Early life adversity (e.g., abuse, poverty) is a well-established risk factor for alcohol misuse in midlife and beyond. Neighborhood environments may also influence alcohol use and shape the extent to which early adversity contributes to misuse later in life, yet little is known about these relationships among midlife and older adults. Using a cross-sectional sample of 9759 adults aged 51+ from the Health and Retirement Study and a series of multilevel mixed effects logistic regression models, this study examined whether adult residential characteristics moderate the associations between three domains of childhood adversity and two problematic drinking outcomes (heavy episodic drinking and hazardous drinking). Findings showed that exposure to two or more risky parental (e.g., abuse) or any adolescent (e.g., trouble with police) behaviors increased the odds of hazardous drinking, while exposure to multiple childhood socioeconomic disadvantages (e.g., poor family finances) was associated with lower odds of hazardous drinking. Among residential characteristics, neighborhood social ties were associated with higher odds of both heavy episodic and hazardous drinking. Neighborhood affluence, however, was a protective factor for problematic drinking. Significant cross-level interactions indicated that residential context modifies associations between early life adversity and alcohol misuse. Notably, neighborhood social ties amplified the probability of heavy episodic drinking among individuals with childhood socioeconomic disadvantage. These findings highlight the complex and context-dependent nature of alcohol misuse risk in mid- and older-adulthood, and that residential characteristics may function as both protective and risk-enhancing factors.

title: The cyclical and intersecting influence of substance use, homelessness and criminal legal policy on risk among minoritized people who use drugs
abstract: The US has seen an alarming rise in overdose mortality among people experiencing homelessness and incarceration. Drug overdose and homelessness are dual crises that disproportionately impact Black, Hispanic, and American Indian/Alaska Native communities due to historic and ongoing structural racism. Our objective was to better understand the intersection of substance use, homelessness, and criminal-legal involvement among these populations to inform harm reduction and policy. We completed in-depth semi-structured interviews with racially minoritized people who use drugs (PWUD) in Michigan, New Jersey, and Wisconsin. This analysis focused on 54 participants currently or previously experiencing homelessness. We conducted a thematic analysis informed by the risk environment framework, which considers structural factors related to substance use. Participants identified a cyclical relationship between homelessness and substance use that was highly influenced by the policy risk environment. Substance use was shaped by the risk environment of homelessness, and untreated substance use led to homelessness. This synergy was exacerbated by criminal-legal involvement, including incarceration without treatment and exclusion from resources based on criminal histories. Participants described experiences living in racially segregated neighborhoods, which were important potential access-points for social services. Participants also noted the need for housing and treatment outside of the environments where their substance use and homelessness began. Our study describes risk environments that contribute to cyclical substance use, homelessness, and criminal-legal involvement among racially minoritized PWUD. To address overdose trends, it is imperative to expand equitable access to harm reduction and housing and reform criminal-legal policies surrounding substance use and unsheltered living.

title: Rethinking cancer survivorship on social media: A phenomenological study of embodiment, online visibility, and the content object-body
abstract: Studies of cancer survivorship and social media have treated survivors as audiences of online cancer content, examining how cancer survivors receive support and information from what others post. This study, in contrast, shifts attention from the consumption of online cancer content to its creation. In this article, we employed a theory-led phenomenological approach to examine how creating cancer content on social media did not merely represent survivorship, but - in participants' accounts - substantially transformed their embodied experience of illness. Drawing on interviews conducted between January and May 2026 with 18 cancer content creators in the United States and Europe, findings revealed three ways participants described content creation as reshaping how they lived with cancer. 1) Becoming recognizable showed how participants described their own public cancer brands as becoming part of their self-understanding. 2) Becoming believable showed how participants - who reported that followers doubted whether they really had cancer - came to experience visible bodily changes and clinical spaces as evidence that could prove their illness was real. 3) Becoming valuable revealed how participants perceived suffering and medical crisis as drawing greater audience attention than recovery - creating a paradox in their experience of healing. Namely, as participants recovered and audience attention appeared to decline, some participants came to feel less valuable. Building on these findings, this study demonstrates that social media is not only a repository of cancer information, but a lived cancer environment in which survivorship itself takes shape.

title: From Static to Person-Specific Neighborhood Contexts: Comparing Residential and Mobility-Based Environments in Relation to Late-Life Cognition
Making public health guidance trustworthy: Public Health Sensegiving under uncertainty
abstract: Public health emergencies confront officials with the challenge of communicating guidance that evolves as scientific evidence and institutional recommendations change. Although institutional trust is associated with adherence to public health measures, less is known about the interpretive and communicative work through which public officials seek to make changing guidance understandable, legitimate, and credible. Drawing on a comparative qualitative study of Brazil and Japan, this article examines trust-building communication among public officials involved in implementation, coordination, and policy oversight. The study is based on 122 semi-structured interviews and a 239-document corpus covering 2020-2022. Using abductive comparative analysis, we identify Public Health Sensegiving as the process through which officials interpret evolving scientific and institutional guidance and translate it into public-facing explanations. Empirical episodes show a recurrent sequence in which officials interpret ambiguous guidance, communicate workable explanations, and refine them in response to citizen questions. Four practices constitute this process: explaining and translating guidance, contextualizing risk and uncertainty, legitimizing recommendations, and encouraging voluntary cooperation. Comparisons within and across countries show that competing messages increased the need for reconciliation, whereas more consistent messaging allowed greater emphasis on continuity and shared responsibility. These differences reflect contextual communicative demands rather than fixed national types. Rather than demonstrating changes in citizens' trust or behaviour, the findings identify how officials perform trust-building communicative work under uncertainty and highlight interpretive capacity as a public health preparedness capability.

title: Editorial Board
Refractions of tuberculosis and migration in the northern suburb of Paris: Exposure, adherence, and semantic recalcitrance
abstract: France is overall a low endemic country for tuberculosis (TB); however, Seine-Saint-Denis-the poorest department of metropolitan France-has the highest incidence rate in the whole country, excluding overseas territories. At the national level, TB mainly concerns people coming from a country with a high endemicity of TB, people in conditions of absolute poverty, and people living in prison facilities. In this north-eastern Parisian suburb, we conducted qualitative research through a multi-sited ethnography in six university hospitals of the Assistance Publique - Hôpitaux de Paris (AP-HP), two inter-municipal hospital centres, and the Samusocial de Paris, Équipe Mobile de Lutte contre la Tuberculose, a mobile medico-social team dedicated to TB. This study examines the processes through which tuberculosis is experienced and interpreted by migrants undergoing treatment in these facilities. Drawing on 82 in-depth semi-structured interviews with people living with TB (65 men and 17 women, whose estimated mean length of residence in France was about 10 years), this study shows that persistent doubt about the biomedical diagnosis can coexist with almost complete adherence to treatment. While most participants follow the prescribed treatment, many do not fully recognise tuberculosis as an exhaustive explanation of their illness and construct aetiological interpretations anchored in the social, material, and institutional conditions of their lives in France, including the absence of stable work and housing, insecure residence status, and experiences of institutional disaffiliation accumulated over time. We define this specific configuration as semantic resistance: a situated and circumscribed form of agency exercised within the therapeutic relationship through the possibility of accepting treatment without necessarily relinquishing one's own interpretation of illness. These forms of resistance can be read as a denunciation and an unveiling of the social and existential conditions within which suffering is experienced.

title: The impact of diabetes on formal and informal care
abstract: There is limited evidence on how chronic conditions affect the demand and costs for long-term care (LTC), restricting our ability to evaluate interventions. This paper estimates the causal effect of type 2 diabetes (T2D), a highly prevalent chronic condition among the elderly, on formal and informal LTC utilization. We used data from eight waves (2002-2017) of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) (n = 18,166) and employed a Mendelian Randomization approach to address the endogeneity of diabetes status in LTC demand. Our results indicate that T2D increases the probability of using formal care by 6 percentage points and informal care by 27 percentage points. When adjusting for possible pleiotropy via obesity, the impact on informal care reduces to 25 percentage points. Exploration of mechanisms shows that diabetes increases the likelihood of limitations in activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs). These results highlight the broader burden of T2D beyond healthcare costs and can be used in future decision analytic models to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of diabetes interventions.

title: Early-life neighborhood resources and adulthood mortality
When prevention constrains cure: Institutional lock-in and gene therapy access for beta-thalassemia
abstract: On 16 November 2023, the United Kingdom Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), the first CRISPR-based gene therapy for a genetic disease, offering patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (TDT) freedom from lifelong monthly transfusions. Yet in China, which carries the world's largest TDT patient population, no patient has received the therapy through the public health system, and the access gap is not explained by price or manufacturing economics alone. This paper argues that prevention-era institutional architecture constrains cure-era access through three lock-in mechanisms: cognitive (the direction of genetic information flow), infrastructural (the spatial distribution of treatment capacity), and fiscal (the structure of payment responsibility). Drawing on a structured comparison of four countries selected to represent distinct institutional pathway types (Cyprus, ecclesiastical-public certification; China, administrative filing; Thailand, public health universal coverage; India, federal fragmentation), the analysis proposes a typology of barrier configurations and illustrates them through four exploratory cases. The administrative-filing pathway is associated with high barriers across information, geographic, and economic dimensions; trust-intention is not assessable on current evidence. The ecclesiastical-public pathway is associated with medium information and low geographic barriers with medium fiscal and low-confidence trust barriers; the universal-coverage pathway provides a balanced platform that remains under-activated for gene therapy; and the federal-fragmented pathway fails the precondition of patient identification. No pathway simultaneously optimizes all four readiness dimensions. Presented as a hypothesis-generating typology rather than a tested diagnostic model, the framework relates pathway type to barrier configuration and offers testable hypotheses for pathway-specific intervention design and for extension to sickle cell disease, hemophilia, and other genetic conditions entering the curative era.

title: Armed conflict exposure and violent discipline of children at home: Panel evidence from Ethiopia
abstract: Armed conflict has far-reaching effects on household well-being, including increased risk of violence. We examine whether changes in local armed conflict exposure are associated with changes in caregiver-perpetrated physical punishment of children, as reported by mothers. We link six waves (2016-2021) of panel survey data from employed women in Ethiopia (1065 respondents; just over 5000 respondent-wave observations) to geo-referenced conflict events from ACLED. Using respondent and wave fixed-effects linear probability models, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in conflict exposure (19.4 events) increases the probability of physical punishment by any caregiver by 3.4 percentage points (pp) (≈5.2% relative to the mean), father punishment by 2.7 pp (≈6.4%), mother punishment by 3.6 pp (≈5.6%), and punishment by both caregivers by 2.9 pp (≈7.3%). A decomposition into presence versus intensity indicates a sizeable increase at conflict onset, with smaller incremental increases as events accumulate. Conflict exposure also coincides with higher caregiver distress and indicators of economic strain, including reduced labor supply and lower reported income among fathers. These findings suggest that conflict can spill over into harsher parenting, highlighting the importance of integrating child protection, caregiver mental health support, and livelihood assistance into conflict-response programming.

title: Shaping Humanistic Care in Treatment-Centered Public Hospitals: The Active Role of Nonprofit Organizations
Getting the Time to Be Sick: Barriers to Paid Sick Leave Access for Immigrant Restaurant Workers
From urban decay to responsibilized citizenship: Visualizing the racialized geographies of water insecurity in Southwest Illinois, United States
abstract: Water insecurity experiences are shaped by the reciprocal interactions of water with the social and political context-a process called the hydrosocial cycle. In the United States, broad patterns have emerged in which water infrastructure deterioration is linked to racialized migration. In this photovoice project, we examined the experience of water insecurity in East St. Louis and Cahokia Heights, two majority-Black cities in Illinois, United States. From March to May 2024, participants chose the research question "How does the water affect your life?", took photos in their community, and participated in one to four focus groups (n = 10). We analyzed focus group transcripts using thematic analysis and identified themes at the community level (contamination, accountability, deterioration) and individual level (health concerns about "the water", powerlessness and disillusionment, frustration and distress, agency). Together, these themes illustrate how residents perceive that water and sewer infrastructure have exerted multiple forms of harm across decades, including how residents have assumed a responsibilized citizenship, in which the government's failure to maintain water and sewer infrastructure requires residents themselves to shoulder the burden of water safety and accessibility. This case study demonstrates the severe consequences of infrastructural disinvestment for resident wellbeing and water security. Residents often contextualized their severe water insecurity through comparisons with neighboring majority-white communities that do not experience the same degree of flooding and sewage backups, revealing a racialized geography of indifference. These lessons can be used to improve infrastructural investment decisions in ways that address existing critical water insecurity issues and avoid repeating these patterns of disinvestment in the future.

title: When biological explanations undermine confidence in psychotherapy: Identifying and countering causal discounting
abstract: Both laypeople and clinicians tend to judge psychotherapy as less effective when a mental disorder is attributed to biological causes. This tendency is unwarranted, given that the combination of medication and psychotherapy is generally considered the optimal treatment. Among the mechanisms proposed for this effect, the present study examines causal discounting, the assumption that biological causes are sufficient to explain symptoms, overlooking psychosocial causes. To counteract this assumption, we developed an intervention explaining how biological and psychosocial causes are interdependent. Three pre-registered studies found that laypeople with and without elevated depressive symptoms (Study 1: N = 428; Study 2: N = 566) and mental health clinicians (Study 3: N = 495) discounted psychosocial causes and rated psychotherapy as less effective upon learning that a depression case had biological causes. However, our intervention improved perceived psychotherapy effectiveness more than materials from the National Institute of Mental Health and a popular commercial health website (WebMD) listing both types of causes. These findings suggest that explaining the interplay between biological and psychosocial factors may help prevent biological explanations from inadvertently diminishing perceived effectiveness. Future studies can test the intervention in real-life settings with direct measures of psychotherapy uptake and adherence.

title: Making medicine sacred, making religion healthy: Navigating medical pluralism among Christian African immigrants in the United States
abstract: This study examines how individuals from societies, where religion and medicine have operated as cooperative institutions, describe that relationship upon migrating to the United States, where medicine is institutionally dominant. Drawing on qualitative interviews with 37 Christian African immigrants in Houston, I find that respondents describe religion and medicine as complementary pathways to health. They articulate this complementarity through two interpretive frames: making medicine sacred, whereby medical professionals are interpreted as instruments of divine healing, and making religion healthy, whereby practices such as prayer and fasting are described in terms of their physical and psychological benefits. In accounting for medicine, respondents locate healing in God and describe medical practices as the means through which it comes. They place traditional healers in the same terms, conceding their efficacy but judging their legitimacy by whether the practitioner acknowledges where healing originates. Respondents further describe congregations in both settings as engaged with health. These findings suggest that reasoning about the source of healing can hold a plural health field together, and that congregations are plausible partners in health promotion.

title: The good participant paradox: Benevolent Misrepresentation as a response to research exclusion
abstract: RATIONALE: Research participation fraud is typically framed as incentive-driven dishonesty, yet altruistic motivation is near-universal among research candidates. A paradox is created when well-intentioned individuals misrepresent their eligibility information to join studies they believe will help others, rather than for personal gain. This phenomenon, termed benevolent misrepresentation, is poorly understood and increasingly consequential as online research recruitment and screening become more widespread. OBJECTIVE: This study examined when and why well-intentioned individuals misrepresent their eligibility during health research screening. METHODS: A sequential mixed-methods design was employed, including observational analysis of 10,734 screening submissions from a large-scale urinary microbiome study, qualitative analysis of excluded candidate correspondence (n = 25), and a quantitative survey of individuals from the same patient population (n = 438). RESULTS: Misrepresentation was predominantly situational rather than a reflection of persistent underlying dishonesty. A Two-Stage Model emerged: emotional responses, altruistic salience, and perceived eligibility predicted whether individuals resisted exclusion, while perceived eligibility alone differentiated whether resistance took the form of legitimate challenge or misrepresentation. 24.01% misrepresented their eligibility in at least one scenario. Exclusion criteria that dismissed experiential knowledge in favour of clinical diagnosis elicited the highest misrepresentation rates; unspecified exclusion criteria elicited the lowest. CONCLUSION: These findings, grounded in procedural justice and moral self-licensing theory, challenge fraud-detection models by suggesting misrepresentation is strongly associated with perceived injustice rather than intentional dishonesty. The psychological mechanisms of benevolent misrepresentation in unremunerated research are explored through the lens of a Two-Stage Model of Benevolent Misrepresentation, and practical recommendations are provided to help researchers avoid the identified triggers.
